Start here

How this course works

You have 6 years of mobile design behind you. This course converts that experience into web, product, systems and AI design skill — by making you design, tear down and rebuild real interfaces, every single week. The web & SaaS core is 8 weeks; the five tracks beyond it are modular and you choose which ones you need. See How long this actually takes below for the honest numbers.

Your path, step by step

New here? The sidebar is already ordered as a path, top to bottom — this is why it goes in that order.

  1. 1 · Web & SaaS Core (Weeks 1–8). Non-negotiable first. Every track after this assumes grids, type, colour, components and the five screen states.
  2. 2 · Mobile Design (iOS, Android, Motion & Prototyping). Comes next because Design Systems' platform modules build directly on it — you can't design an iOS token system without the HIG first.
  3. 3 · Watch Design. The smallest track. Design Systems' watch module depends on it the same way.
  4. 4 · Design Systems. Now that you know web, iOS, Android and watch conventions, this is where you formalise all of it into token systems, specs and documentation — the single highest-value track for employability.
  5. 5 · Advanced Web Craft. Builds on the Design System Kits shipped by the previous track. Motion, 3D, and shipping without a developer.
  6. 6 · AI for UI/UX. Last on purpose — you get the most out of AI tools once you already have the judgment to evaluate what they produce.
Don't want the full path?You don't have to do every track, or in this exact order beyond step 1. See "Pick a route, not the whole map" below for four shorter, tested combinations — just note that Design Systems' iOS/Android/Watch modules (d3–d5) assume you've done the matching Mobile/Watch lessons first. And whichever route you pick, the full resource index is organised in this same order, section by section.

The weekly rhythm (8–10 hrs/week)

This is the rhythm for any week of the course, in any track.

BlockTimeWhat you do
Learn~3 hrsWatch the lesson videos, read the core lesson text and 1–2 assigned articles.
Steal like a designer~2 hrsOpen the Mobbin references in each practice lesson. Don't scroll — analyze. Answer the teardown questions in writing (a Figma sticky or notes file).
Build~4 hrsDo the Figma exercise. Every week produces a real artifact you keep.
Test~30 minTake the quiz. Pass mark is 70%. Retake until it sticks.

Ground rules

  • Design at 1440×900 by default. That's your new "iPhone frame". Desktop-first for SaaS apps, then adapt down (Week 8 covers when to flip this).
  • Copy before you create. Weeks 1–4 you'll rebuild existing screens pixel-close. That's not cheating — it's how you internalize web conventions fast. Original work starts Week 5 and takes over by Week 8.
  • Everything in one Figma file. Create a file called SaaS Web Design Course with one page per week. By Week 8 it becomes your process portfolio.
  • Write your teardowns. One paragraph per Mobbin analysis. Verbalizing what a layout does is what turns looking into learning.
Your progress is savedProgress and quiz scores save automatically in this browser (localStorage). Keep opening this file in the same browser. The sidebar tracks completion; each lesson ends with a "Mark complete" button.

What you'll be able to do by Week 8

  • Design a complete SaaS product — marketing site, auth, onboarding, dashboard, settings, billing — in any niche.
  • Design any other kind of website with confidence: e-commerce stores, content/editorial sites, portfolios, local business and agency sites (Week 7 covers their specific anatomy).
  • Set up grids, type scales, spacing and color tokens like a web-native designer.
  • Design dense, data-heavy screens (tables, dashboards) that mobile design never asked of you.
  • Make everything responsive and accessible, and hand it off with proper tokens.

Tools you need

Figma (you have it), Mobbin (connected — links throughout open real screens), and a browser with DevTools — you'll use Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+C to inspect real sites' spacing, type sizes and breakpoints constantly. Inspecting live sites is the web designer's superpower that mobile never gave you.

How long this actually takes

The honest numberThis course used to say "8 weeks". That was true when it was 42 lessons. It is now 122 lessons across six tracks — about 354 hours of study and practice. At a sustainable 8–10 hours a week, the whole thing is 8–10 months.

That is not a reason to be discouraged. It is a reason to stop treating it as one course. The web & SaaS core is a real 8-week course that stands on its own. Everything after it is a track you add because you want the thing it teaches.

Where the hours actually are

TrackModulesHoursAt 8 hrs/wkStatus

Roughly two thirds of those hours are practice, not reading. That ratio is deliberate — and it's why the number is large. A course you can finish in a weekend produced nothing you can show anyone.

Pick a route, not the whole map

RouteTracksHoursAt 8–10 hrs/wkYou end up able to…
1 · Web designer
the minimum viable transition		W1–W8~97 h2.5–3 monthsDesign and defend real SaaS and marketing screens on a grid, with a type and colour system, all states, responsive and accessible
2 · Product designer
the recommended default		W1–W8 + d1–d5 + a1–a2~228 h6–7 monthsEverything above, plus ship a published design system and work fluently with AI — the two things most product-design roles now screen for
3 · Cross-platform designerW1–W8 + x1–x4 + d1–d5~227 h6–7 monthsDesign credibly for web, iOS, Android and watch, with one system underneath — your mobile background makes this the fastest of the long routes
4 · Craft / studio designerW1–W8 + c1–c4 + a1–a2~221 h6–7 monthsBuild award-level marketing sites with motion and 3D, and ship them yourself without a developer
5 · The full pathEverything~351 h9–11 monthsThe complete portfolio: product, system, mobile, craft, AI. This is a year of deliberate practice, not a course you finish.
If you only read one rowTake route 2. The core plus design systems plus AI is roughly six months and produces the three artefacts that hiring conversations actually turn on: a data-dense product surface with every state, a published design system, and an honest account of how you work with AI. Add the mobile track later — you already have six years of that instinct; it converts fast when you need it.

The rules that make a long course finishable

RuleWhy
Finish the core before starting a trackEvery later track assumes grids, type, colour, components and states. Skipping ahead means relearning them badly.
One track at a timeParallel tracks feel productive and finish nothing. Sequence them.
Do the practice, skip nothing elseThe reading is a third of the hours and all of the vocabulary. The practice is two thirds and all of the portfolio.
Ship something at the end of every trackA published system, a live site, a case study. Unshipped work decays; shipped work compounds.
Two hours beats zero8–10 hrs/week is the plan, not the requirement. At 4 hrs/week route 2 takes a year — which is still a transition, and still faster than not starting.
Re-do, don't just proceedRebuilding a Week 6 screen after the design-systems track teaches more than a new screen would

What "done" looks like

Not a completion percentage. Three case studies and one live URL. Whichever route you take, you are finished when you have: a product surface with all five states across three breakpoints, a published and documented design system, one piece of craft work with a real domain, and a written account of your own process — including where it went wrong. The progress bar is a motivational device; those four artefacts are the actual deliverable.

Your resource library

Everything referenced in this course, in one place. Bookmark-worthy. Come back here whenever a lesson cites something.

Books (in reading order)

Weeks 1–4
Refactoring UI — Adam Wathan & Steve Schoger

The single highest-leverage book for this course. Tactical visual design for interfaces: spacing, type, color, depth. Short, dense, all practice.

Week 1
Laws of UX — Jon Yablonski

Psychology principles behind every design decision. The companion site lawsofux.com is free and covers most of it.

Weeks 2–3
Practical Typography — Matthew Butterick (free online)

The best typography book, period, and it's a website. Read "Typography in ten minutes" and "Summary of key rules" first.

Week 5+
Designing Interfaces (3rd ed.) — Jenifer Tidwell et al.

A pattern encyclopedia: navigation, forms, lists, tables. Use as reference, not cover-to-cover.

Anytime
Don't Make Me Think (Revisited) — Steve Krug

Web usability classic. A 2-evening read that permanently changes how you judge web pages.

Anytime
Grid Systems in Graphic Design — Josef Müller-Brockmann

The origin of everything Week 2 teaches. Optional, but foundational if you fall in love with layout.

Starter kits that ship with this course

The Design System Kits folder sits next to this course file. These are working artefacts you build from, not demos you look at — modules d1–d5 use them directly.

Read 1st
README.md

What each file is, how the colour ramps were generated, the verified contrast table, and how to get everything into Figma and into code.

Tokens
saas-tokens.css

The full three-tier token set — primitives, semantic roles, component tokens — with light and dark modes and a reduced-motion pass. Used throughout module d1.

Tokens
saas-tokens.json · saas-tokens.figma.json · saas-tokens.tailwind.css

The same tokens in DTCG format, as a flat map for Figma variable-import plugins, and as a Tailwind v4 theme block.

Web
marketing-web-tokens.css

Fluid type, section rhythm, containers and art-direction slots for marketing pages. Loads on top of the SaaS tokens. Module d2.

Mobile
ios-tokens-reference.md · android-m3-tokens-reference.md · watch-tokens-reference.md

Platform token sheets: Dynamic Type and semantic colours; the M3 ref/sys/comp architecture with the full role table; watchOS and Wear OS constraints. Modules d3, d4, d5.

Process
component-spec-template.md · audit-checklist.md

The thirteen-section spec every component gets filled in against, and the pass/fail list you score your system on before calling it v1.

If a link above doesn't openThese are local files. Open the Design System Kits folder directly in Finder or Explorer — the .css, .json and .md files open in any text editor, and the Markdown ones render nicely in VS Code or any Markdown viewer.

Week 1 · Lesson 1.1

UX fundamentals, rebuilt from zero

You asked for everything from scratch — so we start with the psychology that governs every interface, mobile or web. Even familiar principles land differently once you view them through a web lens.

Watch

▶
Jon Yablonski — Laws of UX: Using Psychology to Design Better Products
The author of Laws of UX walks through the core principles with product examples.
▶
The Laws of UX — 19 Psychological Design Principles
Rapid-fire summary — good as revision after the first video.

The laws you'll use weekly in SaaS design

LawWhat it saysWhere it bites in SaaS
Jakob's LawUsers expect your product to work like the products they already use.Why your sidebar should look like Linear's/Notion's, your settings like everyone's settings. Convention beats novelty in tools people use 8 hrs/day.
Fitts's LawTime to hit a target depends on its size and distance.On web, cursor precision is high but travel cost is real: keep row actions near rows, put primary CTAs where the eye already is. Screen edges are "infinite" targets.
Hick's LawMore choices = slower decisions.Pricing pages (3 plans, one highlighted), toolbars (progressive disclosure), onboarding (one question per step).
Miller's LawWorking memory holds ~7±2 chunks.Chunk nav into groups of 4–6; group form fields into labeled sections; don't show 14 KPIs at once.
Tesler's LawComplexity can't be destroyed, only moved.Every "simple" UI pushes complexity somewhere — good SaaS design moves it away from the user (smart defaults) not just off the screen.
Aesthetic–UsabilityBeautiful things are perceived as easier to use.Why Week 3–4 (type & color) matter commercially, not just aesthetically.
Peak–End RulePeople judge experiences by the peak and the end.Design the "aha" moment of onboarding and the success states of flows with extra care.
Von RestorffThe different thing gets remembered.One (and only one) highlighted plan, one primary button per view.

The rest of the foundation

Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics are the vocabulary of every design critique you'll ever be in. Read the canonical article and, for each heuristic, name one example from an app you use daily: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design (NN/g).

Information architecture — on web this becomes URL structure, nav hierarchy, and search. A SaaS app is a tree: workspaces → projects → items → detail. Users must always know where they are (breadcrumbs, highlighted nav, page titles answer this).

User flows — you know these from mobile. The web difference: flows can branch through multiple entry points (deep links, email links, shared URLs, SEO landings). A web screen never gets to assume "the user came from the previous screen."

Mental models — write down what the user believes is happening ("my draft is saved", "this filter is temporary"). Interfaces fail where the model and the system disagree. Autosave indicators, optimistic UI, and undo exist to close these gaps.

Week 1 · Lesson 1.2

Mobile → Web: everything that changes

This is the most important lesson in the course. Web isn't "a bigger phone" — it's a different medium with a different input device, different viewport physics, and different user posture.

1. The canvas is fluid, not fixed

Mobile gave you a handful of known devices. Web gives you a continuum from 320px phones to 3840px ultrawides — and users resize windows mid-session. You don't design "a screen"; you design a system of rules that produces the right screen at every width. That's why grids (Week 2) and responsive logic (Week 8) are core skills, not add-ons.

RealityMobileWeb
Viewport~390×844, fixed, portrait320→3840px wide, user-resizable
Design frameDevice frame1440×900 artboard + a max-width container (usually 1200–1280px) with rules for what stretches
OrientationPortrait-firstLandscape-first; vertical space is the scarce resource

2. The pointer changes everything

A finger is ~9mm of imprecise meat with no position until it touches. A cursor is 1px-precise and always present — which unlocks an entire layer mobile doesn't have: hover.

  • Hover states — every interactive element needs one (buttons, rows, cards, links). Hover is how web users probe "is this clickable?"
  • Hover-revealed actions — row actions in tables, card menus, comment buttons. Density without clutter. (Rule: hover-revealed must also be reachable by keyboard.)
  • Tooltips — hover explains icons and truncated text. There is no long-press.
  • Cursor changes — pointer for clickable, text for selectable, grab for draggable. Free affordance.
  • Smaller targets are OK — 32–40px buttons instead of 44pt minimums; 13–14px UI text instead of 16–17pt. This is where SaaS density comes from.

And the keyboard becomes a first-class input: focus states (visible rings on the focused element), Tab order, Enter to submit, Esc to close, and power-user shortcuts (Cmd+K command palettes). Every component you design now needs states mobile never asked for: defaulthoverfocusactivedisabledloading

3. Reading behavior: scanning patterns

On wide screens, eyes don't read — they scan. Two patterns you design for:

  • F-pattern — on text-heavy pages users read the first lines, then scan down the left edge. Front-load headings and list items with keywords; left-align what matters. Read: NN/g on the F-pattern.
  • Z-pattern — on sparse marketing layouts the eye sweeps top-left → top-right, diagonals down, ends bottom-right. Logo top-left, CTA top-right and again at the diagonal's end — the classic landing header follows the Z.

4. Scroll, chrome, and the fold

  • Scrolling is cheap, but the top ~600px ("above the fold") still decides whether users continue. Marketing pages must state value + CTA before any scrolling.
  • Browser chrome exists — the URL is UI (readable, shareable, deep-linkable). Back button must never break. New-tab behavior matters (marketing links may open new tabs; in-app navigation never).
  • Sticky elements — headers, table headers, sidebars, and in-page section navs can stick while content scrolls. Powerful and easy to overuse: every sticky element permanently taxes the scarce vertical space.

5. Posture and session shape

Mobile sessions are 30-second bursts on the go. SaaS web sessions are 30-minute-to-8-hour work sessions at a desk. Consequences: information density is a feature (fewer clicks > more whitespace), multitasking is normal (your app lives in one of 12 tabs — favicons, page titles and notification badges matter), and efficiency compounds (bulk actions, keyboard shortcuts, saved views: features that would be overkill on mobile are table stakes in SaaS).

Start doing
  • Design hover + focus states for every component
  • Design at 1440 with a 1200–1280px container
  • Treat vertical px as the scarce resource
  • Ask "what does the URL say?" for every screen
  • Add tooltips to every icon-only button
Stop doing (mobile habits)
  • 44pt touch targets everywhere
  • Bottom nav / thumb-zone thinking
  • Hiding actions behind long-press or swipe
  • One-thing-per-screen pacing for work tools
  • Assuming users arrived from the previous screen

Week 2 · Lesson 2.1

The 12-column grid, properly

The grid is the skeleton of every web page you'll ever design. Mobile mostly hid this from you — a phone is basically one column. On web, the grid is the design.

Watch

▶
How to Set Up a 12-Column Grid System in Figma
Follow along in Figma — set this up before reading on.

The vocabulary

TermMeaningTypical web values
ContainerThe max width your content lives in; centered, with side margins1200–1280px (marketing), fluid/full-width (apps)
ColumnsVertical slices content snaps to12 (marketing & dashboards), 8 (tablet), 4 (mobile)
GutterGap between columns24px (also 16, 20, 32)
MarginSpace between the grid and the viewport edge≥32px desktop, 24px tablet, 16px mobile

Why 12?

12 divides by 2, 3, 4 and 6 — so one grid supports halves, thirds, quarters and sixths without changing anything. A pricing page with 3 plans = three 4-column blocks. A blog with sidebar = 8 + 4. A form next to an illustration = 6 + 6. Every layout decision becomes "how many columns does this get?" — which is exactly the kind of constraint that makes design faster.

Your default Figma setup (memorize this)

  • Frame: 1440×900
  • Layout grid: 12 columns, Stretch, gutter 24, margin 120 → yields a 1200px content container
  • Alternative for denser marketing: margin 80 → 1280px container
  • Add a second grid: Rows, 8px (10% opacity) — this is your spacing ruler (next lesson)
Stretch vs Fixed columnsSet columns to Stretch, not fixed-width. Stretch mirrors how CSS grids actually behave when the viewport changes — your design intent survives translation to code. Fixed-width columns are a mobile-designer habit that breaks responsive thinking.

Apps vs marketing pages use grids differently

  • Marketing pages — content sits inside the centered container; the 12 columns govern every section. Backgrounds can bleed full-width while content stays in the grid ("full-bleed section, contained content" — look at any Stripe page).
  • SaaS apps — the app shell (sidebar + top bar) is not on the 12-col grid; it's a fixed-width sidebar (240–280px) plus a fluid content region. Inside that content region you re-apply a grid or a card system. Dashboards often use 12 columns inside the content area for arranging widgets.

Breakpoints (preview — Week 8 goes deep)

NameRangeColumnsDesign frame
Mobile320–7674, gutter 16, margin 16390
Tablet768–10238, gutter 24, margin 24–32834
Desktop1024–143912, gutter 24, margin 32+1280
Large1440+12, container caps at 1200–12801440

Week 2 · Lesson 2.2

Spacing systems & vertical rhythm

Columns handle horizontal structure. Vertical structure comes from a spacing scale — and consistent spacing is the single most visible difference between amateur and professional web design.

The 8-point system

All spacing (padding, gaps, margins) comes from multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 80, 96, 120, 160 — with 4 and 12 allowed for fine-grained UI (icon gaps, badge padding, dense tables). Why it works: it's divisible, it renders crisply at every screen density, and it kills the "is this 27 or 29px?" micro-decisions that eat your day.

Spacing communicates grouping (this is the real skill)

Proximity is hierarchy. A label sits 8px from its input, but 24px from the previous field — so the eye pairs them correctly without a single divider line. The general rule: space within a group < space between groups < space between sections. When a design feels "off" and you can't say why, it's almost always spacing that contradicts grouping.

RelationshipTypical value
Icon ↔ its label4–8
Label ↔ its input6–8
Between form fields16–24
Card internal padding16–24 (dense UI) / 24–32 (marketing)
Between cards16–24
Between page sections (app)32–48
Between page sections (marketing)96–160
Marketing spacing will feel wrong at firstMobile trained you on tight vertical budgets. Marketing sections breathe with 96–160px between them. When your landing page feels cramped, double the section spacing — seriously, double it — before touching anything else.

White space is doing work

It buys hierarchy without adding lines or boxes (Refactoring UI's "start with too much white space, then remove"), it signals quality (luxury = space; discount = cramming — think Apple vs a flight-deals site), and it sets reading pace. Dense SaaS tables minimize it deliberately; long-form content maximizes it deliberately. Density is a decision, not an accident.

Vertical rhythm

Keep vertical gaps from the same scale so repeated patterns (cards in a grid, rows in a list, sections down a page) create a steady beat. Turn on your 8px row grid and nudge until things land on it. Don't be religious — optical alignment beats mathematical alignment when they conflict (more in Week 3).

Read

Book ch.
Refactoring UI — "Layout and Spacing" chapter

The definitive treatment. Read it this week.

Week 2 · Lesson 2.3

Web layout patterns that repeat forever

Almost every web page you'll ever design is a remix of about a dozen layouts. Learn them by name and you'll never face a blank canvas again.

Page-level archetypes

PatternStructureUsed for
Single columnOne centered column, 640–760pxArticles, blogs, docs, settings pages, checkout
Sidebar app shellFixed sidebar (240–280px) + fluid contentAlmost every SaaS app: Linear, Notion, Slack
Double sidebarNav sidebar + list panel + detail ("holy grail")Email clients, CRMs, messaging — master-detail data
Top-nav containerHorizontal nav + centered 1200px contentMarketing sites, e-commerce, GitHub-style apps
Split screen50/50 or 60/40 two-paneAuth pages (form + brand panel), landing heroes
Card gridRepeating cards, 2–4 per rowDashboards, galleries, pricing, integrations pages
FeedSingle scrolling column + side railsSocial, activity streams, notifications

Section-level patterns (marketing pages are stacks of these)

  • Hero — headline + subhead + CTA(s) + visual. Variants: centered (text over/above visual), split (text left, product right), full-bleed background.
  • Logo bar — "Trusted by" strip of 5–8 customer logos, greyscaled to not compete.
  • Feature trio — 3 columns of icon + title + 2 lines. The workhorse.
  • Zig-zag — alternating image/text rows (image left, then image right…). Rhythm for long feature lists.
  • Bento grid — asymmetric card mosaic showing many features at once; the current-era pattern (Apple, Vercel, Linear all use it).
  • Social proof — testimonial cards, case-study stats ("300% increase in…"), review badges.
  • Pricing — 3 tiers, middle highlighted (Week 7 goes deep).
  • Final CTA — big headline + one button on colored background, right before the footer.
  • Footer — 4–5 link columns + legal row. Mega-footers double as sitemaps and SEO.

Visual hierarchy on wide screens

Three levers, in order of power: size (biggest thing wins — one per screen), contrast (dark text/strong color pulls focus; muted grays recede), position (top-left of the F-pattern; the Z's endpoints). If everything is big and bold, nothing is — pick winners deliberately. A good self-test: squint until the page blurs. Whatever still stands out is your actual hierarchy; check it matches your intended one.

Do
  • Pick an archetype before opening Figma
  • Limit line length even when the screen is wide
  • Let sections alternate background tint (white / gray-50) to separate them
  • Anchor every element to the column grid
Don't
  • Stretch content edge-to-edge on 1920px screens
  • Center-align long body text
  • Invent a new layout when a named one fits
  • Fill horizontal space just because it exists

See the patterns live

Origin — centered heroHeadline → subtext → single CTA → product visual. Textbook. Craft — centered hero variantSame skeleton, different type & color personality

Neo-grotesque sansNeutral, modern, "product"Inter, Helvetica Now, SF Pro, Roboto
Geometric sansFriendly, techy, startupPoppins, Futura PT, Circular, DM Sans
Humanist sansWarm, readable, trustworthySource Sans 3, Open Sans, Frutiger
Transitional/old-style serifEditorial, established, premiumGeorgia, Freight Text, Source Serif 4
Display serifLuxury, fashion, opinionatedCanela, GT Sectra, Fraunces
MonospaceTechnical, developer-brandJetBrains Mono, IBM Plex Mono, Geist Mono

Notice the current SaaS pattern: a neutral sans for UI (Inter is everywhere) + one personality font for marketing headlines (a display serif or distinctive sans). Origin's landing page from Week 2 does exactly this — serif headline, sans everything else.

Rules for choosing UI type

  • Tall x-height, open apertures — legible at 13px. This is why Inter, not Futura, runs your dashboard.
  • Real weights — you need at least 400 / 500 / 600. (Faux-bolding is a crime the browser will happily commit for you.)
  • Tabular figures available — numbers that align in columns. Non-negotiable for tables and dashboards (Week 6).
  • Variable font versions — one file, all weights, faster loads. Inter, Fraunces, Source families all ship variable.

Pairing without pain

  • The safest pair is no pair — one family, many weights/sizes. Most great SaaS products are single-typeface.
  • Pair by contrast, not similarity — display serif + neutral sans works; two similar sans faces just looks like a mistake.
  • One does headlines, one does everything else. Never alternate mid-hierarchy.
  • Steal proven pairs: Google Fonts Knowledge and the specimen pages on fonts.google.com show live pairings.

Web-only concerns mobile never taught you

  • Loading — webfonts download. Fewer families/weights = faster paint. System-font stacks cost 0ms (GitHub uses one).
  • Fallbacks — specify what shows if the font fails: Inter, -apple-system, sans-serif. Design shouldn't collapse on fallback.
  • Licensing — Google Fonts = free anywhere. Foundry fonts (Circular, Canela…) need web licenses priced by pageview. Check before you fall in love.

Book

Then skim "Summary of key rules". 15 minutes, permanent upgrade.

Week 3 · Lesson 3.2

Setting type: scale, rhythm, measure

Choosing a font is 10% of typography. The other 90% is setting it: sizes, line-heights, line lengths, and the relationships between them.

Units: px, rem, em

You design in px in Figma, but developers build in rem (1rem = 16px by default, scales when users change browser font size). Keep every font size divisible into sensible rems (13, 14, 16, 18, 20, 24…) and note rem equivalents in handoff. em is relative to the parent element — used for things that should scale with their context, like an icon inside a button.

Type scales

Pick sizes from a ratio, not from vibes. Generate one at typescale.com:

RatioFeelBest for
1.125 (major second)Subtle stepsDense app UI
1.2 (minor third)BalancedThe default choice — apps + content
1.25 (major third)Confident jumpsMarketing pages
1.333–1.5DramaticEditorial, big-brand landings

A practical dual-scale setup for a SaaS product: App UI: 12 · 13 · 14 (body) · 16 · 18 · 20 · 24. Marketing: 16 · 18 (body) · 20 · 24 · 32 · 40 · 56 · 72. Marketing headlines go far bigger than mobile ever allowed — a 64px H1 at 1440 is normal, not shouting.

Line height (leading)

TextLine heightExample
Big headlines (40px+)1.0–1.1556px / 60px
Subheads (20–32px)1.2–1.3524px / 32px
Body (14–18px)1.5–1.716px / 26px
Dense UI text (12–14px)1.35–1.513px / 18px

The inverse law: the bigger the text, the tighter the leading. Mobile rarely showed you 56px headlines, so this is a new muscle — a 56px headline at 1.5 line-height looks broken.

Measure (line length) — the most-violated web rule

45–75 characters per line; ~66 is ideal. At 16px that's roughly a 640–700px column. This is why article text sits in a narrow centered column even on a 1920px monitor — and why "stretch the text to fill the space" is always wrong. Wide lines make eyes lose their place on the return sweep; short lines create choppy, fatiguing rhythm.

Letter-spacing (tracking)

  • Big headlines: slightly negative (-1% to -3%) — large glyphs look loose by default. This is the "designed" look of modern SaaS headlines.
  • Body: leave it alone (0).
  • ALL-CAPS labels: positive (+4% to +8%) — caps need air. (Like the section labels in this course's sidebar.)

Hierarchy without size

Before making something bigger, try: heavier weight, darker/lighter color (ink vs muted gray), or more surrounding space. Refactoring UI's trick: a hierarchy of three text colors (primary #0F172A-ish, secondary #64748B-ish, disabled/hint #94A3B8-ish) does more work than five font sizes. Size changes are the loudest tool — save them for real structure.

Do
  • Define the full scale before designing screens
  • Keep body text 16–18px on marketing, 13–14px in dense UI
  • Cap text columns at ~70ch regardless of screen width
  • Tighten tracking on 40px+ headlines
Don't
  • Invent a new size per screen ("size soup")
  • Use pure black text on pure white (harsh; use near-black)
  • Center-align paragraphs longer than 2 lines
  • Justify text on the web (rivers everywhere)

Book

Week 3 · Lesson 3.3

UI typography for SaaS products

Marketing typography seduces; product typography disappears. Inside the app, type succeeds when nobody notices it for eight working hours.

The SaaS type kit

Nearly every serious web app runs on a variation of this — steal it, then adapt:

RoleSize/weightNotes
Page title20–24 / 600One per page, top-left region
Section / card title16–18 / 600
Body / default UI14 / 40013px in dense tools (Linear runs 13)
Secondary / meta13 / 400, muted colorTimestamps, descriptions, helper text
Labels / overlines11–12 / 500–600, +5% tracking, caps optionalTable headers, form labels, nav groups
Numbers in dataSame size as body, tabular lining figuresFigma: OpenType features → tnum

Truncation & overflow — the web's daily reality

User-generated text will be longer than your mock. Decide per element: truncate with ellipsis (single-line titles in tables — pair with a hover tooltip showing full text), line-clamp (card descriptions, 2–3 lines max), or wrap freely (comments, docs). Design every text component with a "worst realistic string" — a 47-character company name, a German compound word, an email like anjum.ayoub.design+test@gmail.com.

Small rules with big payoffs

  • Align numbers right in table columns; align text left. Never center data columns.
  • Weight beats size in rows — a 14/600 name over a 13/400 email reads perfectly without any size drama.
  • Links inside app UI usually drop the underline and use color + hover-underline instead; body-copy links keep underlines (accessibility: color alone can't signal links in flowing text).
  • Sentence case everywhere (buttons, titles, labels) is the modern SaaS default — Title Case Feels Older and slows scanning. Pick one and never mix.
  • Placeholder ≠ label. Placeholder text is a hint, disappears on typing, fails recall — it can never replace a label (Week 5 hammers this).
Study this course fileThis page you're reading applies the whole week: ~17px body, 66ch measure, 1.65 line-height, negative tracking on the H2, muted secondary color, +4% tracked caps labels in the sidebar. Open DevTools and inspect it.
Week 3 · Practice

Practice: type teardown + build a type system

Typography is learned through the fingers. Two build tasks and one forensic task.

Task 1 · ~45 minForensic teardown with DevTools Open stripe.com and linear.app. Using inspect (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+C), record for each: font families in use, H1 size/line-height/letter-spacing, body size/line-height, and the measure of the widest paragraph (count characters). Compare marketing pages vs app screenshots — notice the dual system from lesson 3.2.
Task 2 · ~90 minBuild your dual type system in Figma Create text styles for a fictional SaaS product: the full marketing scale (H1→caption, with line-heights and tracking baked into the styles) and the full app UI kit from lesson 3.3. Choose your own pairing (or single family) using lesson 3.1's rules — not Inter, force a real decision. Name styles properly: Marketing/H1, App/Body, App/Label…
Task 3 · ~60 minSet a real article Grab any long blog post's text. Set it at 1440 as a proper article layout: title, byline, lede, body with subheads, a pull quote, an image caption. Apply everything: measure 60–70ch, correct leading, hierarchy via weight/color before size. Then break it on purpose — make a copy with 90ch lines, 1.2 body leading, and centered paragraphs. Put them side by side. Feel the difference; this calibrates your eye.
DeliverableA published type-style sheet in your Figma file + the article set correctly (and its deliberately broken twin).

Week 4 · Lesson 4.1

Building a color system

Web products don't use colors — they use color systems: structured ramps of shades that make every future decision automatic.

Watch

▶
Super Practical Guide to Color Theory, Color Models & Perfect Palettes

Think in HSL, not hex

Hex codes are for computers. Design in Hue (0–360° on the wheel), Saturation (gray→vivid), Lightness (black→white). Every skill in this lesson is an HSL manipulation: shades of a color = same hue, stepped lightness (with saturation adjusted); a "warmer gray" = a gray with 2–5% saturation of an orange hue; a harmonious palette = controlled hue relationships.

What a real UI palette contains

GroupContentsJob
Primary/brand1 hue × 9–10 shades (50→900)Buttons, links, active states, focus rings
NeutralsGray ramp × 10 shades — where 90% of your UI livesText (3 levels), backgrounds, borders, disabled
SemanticGreen (success), red (danger), amber (warning), blue (info) — each with a pale background shadeFeedback: alerts, toasts, validation, badges
Accents (optional)1–2 supporting hues, data-viz rampCharts, tags, illustration, marketing moments

Build ramps like the pros: pick your brand color as the ~500 shade, then step lightness both ways — but desaturate slightly toward white and shift saturation/hue subtly toward the extremes, or the pale shades look washed-out and the dark ones dead. Compare your handmade ramp against Tailwind's palette — the most battle-tested open ramp set on the web (and the palette this course file uses).

Proportions: 60-30-10, translated for UI

In practice: ~60% neutral backgrounds, ~30% neutral text/borders/surfaces, ~10% brand color — and semantic colors only at moments of feedback. New web designers' most common mistake is 10× too much brand color. Open Linear or Stripe's dashboard: they're gray products where color means something is interactive or something happened.

Saturated colors are for small areasA full-saturation indigo works at button scale, but as a page background it exhausts. Big areas → very pale tints (your gray-50/indigo-50); high saturation → small, meaningful moments.

Choosing the brand hue

  • Blue/indigo/violet: trust, tech, the SaaS default (for a reason — safest, and renders well on screens)
  • Green: money, health, growth, "go"
  • Warm hues (orange/coral): energy, consumer-friendly, creative tools
  • Black/near-black as brand: premium, developer-brands (Vercel, Linear's marketing)
  • Check the niche's conventions on Mobbin first — fintech skews blue/green + dark; creative tools go bolder. Differ deliberately, not accidentally.

Read

Article
Erik Kennedy — Color in UI Design: A Practical Framework

The single best article on UI color. His "adjust HSB, not opacity" method will change how you make shades.

Book ch.
Refactoring UI — "Working with Color"

Why you need more grays than you think, and how to make color palettes that scale.

Week 4 · Lesson 4.2

Color in practice: contrast, tokens, dark mode

A palette is potential. This lesson is application: making color readable, systematic, and theme-able.

Contrast — the non-negotiable

WCAG contrast ratios run 1:1 (identical) to 21:1 (black on white). The AA standard you design to:

ElementMinimum ratio
Body text (<24px)4.5:1
Large text (≥24px, or ≥18.7px bold)3:1
UI components & meaningful icons/borders3:1

Check every text/background pair with WebAIM's checker or a Figma plugin (Stark, Contrast). The classic failures: muted gray helper text on white (your gray-400 probably fails — use gray-500+), white text on brand-500 buttons (often needs brand-600), and placeholder text nobody can read.

Color is never the only signalColorblind users (~8% of men) can't rely on red-vs-green. Pair color with an icon, label, or pattern: error states get an icon + message, not just a red border; chart series get distinct shapes or direct labels, not just hues.

Text on colored & image backgrounds

  • On brand-colored surfaces, white text usually needs the surface to be ≥500-level dark. Check it — don't eyeball it.
  • On photos: add a scrim (dark gradient overlay), blur the image region, or anchor text to a solid panel. Never raw white-on-photo.
  • "Colored text on colored bg" (like this course's callout boxes): use the 700–800 shade for text on the 50 shade background of the same hue.

Semantic tokens — naming color by job

Raw shades (indigo-600) are primitives. Products map them to semantic tokens named for their role: bg/surface, bg/subtle, text/primary, text/secondary, border/default, action/primary, action/primary-hover, feedback/danger… Components reference tokens, tokens reference primitives. Change what action/primary points to and the whole product rebrands. This two-layer structure is exactly what Figma Variables model (Week 8 builds it).

Dark mode basics (SaaS table stakes)

  • Not inverted, re-mapped: dark surfaces are dark-gray (slate 900/950), never pure black; elevation = slightly lighter surface, since shadows die in the dark.
  • Desaturate: vivid brand colors vibrate on dark — use the 400 shade where light mode used 600.
  • Soften text: pure white glows; use gray-100/200 for primary text. Contrast rules still apply, same math.
  • Semantic tokens make dark mode a re-mapping exercise instead of a redesign — the reason the token layer exists.

Week 4 · Lesson 4.3

Depth & polish: shadows, borders, radius

The gap between "fine" and "polished" lives in the details this lesson covers. It's also the lesson where Steve Schoger makes you dangerous.

Watch

▶
Steve Schoger — Refactoring UI (CSS Day)
A live redesign masterclass. Watch him apply everything from Weeks 2–4 in real time.

Elevation: a shadow scale, not random shadows

Define 4–5 elevation levels and use them consistently — shadows communicate what floats above what:

LevelUseRecipe (roughly)
0 — flatPage background, inputsnone (border instead)
1 — raisedCards, table rows on hover0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,.08)
2 — floatingDropdowns, popovers, sticky bars0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,.10)
3 — overlayModals, command palettes0 16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18)

Good shadows are large-blur, low-opacity, slightly downward (light comes from above). Two-layer shadows (a tight one + a soft one) look most natural. Dark, tight, high-opacity shadows are the #1 "designed in 2012" tell.

Borders vs shadows vs background shifts

Three ways to separate surfaces: borders (crisp, dense-UI friendly — use gray-200-ish, 1px), shadows (soft, floaty, marketing-friendly), background contrast (white cards on gray-50 page — no outline needed at all). Modern SaaS often uses background-contrast + hairline borders and saves shadows for genuinely floating elements. Pick a strategy per product, not per screen.

Corner radius is a personality dial

RadiusPersonalityExamples
0–2pxSerious, technical, enterpriseBloomberg, older enterprise tools
6–10pxThe modern-professional defaultStripe, Linear, this course (10px)
12–20pxFriendly, consumer, approachableNotion cards, consumer fintech
Full (pill)Playful buttons/chips or iOS-flavoredSpotify buttons, filter chips

Rules: define a small scale (e.g., 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / full) and stick to it; nested radii — inner element radius ≈ outer radius − padding, or the corners fight; consistency matters more than the value you choose.

Icons, imagery, gradients

  • One icon set, one stroke weight. Lucide, Phosphor, or Heroicons — 16/20/24px UI sizes, aligned to the pixel grid. Mixing sets is instantly visible.
  • Product screenshots are SaaS marketing's hero imagery: frame them in browser chrome, tilt or overlap them for life, always retina-sharp.
  • Gradients are back (subtle, two neighboring hues, or as mesh backgrounds). Keep text off busy gradient regions or scrim it.
  • Illustration sets tone fast but ages fast — the generic "corporate flat people" era is a cautionary tale. Prefer abstract shapes or real product visuals.
Week 4 · Practice

Practice: one screen, two brands

Color systems prove themselves under change. Build one, then bend it.

Task 1 · ~60 minBuild your palette as Figma styles/variables Construct: a 10-step neutral ramp (with a subtle hue temperature — decide warm or cool), a 10-step brand ramp around your chosen 500, and 4 semantic colors each with a pale-bg partner. Verify: brand-600 on white ≥ 4.5:1, white on brand-600 ≥ 4.5:1, gray-500 on white ≥ 4.5:1. Name them as primitives (gray/500) and add a semantic layer (text/secondary → gray/500).
Task 2 · ~90 minColor a wireframe twice Take your Week 2 rebuilt hero + app shell (gray boxes). Apply your system fully: version A as a trustworthy fintech, version B as a playful creative tool — different hue, radius scale, shadow strategy, imagery treatment. Same skeleton, two personalities. This is the exercise that proves layout and style are independent layers.
Task 3 · ~45 minContrast audit on a real product Pick any Mobbin screen from this course. Sample its text/background pairs into WebAIM's checker. Find at least two failures (most products have them) and propose the minimal fix (usually: one shade darker). Study how these two data-dense screens handle color proportions while you're there:
Etsy — Shop statsNear-monochrome + one accent; classic 60-30-10 Indeed — AnalyticsSemantic color reserved for data; chrome stays neutral
DeliverablePublished color styles (primitives + semantic), the two-brand screen pair, and a short contrast-audit note.

Week 5 · Lesson 5.1

The component encyclopedia

Every web interface is assembled from ~25 recurring components. You know many from mobile — but each carries web-specific rules, states, and conventions. This is your reference lesson; return to it often.

Buttons

  • Hierarchy: primary (filled, brand — one per view), secondary (outline/tonal), tertiary/ghost (text-only), destructive (red, for irreversible actions), icon-button (needs tooltip).
  • Sizes: sm 28–32px, md 36–40px (default), lg 44–48px (marketing CTAs). Padding ≈ 2× vertical padding horizontally.
  • All six states from Week 1 — hover darkens/lifts, focus shows a ring, loading swaps label for spinner without changing width.
  • Labels: verbs ("Save changes", "Create project"), never "Yes"/"OK" alone. In dialogs, buttons state the outcome: "Delete 14 items" beats "Confirm".

Inputs & selection controls

  • Text input: label above (not placeholder-as-label), 36–44px tall, visible border (3:1 contrast), focus ring, error state with icon + message below, optional helper text. Prefix/suffix slots ($ 0.00 USD).
  • Select vs radio vs combobox: ≤5 options visible → radio group; 6–15 → select dropdown; >15 or user-known values → combobox with type-ahead search.
  • Checkbox = independent toggles / multi-select; radio = exactly one; switch = instant on/off with immediate effect (no save button); if a save button exists, use checkboxes, not switches.
  • Specialized: date pickers (allow typing too — pickers alone infuriate), steppers, sliders (only for imprecise ranges), file dropzones, tag inputs.

Overlays

ComponentUse whenWeb rules
ModalFocused task or confirmation that must interruptMax ~480–640px wide, close via X + Esc + (usually) backdrop click, never stack modals, primary action bottom-right
Drawer/panelDetail view or editing without losing list contextSlides from right, 360–480px; the SaaS favorite for record details
PopoverSmall contextual UI anchored to a trigger (filters, pickers)Dismiss on outside click; keep within viewport
TooltipName/explain on hover — icons, truncations, shortcutsAppears on hover+focus, ~300ms delay, never contains actions
ToastAsync feedback that shouldn't block ("Saved", "Export ready")Top/bottom-right, auto-dismiss 4–6s, include Undo where possible
The modal testBefore designing a modal ask: could this be inline, a drawer, or a dedicated page? Modals that contain whole workflows (scrolling forms, tabs!) are the most common SaaS design smell. Interrupt only to confirm or capture one focused thing.

Structure & wayfinding

  • Cards: a bounded surface = one unit of content. Don't nest cards; don't card everything — tables beat card-grids for comparing records.
  • Tabs: peer views of one object (Profile / Security / Notifications). Selected tab must be obvious; never tabs inside tabs.
  • Accordion: progressive disclosure for long optional content (FAQs, advanced settings). Not for content everyone needs.
  • Breadcrumbs: hierarchy path on deep structures (Workspace / Project / Issue). Marketing sites skip them; docs and consoles need them.
  • Pagination vs infinite scroll: data/work UIs paginate (position, linkability, footer reachable); feeds scroll infinitely. Show "1–50 of 1,204".
  • Badges/tags: status dots + label (colorblind-safe), count badges, removable filter chips.
  • Avatars: 24/32/40px, initials fallback with deterministic color, stacked "+4" groups.
  • Skeletons > spinners for initial loads (perceived speed); spinners for short unknown waits; progress bars when duration is estimable.

Study a real system

Open Shopify Polaris components and read 5 component pages end-to-end (Button, TextField, Modal, Banner, DataTable). Notice what a complete spec includes: anatomy, all states, content guidelines, accessibility, and when-not-to-use. That's the completeness bar for your own libraries.

The component decision tables

Most component mistakes are selection mistakes, not styling ones. These three tables settle the arguments that recur forever.

You need the user to…UseNot
Choose one of 2–5 visible optionsRadio group, or segmented control if they're viewsA dropdown — it hides the options
Choose one of 6+SelectA radio group that fills the screen
Choose several independent optionsCheckbox groupA multi-select dropdown, unless there are many
Flip a setting that applies immediatelySwitchA checkbox — that implies a Save step
Filter a list by known valuesFilter chips or faceted dropdownsA free-text search box alone
Pick from a large, searchable setCombobox / autocompleteA 400-item select
Enter a number in a small rangeStepperA slider, if precision matters
Enter a dateText input plus a calendar pickerA calendar alone — typing is faster for known dates
Take an action from a list of optionsMenuA select — selects hold values, menus fire actions

Density variants

ComponentCompactDefaultComfortable
Button32 px40 px48 px
Input / select32 px40 px48 px
Table row36 px48 px60 px
Menu item28 px32 px40 px
List item40 px56 px72 px

Pick one density as the product default and offer compact as a user preference on data-heavy surfaces only. Mixing densities within a screen is one of the most common causes of "this feels off" feedback.

The nine states, as a checklist

StateApplies toMost common failure
DefaultEverything—
HoverPointer devicesBeing the only way to discover an action
Focus-visibleEverything interactiveRemoved for aesthetics — an outright accessibility failure
Active / pressedButtons, rows, tabsSkipped, so taps feel unresponsive
LoadingAnything asyncWidth not locked, so the layout jumps
DisabledContextual controlsNo explanation of why it's disabled
ErrorInputs, formsColour only, no icon or message
SelectedRows, chips, tabs, cardsIndistinguishable from hover
Read-onlyInputsStyled identically to disabled, so text can't be copied
Task · ~60 minThe selection audit Open a product you use daily and find five controls. For each, check it against the first table: is it the right component for the job? You will reliably find a dropdown holding three options, a checkbox that applies immediately, and a select being used as an action menu. Redesign the worst one and write the one-line rule it broke.

Week 5 · Lesson 5.2

SaaS navigation patterns

Navigation is the skeleton users feel but never look at. Web apps have converged on a small set of patterns — know exactly when each applies.

The big three

PatternChoose whenExamples
Left sidebar (240–280px, collapsible to 56–64px icon rail)>6 destinations, hierarchical content, workspace switching — the SaaS defaultLinear, Notion, Slack, Figma
Top nav≤6 flat destinations; content deserves full width; marketing-adjacent productsGitHub, Vercel dashboard, most e-commerce
Hybrid (top for product areas + side for section)Big multi-module productsAWS console, Atlassian, HubSpot

Sidebar anatomy (memorize)

Top: workspace/org switcher + search. Middle: primary destinations (icon + label, groups of 4–6 with labeled dividers — Miller's Law), then pinned/favorite items, then dynamic lists (projects, channels). Bottom: settings, help, user account. Active item gets a filled background; hover gets a lighter one; groups collapse. Look at this course's sidebar — same skeleton.

Universal SaaS furniture

  • Command palette (Cmd+K): search + actions + navigation in one. Now expected in professional tools; design it early, it shapes IA.
  • Global search: scoped results (projects vs docs vs people), recent items on focus, keyboard navigation.
  • Breadcrumb header in the content area: where am I + page-level actions on the right (the "page header" pattern: title left, primary button right).
  • User menu: profile, theme toggle, keyboard shortcuts, sign out. Org switcher separate from user menu.
  • Notifications: bell + badge count, popover inbox with read/unread, mark-all-read. Deep-links into the app (multiple entry points again).

Navigation depth rules

  • Primary nav shows place, not actions. "Create new" is a button, not a nav item.
  • Two levels max in a sidebar; a third level lives inside the page (tabs).
  • The URL mirrors nav depth: /projects/website-redesign/settings. If you can't express a screen as a URL, your IA has a hole.
  • Persistent selected states everywhere — users glance at nav to answer "where am I" dozens of times per session.

Choosing the shell

PatternUse whenBreaks down when
Fixed sidebar5–15 destinations; users live in the app all dayBeyond ~20 items without grouping and search
Collapsible sidebarThe same, but screen real estate is contestedIcons alone are ambiguous — always keep tooltips
Top nav3–7 destinations; content is wideDeep hierarchies; it forces dropdowns
Top nav + sidebarTwo axes: product areas on top, sections within one on the sideThe two levels aren't genuinely distinct — then it's just noise
Command menu (⌘K)Once you pass ~20 destinationsAs the only route — it's undiscoverable alone
Workspace / org switcherMulti-tenant productsPlaced where it can be mistaken for the account menu

Sidebar anatomy

ZoneContainsRule
TopLogo, workspace switcherWorkspace identity must be unmistakable in multi-tenant products
PrimaryMain destinations, grouped, 5–12Group labels are not clickable. Active state is a filled or tinted row, not just bold text.
ContextualFavourites, recent, pinnedOptional but it is what makes a sidebar feel personal
BottomSettings, help, account, plan statusAnchored to the bottom so it doesn't move as the list grows
Width240 px expanded / 64 px collapsedPersist the user's choice
Active state is more important than it looksIn a sidebar with fifteen rows, "which page am I on?" must be answerable in a glance from across the room. Bold text alone fails that test. Use a filled or tinted row plus a weight change — two signals, because one of them will be invisible to someone at some point.

Navigation rules that hold everywhere

  • Every destination has a URL. If a view can't be linked to, it isn't navigation — it's state.
  • Breadcrumbs when the hierarchy is three levels or deeper, and they must be clickable at every level.
  • Never more than two levels of nesting in a sidebar. A third level means you need a section landing page.
  • Search is navigation. Once you pass ~20 destinations, ship ⌘K.
  • Badges (counts, "New") belong on rows, but cap them — a sidebar where every row has a badge communicates nothing.
  • The mobile version is a decision, not a shrink: bottom bar for 3–5, drawer for more.
Task · ~75 minThree shells, one product Take your Week 6 dashboard and design its shell three ways: fixed sidebar, top nav, and top nav + sidebar. Same content, same destinations. Then write a paragraph on which you'd ship and why — referencing destination count, session length and content width. Being able to argue this is a large part of what a senior product designer is asked to do.

Study these

Linear — grouped sidebarAccount / Issues / Projects / Features / Administration. Scopes never mix, and the active row is unmistakable. Linear — the shell proportionsSlim sidebar, quiet chrome, content dominant. The proportions most SaaS apps converge on. Vapi — command menu as navigationWhat navigation becomes past twenty destinations. Mixpanel — sidebar with favourites and pinnedThe contextual zone doing real work for daily users.

Week 5 · Lesson 5.3

Forms that don't lose users

Forms are where products make money and lose users. Signup, checkout, settings, record creation — all forms. This is the highest-ROI component skill on the web.

Watch

▶
Vitaly Friedman — UX Best Practices for Forms: Preventing Error Messages
▶
Multi-Step Form UX — Best Practices

Layout laws

  • Single column. The most replicated form finding: one column completes faster with fewer errors. Exceptions only for tightly-coupled pairs (First/Last name, City/Postcode, MM/YY · CVC).
  • Labels above fields, left-aligned. (Left-of-field labels are for dense enterprise settings pages only.)
  • Field width hints expected content: a postcode field shouldn't be 600px wide. Cap the whole form at ~400–480px.
  • Group with headings + spacing (Week 2's proximity rule), not boxes-inside-boxes.
  • One primary button, left-aligned with the fields (or full-width in narrow auth forms), labeled with the outcome: "Create account", "Pay $49".

Reducing friction (the real design work)

  • Cut fields ruthlessly. Every field costs conversion. No "fax number". Ask: could we get this later, infer it, or live without it? ("Progressive profiling" = ask later, in context.)
  • Smart defaults + inference: country from IP, city from postcode, name parsed from email. Tesler's Law applied.
  • Show, never punish: input masks/formatting as they type (card numbers grouping into 4s), password requirements listed upfront with live checkmarks, caps-lock warnings.
  • Optional is labeled, required is not (when most fields are required). "(optional)" beats asterisk soup.

Validation & errors

  • Validate on blur (leaving a field), not on every keystroke (premature reds while typing) and not only on submit (error avalanche). Exception: live-validate positively — turning requirements green as they're met.
  • Error anatomy: red border + icon + specific message below the field. "Password needs 8+ characters" not "Invalid input". Never color alone.
  • On failed submit: scroll to the first error, keep everything the user typed, summarize errors at top for long forms.
  • Never clear the form. Ever.

Multi-step forms (wizards)

  • Split by mental topic (Your details → Company → Preferences), 3–5 steps, one topic per step.
  • Progress indicator with named steps; allow going back without data loss; autosave state.
  • Start with the easy/engaging question, ask the sensitive stuff (phone, billing) last — commitment escalates.
  • Final step = review + edit links. The Coda/ClickUp onboarding flows you'll study in Week 7 are exactly this pattern.

Read

Article
NN/g — Website Forms Usability: Top Guidelines

The evidence-based checklist.

Guide

Week 6 · Lesson 6.1

Data tables masterclass

Tables are the beating heart of SaaS — and the component mobile design prepared you for least. Master tables and you can design CRMs, admin panels, and every "manage things" screen on earth.

Watch

▶
A Better UX Design for Large Data Tables

Anatomy of a serious table

Top to bottom: table toolbar (search, filter button + active filter chips, view switcher, column customizer, primary action), header row (sticky on scroll; sortable columns show direction arrows), rows, footer (pagination "1–50 of 1,204" + rows-per-page). Selection adds a checkbox column and a bulk-action bar that replaces/overlays the toolbar when items are selected ("3 selected · Delete · Export · Assign").

The formatting rules

RuleWhy
Text left, numbers right, with tabular figuresNumbers compare by magnitude down the column
Never center data columnsRagged both sides = unscannable
Row height 40–48px (relaxed) / 32–36px (dense); offer a density toggle for power usersDensity is a user preference in data tools
Align header with its column's alignmentHeaders are part of the scan line
Zebra stripes OR row borders OR generous spacing — one, not allGridlines everywhere = prison bars; modern tables use hairline row borders only
First column = the identity column (name), medium weight, often linkedIt's the answer to "what is this row?"
Truncate long text with tooltip; wrap only descriptionsRow height consistency beats completeness
Status as dot+label badge; dates as relative ("2h ago") with exact on hoverScannable and precise

Row interactions

  • Hover: row tint + revealed quick actions on the right (edit, more-menu). Keep destructive actions inside the ⋯ menu.
  • Click target: decide what a row-click does — usually opens the record (in a drawer for quick tasks, full page for deep ones). Make the whole row clickable, not just the name.
  • Inline edit for spreadsheet-like tools: click-to-edit cells with clear editable affordance. Expensive to do well — default to drawer editing.

Filtering & sorting UI

  • Search box for free text; Filter button opening a popover (field → operator → value); applied filters as removable chips next to the button.
  • Saved views (filter+sort+column sets with names) — the power feature that turns a table into a workspace: "My open deals", "Churn risks".
  • Sort by clicking headers; show the active sort arrow; secondary sort for ties if the tool is serious.

Study the masters

Zoho CRM — DealsFilter sidebar + sort popover + bulk checkboxes, all at once Juicebox — ContactsColumn customizer popover — user-controlled tables

Read

Article
Pencil & Paper — Enterprise Data Tables UX Patterns

The best single write-up on tables. Read fully.

Collection
Stéphanie Walter — Complex Data Table Resources

A curated rabbit hole when you need table edge cases.

Column types — decide the format once, apply it everywhere

Every column in your product is one of about eight types. Spec each type once and you never argue about alignment again.

TypeAlignFormat rulesOverflow
Text / nameLeftOften the row's primary identifier — make it the link. Add a secondary line (email, ID) if it aids scanning.Truncate with ellipsis + tooltip. Never wrap the identity column.
Number / currencyRightTabular numerals, fixed decimals, thousands separators, unit in the header not the cell ("Revenue (USD)")Never truncate a number — shrink the column or abbreviate (1.2M)
Date / timeLeft or right (pick one)Relative for recent ("2h ago"), absolute beyond a week. Absolute value in the tooltip, always.Fixed width — dates are predictable
StatusLeftBadge with icon + word. Never colour alone. Cap at ~6 statuses; more means you need a second column.Fixed width
User / entityLeftAvatar 24 px + name. Stack up to 3 avatars then "+N".Truncate name, keep avatar
Tags / multi-valueLeftShow 2, then "+3" that opens a popoverNever wrap to a second line — it breaks row height
Progress / sparklineLeftInclude the number; a bar alone is unreadableFixed width, min 80 px
ActionsRightGhost icon buttons + overflow menu. Sticky right if the table scrolls horizontally.Fixed width

Row anatomy and density

DensityRow heightFontCell padding-yBest for
Compact36 px13–14 px8 pxPower users scanning hundreds of rows
Default48 px14 px14 pxEverything, until told otherwise
Comfortable60–64 px14 px20 pxTwo-line cells, avatars, touch

Make density a persisted user preference, not a designer decision. The person who lives in this table eight hours a day has an opinion, and it is more informed than yours.

Zebra striping is usually the wrong fixIf rows are hard to track, the cause is almost always too little horizontal rhythm or too many columns. Try: a 1 px border-subtle rule between rows, a strong hover wash, and cutting two columns. Striping adds visual noise to every row to solve a problem that only appears on wide tables — reach for it last, not first.

Filtering — four patterns, four jobs

PatternUse whenSpec notes
Search boxUsers know the name of what they wantDebounce ~300 ms, search across visible columns, show which fields matched, clear button
Quick filters (chips/segments)2–6 common, mutually understood cuts ("Active", "Mine", "Overdue")Show counts. These are shortcuts, not the whole filter system.
Faceted dropdownsFiltering by known dimensions — status, owner, typeMulti-select with counts; show applied filters as removable chips above the table
Filter builderAnalysts building precise queriesField + operator + value rows, AND/OR grouping, "Clear filters". Powerful and intimidating — never the only path.
Saved viewsThe same filter set is used repeatedlyThe real endgame. Name it, share it, set a default. Turns a filter chore into one click.

Always display the result count ("1,779 results") and always offer one-click Clear filters. The most common table complaint in usability testing is "I don't know why I'm seeing nothing" — an empty state that names the active filters solves it.

Selection and bulk actions

QuestionAnswer your spec must give
What does the header checkbox select?The current page. Then offer "Select all 312 matching" as a separate, explicit link.
Indeterminate state?Yes — a dash, not a tick, when some rows are selected
Where do bulk actions appear?A bar that replaces the toolbar or floats above the table. Never a hidden menu.
What does the bar say?"12 selected" + the actions + a clear (✕). Destructive actions are separated and last.
Does selection survive pagination?Decide, then tell the user in the bar. Silent loss of selection is a trust killer.
Undo?Bulk destructive actions need undo or a confirm naming the count. Preferably undo.

Responsive tables — four strategies, ranked

StrategyHowUse when
1 · Prioritise columnsHide low-priority columns at each breakpoint; keep identity + status + one metricAlmost always the right first move
2 · Horizontal scroll + frozen first columnIdentity column sticky-left, rest scrollsComparison matters and all columns are needed
3 · CardsEach row becomes a stacked card below ~640 pxFew rows, rich content, touch-first audiences
4 · Row expandTwo key columns visible; tap to reveal the restLast resort — hides data behind an extra interaction

Accessibility — the six that get missed

  • Real semantics: <table>, <th scope="col">, <caption>. A grid of divs is unusable with a screen reader.
  • Sortable headers are buttons with aria-sort announcing ascending / descending / none.
  • Row actions must appear on keyboard focus, not only hover.
  • Every checkbox needs an accessible name ("Select Bianca Doyle", not "Select row").
  • Result count and filter changes announced via a live region.
  • Horizontal scroll containers must be keyboard-scrollable and have a visible focus style.

Study these

Deel — bulk edit, all selectedFacet dropdowns across the top, every row checked, action bar pinned bottom-right. Retool — filter builderField + operator + value, with 'Add' and 'Clear filters'. Result count under it. Dovetail — column show/hideEvery column type in one table: text, date, tags, status, numeric. Plus reorder handles. Linear — the restraint benchmarkSix columns. No striping. Hierarchy from type weight and one accent. Study what's absent.
Task · ~60 minThe column-type audit Take any table from a product you use daily. For every column, name its type from the table above and check it against the alignment and format rules. Log every violation — right-aligned text, truncated numbers, status by colour alone, dates with no absolute tooltip. Most real tables fail three or more. Then write the corrected spec.

The classic. Row height, alignment, and the case against zebra stripes.

Week 6 · Lesson 6.2

Dashboards & data visualization

A dashboard is not a place to display data — it's a place to answer questions. Design the questions first.

Watch

▶
Designing a Modern Dashboard UI in Figma — Real-World SaaS Project

Dashboard anatomy

  • Global controls first: date-range picker (with compare-to toggle), scope filters (which project/team/segment). They govern everything below — top of page, sticky if long.
  • KPI row: 3–5 stat cards — big number (tabular figures!), label, delta vs previous period (▲ 12% green / ▼ red — plus sign or arrow, never color alone). Most important metric top-left (F-pattern).
  • Charts zone: 12-col grid: hero chart full-width or 8-col, supporting charts 4–6 col. Every chart: title as a question it answers, axis labels, hover tooltips with exact values.
  • Detail zone: a table of the underlying records — dashboards summarize, tables let users act.

Chart choice in one table

QuestionChart
How did it change over time?Line (trend) / area (volume feel)
How do categories compare?Horizontal bar (long labels) / vertical bar (few categories)
What are the parts of the whole?Stacked bar or donut — max 4–5 segments, else "Other"
How are two measures related?Scatter
Where's the single number now?Stat card, gauge, or bullet — not a chart at all
Chart sins3D anything; pies with 7 slices; truncated bar axes that exaggerate change; rainbow category colors (use one hue + emphasis, or your data-viz ramp); legends when direct labels fit; charts where a sentence would do ("Uptime: 99.98%").

Dashboard honesty

Fewer, better: every widget competes for attention (Miller again — 5–7 widgets, not 20). Empty and loading states for each widget individually (skeletons shaped like the chart), never a full-page spinner. And decide the dashboard's job: monitoring (glanceable, alarms), analysis (filters, drill-down), or reporting (export, share) — mixing all three makes mush.

Etsy — KPI row + hero trend lineQuestion-first: "how's traffic?" answered in one glance Indeed — date compare + saved viewsGlobal controls governing the whole page

Pick the chart from the question, not from the chart picker

The user's questionChartWatch out for
How has this changed over time?LineMore than 5 series is spaghetti — small multiples instead
How much, over time, in total?Area / stacked areaOnly the bottom band is readable; put the important series there
How do these categories compare?Bar (horizontal if labels are long)Always start the axis at zero. Truncating a bar axis is lying.
What's the composition of a whole?Stacked bar > piePie only for 2–3 slices; humans compare angles badly
How are values distributed?Histogram / box plotBin size changes the story — state it
Is there a relationship?ScatterCorrelation is not causation, and your users will forget that
Where do people drop off?FunnelShow absolute counts and step conversion %
What's the single number right now?KPI cardA number with no comparison is decoration
Which items rank highest?Ordered bar / top-N listSay what "top" is measured by
How dense is activity across two dimensions?HeatmapNeeds a legend and a sequential (not rainbow) scale
The three unbreakable rules1. Bar charts start at zero — always. 2. No dual y-axes; they let you manufacture any correlation you like. Use two stacked charts sharing an x-axis. 3. No 3-D, no drop shadows on data, no rainbow scales. Every pixel of ink that isn't data is competing with the data.

The KPI card, specified

PartRequiredSpec
LabelYestext-sm, text-secondary. Name the metric precisely — "Active users (7-day)" not "Users".
ValueYes28–36 px, 600, tabular numerals. Abbreviate above 5 digits (1.2M) with the exact value in a tooltip.
ComparisonYesDelta + direction + period ("+12.5% vs last month"). A number without a baseline cannot be judged.
TrendRecommendedSparkline, ~40 px tall, no axes. Shape, not values.
InfoRecommendedⓘ tooltip with the definition. Half of all dashboard confusion is metric definitions.
Empty / loadingYes"—" with a reason, and a skeleton at the exact final height

Delta colour is a decision, not a default: for churn or cost, up is bad. Bind the sentiment to the metric, not to the arrow direction.

Four dashboard archetypes

TypeQuestion it answersDesign consequence
Monitoring"Is anything wrong right now?"Glanceable, thresholds and alerts, auto-refresh, big status. Often on a wall screen — no hover, no tooltips.
Analytical"Why did that happen?"Filters, date ranges, segments, drill-down, export. Density is fine; exploration is the point.
Operational"What do I do next?"A worklist, not a chart wall. Every item leads to an action.
Strategic"Are we on track?"Few metrics, long horizons, targets and variance. Low interactivity, high clarity.

Naming the archetype before you open Figma prevents the most common dashboard failure: a monitoring layout being used for analysis, or an analytical wall being shown to an executive who wanted four numbers.

Layout and controls

  • Inverted pyramid. Row 1: 3–5 KPI cards. Row 2: the primary chart, full width or 2/3. Row 3+: supporting breakdowns and tables. Detail lives one click away.
  • Grid, not free placement. 12 columns; cards span 3/4/6/12. Every card the same vertical rhythm.
  • Global controls at the top: date range, comparison period, segment. They apply to everything below — and say so.
  • Date range presets (7d / 30d / 3m / 12m / custom) plus an explicit "compared to" control. Always print the resolved dates; "Last 30 days" is ambiguous about whether today counts.
  • Timezone and freshness. "Updated 4 min ago", in the user's timezone. Stale data presented confidently is worse than no data.
  • Every chart earns its place. If nobody can name a decision it changes, delete it.

Number formatting

CaseRule
Large numbersAbbreviate consistently — 1.2K, 45.8M. Never mix "1,200" and "1.2K" in one view.
PercentagesOne decimal max. 0 decimals if the range is wide.
CurrencySymbol + code where ambiguity exists (US$1,200). Consistent decimals within a column.
Zero vs null0 and "no data" are different. Show 0 as 0 and null as "—". Charts must break the line, not plot zero.
RoundingRound for display, never for the total. A column of rounded values that doesn't sum destroys trust.
Small samplesBelow ~30, show the count, not just the percentage. "100% (2 of 2)".

Colour in charts

Three palettes, three jobs. Categorical — 6 hues, maximally distinguishable, no implied order. Sequential — one hue, light→dark, for magnitude. Diverging — two hues with a neutral midpoint, for above/below a baseline. Never use a categorical palette for magnitude, and never use a rainbow for anything. Test every palette in greyscale and in a deuteranopia simulator; add pattern or direct labels wherever hue is doing the work alone.

Study these

Whop — KPI grid, editableSix cards on a grid, each with value + delta + sparkline. Date range and comparison up top. Base44 — customise panelUsers choose which modules appear. Note the reorder handles and per-module toggles. Uxcel — period comparisonThis-period vs previous-period stated as two numbers before any chart. Very readable. Mixpanel — analytical archetypeFunnels, retention, conversion. Density is correct here — this is a tool for asking why. Posh — the inverted pyramidKPIs, then one primary chart, then a table. Textbook structure. Lovable — generated dashboardWhat an AI builder considers a default dashboard. Critique it against the archetype table.
Task · ~90 minThe chart-swap exercise Find a dashboard with at least six charts. For each one, write the question it answers in plain language, then check it against the selection table. Redesign every mismatch — and delete any chart whose question you cannot state. Typically a third of the charts go. Present the before/after side by side; the deletions are the strongest part of the case study.
