Week 6 · Lesson 6.3

The five states of every screen

Mockups show the ideal state. Real products live in the other four. Designing all five is what separates product designers from screen painters.

The five

StateDesign job
1. EmptyTeach + activate: explain what will live here, give the primary action, consider a template/sample-data shortcut. First-run empty ≠ cleared-out empty ≠ no-search-results — three different messages.
2. LoadingSkeletons matching final layout (no layout shift); per-widget, not per-page; optimistic UI for user actions (show the change instantly, reconcile after).
3. Partial1 item, not 50: does the layout still look intentional? 3 of 5 fields filled: does the record page collapse gracefully?
4. ErrorWhat broke, in humans' words + what to do next (retry, contact, go back). Inline for fields, banner for sections, full-state for dead pages. Never a dead end.
5. IdealThe one you were already designing — now with realistic data: long names, 0 and 9-digit numbers, missing avatars.

Empty states are a growth surface

SaaS onboarding lives or dies in first-run empty states — they're where activation happens. The pattern: illustration (optional), one line of value ("Reports show you where your time goes"), one primary CTA ("Create your first report"), one escape hatch ("Import from CSV" / "Use sample data"). Study:

Laravel Cloud — first-run emptyIllustration + one line + one action. Nothing else. Etsy — create your first reportAction-first empty state
Habit to build nowFor every screen you design from this week on, duplicate the frame 4× and fill in the other states. In interviews and portfolios, this habit alone signals senior product thinking.

The state matrix — five states × every surface

Junior portfolios show the ideal state. Senior portfolios show all five. This table is the difference, and it is the single highest-return habit in product design.

SurfaceEmptyLoadingPartialErrorIdeal
Table / list3 kinds — first run, cleared, no resultsSkeleton rows at exact row heightSome columns unavailable; show "—" + whyRetry + what failed + what still worksRows
Chart"No data for this range" + range controlSkeleton at final height — never collapse the cardBroken line for gaps, not zeroesInline in the card, keep the titlePlotted
KPI card"—" + reasonShimmer at final heightValue present, comparison missing"Couldn't load" + retry iconValue + delta
Formn/aDisabled + spinner on submitSome fields prefilled, some pendingField-level + a summary at topFilled
SearchRecent / suggestedInline spinner in the fieldPartial results + "still searching""Search unavailable" + browse fallbackResults
PageOnboardingSkeleton of the real layoutSections load independentlyFull-page error with a way outContent

Loading: skeleton, spinner, or nothing

Expected waitShowWhy
< 300 msNothingA flash of spinner reads as a glitch and feels slower than silence
300 ms – 1 sInline spinner on the triggering controlConfirms the click landed, keeps context
1 – 10 sSkeleton matching the real layoutCommunicates what's coming and prevents layout shift
> 10 sProgress + a description of the step + a way to leaveIndeterminate waits over ten seconds feel broken
Background workToast on completion; let them navigate awayNever trap someone on a screen for a job that doesn't need them

Skeleton rules: same dimensions as the real content (this is the whole point), 2–3 grey tones only, a slow shimmer or none at all, and never skeleton something you already have cached. A skeleton whose height differs from the real content is worse than a spinner, because it guarantees a layout jump.

Optimistic UI, and its debtFor actions that almost always succeed — toggling a favourite, renaming, checking a box — update the UI immediately and reconcile in the background. It makes a product feel instant. The debt: you now owe a clear, non-destructive rollback with an explanation when it fails. Optimistic UI without a designed failure path is just a bug you haven't seen yet.

Error taxonomy — five kinds, five different designs

KindCauseWhere it appearsMessage must contain
ValidationUser inputInline, at the field, on blurWhat's wrong + what valid looks like
PermissionNot allowedIn place of the contentWho can grant access, and how to ask
Not foundDeleted or bad linkPage levelWhat was missing + a way back + search
Server / networkNot the user's faultClosest to the failed regionRetry, plainly stated cause, what still works
ConflictSomeone else changed itModal or inline bannerBoth versions and an explicit choice

Message formula: what happened → why → what to do next. Never expose a stack trace, never blame the user, and always keep an error code available (small, copyable) so support can act on it.

Partial — the state nobody designs

Real products load in pieces, and pieces fail independently. Decide per region: does a failed sidebar block the page? Does a missing comparison period hide the KPI or just the delta? Show what you have, mark what you don't, and never let one failed request blank an entire screen. Independent regions with independent states is the architecture; your design has to reflect it.

Study these

Headspace — skeleton pageThe skeleton is the real layout. Compare it to the loaded page and note the exact block sizes. Fabric — two-pane skeletonEach pane loads independently. Study how little detail a skeleton actually needs. Linktree — minimal skeletonThree blocks. Sometimes this is enough — and it never causes a layout shift. Laravel Cloud — empty + toastTwo states in one screenshot: a first-run empty and the toast that explains how it got empty.
Task · ~2 hrsFive states, one screen, no exceptions Take your densest screen from Week 6 and design all five states as separate frames — plus the three empty variants. Then write the exact copy for every message: empty headline and body, each error, the loading label. Copy is most of this work; the visuals are the easy part.
Portfolio note: a single "five states of one screen" board is the fastest way to signal seniority in a portfolio review. Almost nobody has one.

Week 6 · Practice

Practice: design a table + dashboard

The week everything compounds: grid + type + color + components → your first fully original SaaS screens.

Task 1 · ~2 hrsA serious data table Invent a record type you find interesting (deals, candidates, orders, campaigns, projects…). Design the full table screen inside your Week 5 app shell: toolbar with search + filters + primary action, sortable sticky header, 8–10 realistic rows (messy real-world data!), status badges, hover state with revealed actions, bulk-selection state with action bar, pagination footer. Then: the empty state and the loading skeleton.
Task 2 · ~90 minThe dashboard above it Design the overview page for the same product: date-range + scope controls, 4 KPI cards with deltas, one hero chart (draw the line/bars honestly — no decorative squiggles: pick numbers and plot them), 2 supporting charts, and a "recent items" mini-table linking to Task 1's screen.
Task 3 · ~30 minDensity pass Duplicate the table screen and produce a compact version (32px rows, 13px type, tighter paddings). Decide which density is your product's default and write two sentences defending the choice.
DeliverableDashboard + table (default, dense, empty, loading, bulk-selected) — this is a portfolio piece already.

The brief, in five checkpoints

Checkpoint 1 · ~45 minDecide before you draw Write one page: who uses this, which dashboard archetype it is (monitoring / analytical / operational / strategic), the five questions it must answer, and the single decision each answer changes. Then list your table's columns with a type from lesson 6.1 beside each.
Done when: every planned chart maps to one of your five questions. Anything that doesn't, gets cut now rather than designed and cut later.
Checkpoint 2 · ~2.5 hrsBuild the table 1440 frame. Ten columns covering at least six of the eight column types, twenty rows of realistic data — real names, real ranges, real edge cases (a very long name, a null, a zero, a huge number). Include: sticky header, sortable headers with an active sort, a filter bar with two applied filter chips and a result count, three rows selected with the bulk-action bar showing, hover state on one row with its row actions revealed, and a sticky right-hand actions column.
Done when: nothing is lorem ipsum and at least three cells are deliberately awkward.
Checkpoint 3 · ~2.5 hrsBuild the dashboard Four KPI cards (value + delta + period + sparkline + info tooltip), one primary chart chosen from the selection matrix, two supporting charts, and one top-N list. Global date range plus a "compared to" control, and a freshness stamp. All on a 12-column grid with a consistent card rhythm.
Done when: you can point at any chart and state the question it answers in one sentence.
Checkpoint 4 · ~2 hrsAll five states, both screens Table: ideal, skeleton, first-run empty, no-results empty, error. Dashboard: ideal, skeleton, no-data-for-range, partial (one chart failed while the rest loaded), error. Write the real copy for each — headline, body, action label.
Done when: ten frames, all with final copy.
Checkpoint 5 · ~90 minResponsive and dark Take both screens to 768 px and 390 px using a strategy from the responsive table (name which one and why). Then produce a dark-mode version of both using semantic tokens only — if you hand-pick a colour, a token is missing.
Done when: the mobile table is genuinely usable, not just narrower.

Self-review before you call it done

CheckPass condition
NumbersRight-aligned, tabular, consistent decimals, units in the header
StatusIcon or word alongside colour, everywhere
Every KPIHas a comparison and a definition tooltip
Every chartAnswers a listed question; bar axes start at zero; no dual y-axis
Empty statesThree distinct kinds, three distinct messages
SkeletonsExactly the height of the real content
KeyboardRow actions reachable by Tab; sort headers are buttons
Zero vs nullVisibly different in both table and chart
DensityA control exists, and the choice persists
CopyNo lorem ipsum anywhere, including error messages
DeliverableTwo production-grade screens × five states × three breakpoints × two themes, plus the one-page decision brief. This is the strongest SaaS artefact in the course after the design system — and the pairing of a dense table with a well-argued dashboard is exactly what product-design interviews probe for.

Tables, dashboards, and screen states.

Week 7 · Lesson 7.1

Auth & onboarding flows

The first five minutes decide whether a signup becomes a user. This is flow design: sequences, not screens.

Auth pages (the easy part)

  • Signup: email + password + SSO buttons (Google first — it converts best), or passwordless magic-link. Split layout (form + brand panel) or minimal centered card. Ask for nothing else — every extra field costs signups; get the rest during onboarding.
  • Login: same layout for muscle memory, plus "Forgot password" (never hide it), and clear error handling that doesn't reveal whether the email exists.
  • Password reset, verify-email, expired-link pages: boring, essential, usually forgotten by designers — so design them.

Onboarding = the path to the aha moment

Activation isn't account creation — it's the first moment of real value (first report run, first message sent, first design shared). Everything between signup and that moment is onboarding, and every step is a leak. The standard SaaS sequence:

  1. Profiling questions (1 per screen, 3–5 max): role, team size, intent — used to personalize the workspace and route marketing. Progress bar + Skip on every one.
  2. Workspace setup: name it (pre-filled from their name — smart defaults!), invite teammates (skippable, but this is the growth loop — make it attractive).
  3. The shortcut to value: templates, sample data, or an import — never a blank screen. "Start with a template" beats a tutorial every time.
  4. In-product guidance: a getting-started checklist (3–5 tasks with progress — the psychology of the endowed progress effect), plus contextual tooltips. Full product tours get skipped; checklists get finished.

Watch

▶
SaaS Onboarding Teardown — Mailshake
Watch one teardown, then do your own on the flows below — teardowns are the skill, not the content.

Study these full flows on Mobbin

Coda — Setting up account (7 screens)Role question → tool connections → workspace naming ClickUp — Workspace setup (23 screens!)The maximalist version — decide for yourself where it crosses the line

Also read two Growth.Design onboarding case studies this week — their annotation style is exactly the teardown format you should practice.

The sign-up field audit — every field costs conversion

FieldKeep at sign-up?Why
EmailYesThe account identifier. One field.
PasswordYes — or skip itMagic links and OAuth remove it entirely. If you keep it: one field, a reveal toggle, no "confirm password".
Confirm passwordNoA reveal toggle solves the same problem with half the typing and none of the mismatch errors.
Full nameMove itAsk after signup, in context, when you can explain why
Company / role / team sizeMove itThese are sales-qualification fields. They belong in onboarding, where the user is already invested.
PhoneOnly if required for the productHighest-friction field on the form
CaptchaInvisible onlyA visible challenge is a conversion tax on legitimate users

Password rules that survive contact with reality: minimum 8 characters, no composition rules, no forced rotation, allow paste, allow password managers, allow every character including spaces, check against known-breached lists. That is current NIST guidance, and it produces stronger passwords than the "one uppercase, one symbol" theatre.

Auth patterns — pick per audience

PatternBest forDesign obligations
Email + passwordUniversal fallbackReset flow, breach messaging, manager-friendly fields
OAuth / socialConsumer and developer toolsShow which provider they used last time — "you signed up with Google" prevents duplicate accounts
Magic linkLow-frequency products"Check your email" screen must name the address, offer resend with a cooldown, and handle the wrong-browser case
SSO / SAMLEnterpriseEmail-domain routing — type the work email, get redirected. Never make people find a hidden "SSO" link.
PasskeysIncreasingly, everyoneOffer alongside, never as the only route; explain what it is in one line
The three auth screens nobody designs1. "Check your email" — the most-viewed screen in a magic-link flow, and usually the least designed. 2. The expired/invalid link screen, with an obvious way to get a new one. 3. Account-already-exists, which must route to sign-in with the email prefilled rather than accusing the user of an error.

Onboarding — four jobs, in order

JobDoDon't
1 · PersonaliseAsk 2–4 questions that visibly change what they see nextAsk questions that only feed your CRM
2 · Set upConnect data, invite a teammate, import — whatever the product needs to be usefulBlock the product until it's done
3 · ActivateGet them to the aha moment — the first time the product does its actual jobTour the interface instead of using it
4 · HabitChecklist, empty-state nudges, a reason to return tomorrowDeclare victory at first login

Define the aha moment in one sentence before you design anything. "The user sees their own data in a chart." "The user's first invoice is sent." Every onboarding screen either moves toward that sentence or gets cut. Products that skip this step build tours; products that do it build activation.

Onboarding patterns

PatternUse whenRule
Progressive questionsThe product genuinely branches on the answerMax 4 steps, visible progress, skippable
Setup checklistSeveral independent setup tasksShow progress, allow any order, let it be dismissed permanently
Sample data / templateThe product is empty and abstract until populatedMake it obviously sample, and one-click removable
Empty-state teachingAlways — it's freeThe empty state is your best onboarding surface; it appears exactly when it's relevant
Product tour / coach marksRarelyMax 3 stops, dismissible, never on first paint. Tours are what you build when the UI isn't clear enough.

Study these

Render — OAuth-first sign upFour providers above the fold, email below, inline validation. Note: no confirm-password field. Buy Me a Coffee — verification inlineThe email code is collected in the same form, not on a separate screen. Fewer context switches. Duolingo — three fields, no moreName, email, password. Everything else is asked later, inside the product. WorkOS — post-signup profile stepAsked after the account exists, with the email shown as proof of progress.
ClickUp — the full 23-screen setupWalk it end to end. Count how many screens change what you see next versus how many are data collection. Coda — 7-screen setupA tighter flow. Compare its question-to-value ratio with ClickUp's.
Task · ~90 minThe aha-moment teardown Sign up for two SaaS products you have never used. For each, record: number of fields before account creation, number of onboarding steps, which steps changed what you saw next, and how many minutes until the product did something useful for you. Write the aha moment as one sentence for each, then mark every step that did not move toward it. Design the shorter version of the worse one.

Week 7 · Lesson 7.2

Core SaaS surfaces: settings, billing, teams

Every SaaS product ships the same five unglamorous surfaces. Design them by convention — users visit rarely, so familiarity beats cleverness (Jakob's Law at maximum strength).

Settings

  • Architecture: a settings sidebar grouped into Account (profile, security, notifications) vs Workspace/Org (general, members, billing, integrations) — this personal/organizational split is universal; blurring it confuses everyone.
  • Page pattern: single narrow column (~640px) of sections; each section = heading + fields; either autosave with "Saved" feedback per control (modern) or a save bar per section (classic) — never one giant save button for the whole page.
  • Danger zone: destructive actions (delete workspace, transfer ownership) live at the bottom, visually separated in red, with type-to-confirm dialogs.
Obvious — settingsAccount/Workspace/Teams split in the sidebar StackAI — profile settingsSectioned cards + danger zone at bottom

Billing & plan management

  • Current plan card (name, price, renewal date, Manage/Upgrade), payment method row, invoice history table (date, amount, status, download PDF), usage meters when pricing is usage-based.
  • Upgrade moments happen in-product, not on the billing page: paywall modals at feature-touch ("Upgrade to add more than 3 projects"), usage-limit banners at 80% and 100%. Design the moment, then the page.
  • Cancellation: findable (dark-patterning it destroys trust and is increasingly illegal), one honest retention offer max, confirmation of what happens to their data.
Obvious — billingPlan card + payment + history: the whole pattern in one screen Cursor — billing + usageUsage-based pricing needs meters and cycle framing

Members & permissions

  • Members table: avatar+name+email, role (editable dropdown for admins), status (active/invited — resend), last active, remove action. Invite modal: multi-email input + role select + personal message.
  • Roles: Owner / Admin / Member / Guest covers 90% of products. Communicate what each can do at the point of choice (helper text in the role dropdown), not in a distant docs page.
  • Seat-based pricing meets this screen: "8 of 10 seats used" + the upgrade path when full.

Notifications & integrations

  • Notification preferences: a matrix (event types × channels: in-app / email / Slack) with sane defaults and per-project overrides in mature tools. Default to less email than you think.
  • Integrations directory: logo cards with Connect/Connected states, category filter, and a detail view per integration (permissions requested, settings once connected).

Settings information architecture

Settings pages rot faster than any other surface because every feature adds one. The fix is a structure decided up front — not alphabetical, and not chronological by ship date.

ScopeContainsWho can change it
Account (the person)Profile, email, password, MFA, sessions, notifications, appearance, languageThe user, always
Workspace / orgName, logo, domains, members, roles, SSO, audit log, data retentionAdmins
BillingPlan, seats, usage, payment method, invoices, tax detailsBilling role — often not the admin
Project / resourceAnything scoped to one objectObject permissions
IntegrationsConnected apps, API keys, webhooksAdmins, usually
DeveloperKeys, tokens, logs, sandboxDeveloper role

Never mix scopes on one page. "Change my avatar" and "delete the workspace" living under one heading is how people delete workspaces. Label the scope in the page title and repeat it in the confirmation copy.

Settings mechanics

DecisionRule
Save modelPick one per product: auto-save-on-change (switches, selects) or explicit Save. Mixing them is the top settings bug.
Auto-save feedbackInline "Saved" that fades, or a subtle checkmark. Silent saves feel broken.
Explicit saveSticky footer bar appearing only when dirty, with Save + Discard, and a leave-page guard
DescriptionsEvery switch gets one line explaining what changes. If you can't write it, the setting shouldn't exist.
Destructive zoneBottom of the page, visually separated, type-the-name confirmation for anything unrecoverable
SearchOnce you pass ~40 settings, add search. Users don't know your taxonomy.
Permission-gated rowsShow them disabled with "Ask an admin" — hiding them makes users think the feature doesn't exist

Billing — the surface that decides whether you get paid

ElementMust show
Current planName, price, billing period, next renewal date, and what's included
Usage vs limitsA bar per metered dimension with used/total. Warn at 80%, act at 100%.
SeatsAssigned vs paid, cost per additional seat, and what happens mid-cycle (proration — say it plainly)
Payment methodLast four + expiry + a card that visibly expires soon
InvoicesTable: date, amount, status, download PDF. Status is a badge, not colour alone.
Plan changeShow the price difference and the effective date before confirming. Upgrades are instant; downgrades usually take effect at period end — say which.
CancellationFindable. Say exactly what they lose and when, and offer pause or downgrade first. Hiding it converts churn into chargebacks.
Failed paymentA banner everywhere, an email, and a grace period stated in days. This flow saves more revenue than any pricing-page tweak.
Limit-reached is a design surface, not an errorThe moment a user hits a plan limit is the single highest-intent moment in your product. Design it properly: name the limit, show the current usage, state exactly what the next tier gives, and make upgrading one click. A red toast saying "limit reached" wastes the best upsell you will ever get.

Teams, members and roles

SurfaceSpec
Member listAvatar, name, email, role, status (active / invited / suspended), last active, row actions
InviteMulti-email paste, role picker in the same step, optional message, resend + revoke on pending invites
Roles3–5 named roles with a permission matrix the user can actually read. Custom roles only when you must.
OwnershipExactly one owner. Transfer is an explicit, confirmed flow — and you cannot remove the last owner.
RemovalSay what happens to their content: transferred, orphaned or deleted. This is a real decision, not a detail.
Pending stateInvited users appear in the list immediately, greyed, with "Invited 3 days ago · Resend"

Study these

Teachable — plan + usage barsEvery metered dimension has a bar. Note the red 'Limit reached · Add more' row — an upsell placed at the moment of need. Slite — trial + plan stateTrial countdown in the sidebar, plan state, usage, and the billing-period control all on one page. Figma — seat-based billingSeats by type with counts, and the upcoming invoice beside it. Very little else — deliberately. Linear — settings IAScan the sidebar: Account, Issues, Projects, Features, Administration. Scopes never mix.
Task · ~2 hrsDesign the limit-reached moment Design four connected frames: (1) usage at 80% with the in-context warning, (2) the limit-reached state on the surface where the user hit it, (3) the upgrade comparison showing exactly what changes and the prorated price, (4) the post-upgrade confirmation. Write every word. This four-frame sequence is worth more in a portfolio than another dashboard.

Week 7 · Lesson 7.3

Marketing sites, landing & pricing pages

Product design retains users; marketing design wins them. Different rules: persuasion architecture, scanning behavior, and conversion craft. These rules apply to every business's website, not just SaaS.

Watch

▶
Figma Tutorial — Designing a SaaS Landing Page
▶
Let's Design a Landing Page UI in Figma

Landing page = argument structure

A landing page is a persuasive essay in sections (you learned the section patterns in Week 2.3 — now order them as an argument):

  1. Hero: headline states the outcome you buy, in customer words ("Ship websites faster", not "AI-powered workflow platform"). Subhead = how, one CTA (+ optional secondary "watch demo"), visual proof (product shot).
  2. Credibility: logo bar / star ratings — borrow trust immediately.
  3. Problem → solution: name their pain, show the fix — feature sections framed as benefits ("Know where every rupee goes" over "Expense tracking module").
  4. Proof: testimonials with faces + names + companies, case-study numbers ("cut onboarding time 60%").
  5. Objection handling: FAQ, security badges, integrations wall, "works with your stack".
  6. Final CTA: restate the outcome + one button. Then footer.

Rules of thumb: one message per section; the CTA appears every ~2 screens of scroll; every section passes the squint test with its single takeaway; benefit-first headlines with features as supporting detail.

Pricing pages (the highest-stakes page)

  • Three tiers, middle highlighted ("Most popular") — anchoring + Hick's + Von Restorff in one pattern. Enterprise = "Contact sales".
  • Monthly/annual toggle with the annual discount framed as savings ("2 months free").
  • Per-tier: name, price with clear unit (per user/month, billed annually — the fine print that builds or breaks trust), one-line who-it's-for, feature list as differences (not 40 identical checkmarks), CTA per tier ("Start free" vs "Start trial" vs "Talk to us").
  • Below: full comparison table (sticky column headers!), FAQ handling billing objections.
  • Free trial vs freemium vs demo-first is a business decision that reshapes the whole page — know which model the product runs before designing.
Vercel — pricing + proof statsTiers flowing into case-study numbers Framer — plan cardsFeature lists as differences, add-on pricing below

The rest of the marketing site

Feature/solution pages (one landing-page argument per feature or persona), About (team + story — trust for bigger deals), Blog/resources (SEO engine — clean article template with your Week 3 typography), Contact/demo request (a form obeying every Week 5 rule), Careers, Legal. Navigation: 5–7 top items max, mega-menu only when a dropdown genuinely can't hold it, persistent CTA button in the header ("Start free"), and a mega-footer as the sitemap.

The landing page as an argument, section by section

A landing page is not a layout problem. It is an argument, and the sections are its paragraphs. Get the order of the argument right and mediocre visuals still convert; get it wrong and beautiful ones don't.

#SectionThe question it answersFails when
1HeroWhat is this and who is it for?The headline describes a category, not an outcome
2Social proof stripDo serious people use it?Logos nobody recognises, or twelve of them
3ProblemDo they understand my situation?Skipped — the reader never feels seen
4–6Feature blocksHow does it work?Feature names instead of outcomes; no visuals
7Deep proofDid it work for someone like me?Anonymous quotes with no role, company or number
8Pricing / plan previewCan I afford it?"Contact us" as the only option
9Objections / FAQWhat's the catch?Marketing questions instead of the real ones
10Final CTAWhat now?A different action from the hero CTA
11FooterWhere's everything else?—

One page, one action. The hero CTA and the final CTA must be the same verb. Every secondary path — docs, pricing, demo — is a link, not a button.

The hero, dissected

SlotJobRule
EyebrowCategory or audienceOptional. Under 24 characters.
HeadlineThe outcome, in the user's words6–12 words. State a result, not a feature. "Where creators do brand deals" beats "Creator monetisation platform".
SubheadHow, and for whomOne sentence, 15–25 words. This is where the mechanism goes.
Primary CTAThe one actionVerb + outcome. "Start for free" beats "Submit". State the friction: "No credit card".
Secondary CTAThe not-ready pathA link or ghost button. Never equal weight.
MediaProof the thing is realShow the actual product. Abstract 3-D shapes tell the reader nothing.
Proof stripReduce risk immediatelyLogos, a rating, or a user count — one, not all three
The five-second testShow your hero to someone for five seconds, then hide it and ask: what does this company do, who is it for, and what would you click? If they can't answer all three, no amount of gradient fixes it. Run this before you refine anything else.

Feature blocks that actually persuade

Formula per block: outcome headline → one sentence of mechanism → a visual of the real product → optional proof point or link. Alternate media left/right for rhythm, but no more than three alternations before you change format entirely — the pattern stops registering after that. And every screenshot should be legible at the size you're actually showing it; a 40% scale dashboard is a texture, not evidence.

Pricing pages — the highest-stakes marketing surface

DecisionGuidance
Tier count3 is the sweet spot. 4+ needs a comparison table underneath.
Recommended tierElevate exactly one — border, scale or badge. Badging all three cancels out.
Feature lists"Everything in Starter, plus…" — differences, not repeats
Annual toggleShow the saving as a number, and show the monthly-equivalent price when annual is selected
Enterprise tier"Contact sales" is fine — but give a starting price or a qualifying detail, or serious buyers self-disqualify
Currency & taxState whether prices include tax, and detect locale rather than making people convert
The FAQ belowAnswer the real questions: what happens when I exceed a limit, can I downgrade, what counts as a seat, do you delete my data
Comparison tableSticky header with tier names, grouped rows, tooltips on jargon, and a CTA repeated at the bottom of every column

Navigation and the mega menu

Marketing nav is a different component from app nav. Rules: 5–7 top-level items maximum; sign-in as a link and the primary CTA as a button, always in that order; the logo goes home; sticky nav condenses on scroll (don't just shrink — reduce height and drop the sub-items). Mega menus open on click, not hover, on touch devices — and every mega menu needs a keyboard path and an Escape key.

Study these heroes

Passionfroot — outcome headline'Where creators do brand deals.' Six words, states the outcome, names the audience. Headspace — split hero with segmentationHero, then immediately three audience paths. The page branches instead of averaging. Norma — product-photography heroAlmost no copy. Works only because the object is the argument. Study when this fails. Origin — centred heroThe textbook skeleton: headline, subtext, one CTA, product visual.

Proof sections

Miro — 4-up testimonial gridPhoto, logo, quote, name and role on every card. Specific roles make quotes credible. Fibery — single deep quoteOne long, specific quote plus a link to the full story. Depth over volume. Glide — centred single quoteNote what's missing: no company logo. Weaker proof — decide if that trade is worth the calm. Vanta — 3 tiers'Everything in X, plus…' done correctly, with one tier elevated by border alone.
Task · ~2 hrsThe argument audit Pick a landing page you think is good. Write out its sections in order and, beside each, the question it answers from the table above. Find the gaps — most pages skip problem and objections. Then take a page you think is bad and do the same; the diagnosis will almost always be a missing or out-of-order paragraph in the argument, not the visuals.

Week 7 · Lesson 7.4

Beyond SaaS: e-commerce, content & portfolio sites

You asked for all of web design — this is the lesson that maps the rest of the territory. Same foundations (grid, type, color, components), different page anatomies and success metrics per niche.

E-commerce

The conversion funnel is the site: Home → Listing (PLP) → Product (PDP) → Cart → Checkout. Design each for its single job:

  • PLP (listing/category): filter sidebar (price, size, brand — with result counts), sort control, product cards (image dominates, name, price, rating, quick-add), grid of 3–4 columns. Filters are the product-finding UX — treat them as seriously as SaaS table filters (they're the same skill).
  • PDP (product page): gallery left (thumbnails + zoom), buy-box right: title, price (+strikethrough anchor), variant selectors (size/color as swatches — with availability states), quantity, Add to cart (the page's one hero button), shipping/returns reassurance right under it, then reviews, details accordion, cross-sell ("pairs well with").
  • Cart: editable line items, order summary with shipping estimate before checkout (surprise costs are the #1 abandonment cause), promo code field (collapsed — an open one sends people hunting for coupons), trust badges.
  • Checkout: a multi-step form (Week 5.3 rules at maximum stakes): guest checkout first-class, address autocomplete, express pays (Apple/Google Pay) up top, order summary persistent in a right rail, no nav escape routes (the one place stripping navigation is correct).
Etsy — PDP anatomyGallery + buy-box + reassurance line Quicken — checkoutOrder summary rail + payment form + legal fine print

Content & editorial sites (blogs, magazines, docs)

  • The article template is the product: Week 3 typography at full power — 640–700px measure, 18–20px body, clear heading rhythm, pull quotes, figures with captions, estimated reading time, author bio block, "next up" recirculation at the end.
  • Index pages: featured story + card grid, category navigation, honest pagination. Newsletters capture (one polite inline block, not three popups).
  • Docs sites (a niche you'll meet in every SaaS job): three-pane pattern — nav tree left, article center, on-this-page anchors right; search first-class; code blocks with copy buttons; version switcher.

Portfolio, agency & local business sites

  • Portfolio/agency: the work IS the hero — big case-study cards, minimal chrome, personality through type and motion (this is where display serifs and art direction get to play). Case study template: challenge → process → outcome with numbers. One CTA: "Work with us".
  • Local business (restaurant, clinic, salon): the job is answers-fast: what/where/when/how-much above the fold — hours, address with map link, phone that's tappable, menu/services, booking CTA. These sites fail by artistry and win by clarity; mobile traffic dominates, so responsive discipline (Week 8) matters most here.
  • Event/one-pagers: a single scrolling landing argument with anchor nav — everything from 7.3 in miniature.

What changes across niches (the transferable insight)

NicheHero metricDesign center of gravity
SaaSActivation & retentionApp UI density, flows, empty states
E-commerceConversion rate & AOVPDP buy-box, checkout friction, trust
ContentRead time & return visitsTypography, reading experience
Portfolio/agencyInquiriesArt direction, case-study storytelling
Local businessCalls & bookingsFindability of basics, mobile speed

Before designing in any new niche: spend 30 minutes on Mobbin/Land-book studying its top 5 players, list the conventions they all share (that's the Jakob's-Law baseline you must meet), then choose your one deliberate deviation.

E-commerce: the product page checklist

Product pages are the most researched surface in web design — decades of evidence exist. Almost none of it is applied. Here is the short version.

ElementRequirement
ImagesMultiple angles, in-scale/in-context shot, zoom, and the ability to see the product in each selected variant. Thumbnails visible without scrolling.
Title & priceAbove the fold together. Show the original price when discounted, plus the % and the end date if it's time-limited.
VariantsSwatches show the actual colour/material, not a text list. Unavailable combinations are visibly out of stock, not silently missing.
AvailabilityStock status and a delivery estimate as a date, not "3–5 business days". Show it before the cart, not after.
Add to cartOne primary. Secondary paths (save, buy now, make an offer) get lower weight. Confirm with a mini-cart, not a full page redirect.
SpecsA real specification table, not a paragraph. This is the top reason for returns when it's missing.
ReviewsDistribution histogram, filters, customer photos, verified badges, and the negative ones visible. A 5.0 with no criticism reads as fake.
Returns & shippingLinked from the buy box. Uncertainty here kills more carts than price does.
Cross-sellBelow the fold, clearly separated. Never between the price and the buy button.

Checkout

RuleWhy
Guest checkout, alwaysForced account creation is the single largest documented cause of cart abandonment
One columnTwo-column forms cause skipped fields
Show total cost earlyShipping and tax revealed at the last step is the second largest cause
Progress indicator3–4 named steps. People abandon when they can't see the end.
Address autocompleteFewer fields, fewer errors, fewer failed deliveries
Correct input typesNumeric keypad for card and postcode; autocomplete attributes on everything
Card fieldOne field, auto-formatting, auto-detected brand, expiry as MM/YY
Order summary visibleSticky beside or above the form, editable without leaving
Errors inlineNever clear the form on a failed payment. Never.
Wallets firstApple Pay / Google Pay / PayPal above the fold — they skip the whole form

Study these

Walmart — the reviews section done fullyDistribution histogram, customer photos, filter chips by topic, verified badges, sort. This is the benchmark. Etsy — buy box densityPrice, discount, urgency, instalments, three CTAs and trust signals. Count the persuasion devices, then ask which you'd cut. Uvodo — the minimal versionImage, title, price, add-on, quantity, one CTA. Compare its conversion devices to Etsy's — different audiences, different answers. Etsy — category browseHow filtering, sorting and result density work on a marketplace.

Content sites — the reading machine

ElementSpec
Measure65–75 characters. On a 1440 screen your article column stops around 720 px.
Body type18–20 px, line height 1.6–1.75. Larger than app UI, on purpose.
Article headerTitle, dek, author + date, reading time, and the topic — in that order
In-article rhythmA subhead every 300–500 words; images breaking the column; pull quotes sparingly
NavigationSticky progress bar or table of contents for anything over ~1500 words
Related contentAt the end, plus one inline mid-article at most
Dark modeNon-negotiable for a reading surface
Ad slotsIf they exist, design them into the grid rather than letting them punch holes in it

Portfolio sites — the one you'll build for yourself

ElementRule
Above the foldWho you are, what you do, who you do it for — in one sentence. Not a mysterious animation.
Case study count3–4. Depth beats volume; reviewers read two.
Case study structureContext → your role → constraint → process → decisions → outcome. Decisions and outcome are what get you hired.
ProcessShow the messy middle — the rejected direction, the thing that tested badly. Polished-only portfolios read as unexamined.
ImageryReal screens at readable size. No floating iPhone mockups at 12° angles.
ContactAn email address, visible, on every page
Load timeUnder 2 seconds. A designer's own site being slow is a signal, and reviewers read it.
You are building this at the end of the courseThe Week 6 table + dashboard, the Week 7 landing page, and the d1 design system are three case studies. Write each one against the structure above as you finish it — reconstructing your reasoning six months later never works.
Task · ~2.5 hrsThree-genre teardown Pick one e-commerce product page, one long-form article, and one designer portfolio. Score each against its table above, item by item, pass or fail. Then take the lowest scorer and redesign one screen of it, listing the specific checklist items your redesign fixes. Scoring first stops you from redesigning by taste.

Week 7 · Practice

Practice: design the connective tissue

Screens are easy; flows are the job. This week you design sequences — and step outside SaaS once.

Task 1 · ~2 hrsSignup → onboarding → first value For your Week 6 product: signup page → 3 profiling steps → workspace setup → the dashboard's first-run state with a getting-started checklist. 7–9 frames wired with Figma prototyping. Steal structure from the Coda flow; steal restraint by cutting anything ClickUp would have added.
Task 2 · ~90 minPricing page Three tiers for your product (invent honest packaging: what's free, what's pro, what's team-gated), monthly/annual toggle, comparison table, 4-question FAQ. Reference the Vercel/Framer sections from 7.3.
Task 3 · ~90 minNiche crossover: one e-commerce PDP Design a product page for a physical product you own (headphones, a chair, coffee beans…) using the Etsy anatomy from 7.4: gallery, buy-box with variants, reassurance, reviews section. Notice how much of your SaaS kit transfers — and write down the three things that felt genuinely different.
Task 4 · ~45 minOnboarding teardown (Growth.Design style) Sign up for a real product you've never used (any free SaaS). Screenshot every step. Annotate: what they asked, what they defaulted, where you nearly dropped, the time-to-value. One page in Figma.
DeliverableA prototyped onboarding flow, a pricing page, your first e-commerce PDP, and a teardown of a real product's first-run.

The brief, in five checkpoints

Checkpoint 1 · ~45 minWrite the argument before the layout One page: what the product does in a sentence, who it's for, the aha moment, and the eleven-section landing-page argument from lesson 7.3 with your one-line answer to each question. Also decide your single primary CTA verb — it must be identical in the hero and the final CTA.
Done when: a stranger could read the page and predict the design.
Checkpoint 2 · ~3 hrsThe landing page 1440 frame, full page. All eleven sections, real copy, real product screenshots (use your Week 6 dashboard — that's what the connective tissue means). Fluid type and section rhythm from the marketing token kit. Then a 390 px version: what stacks, what's cut, where the CTA goes when the nav collapses.
Done when: the five-second test passes on three different people.
Checkpoint 3 · ~2 hrsPricing + the objection layer Three tiers with one elevated, an annual toggle showing the saving as a number, a full comparison table with a sticky tier header, and an FAQ answering the six real questions (limits, downgrade, seats, data, cancellation, trial). Then the limit-reached → upgrade → confirmation sequence from lesson 7.2.
Done when: someone can answer "what happens if I go over?" without asking you.
Checkpoint 4 · ~2.5 hrsAuth and onboarding Sign up (OAuth-first, minimum fields), the "check your email" screen, the expired-link screen, the account-already-exists screen, then a 3-step onboarding where every step visibly changes what comes next, and finally the first-run empty state that teaches. Write all the copy.
Done when: you can trace an unbroken path from the landing-page CTA to the aha moment with no dead ends.
Checkpoint 5 · ~90 minSettings, billing, team Three screens: an account settings page with a clear save model, a billing page with plan + usage bars + invoices, and a team page with the member list, a pending invite, and the role matrix. All from your component library.
Done when: scopes never mix on one page and every switch has a one-line description.

The connective-tissue test

Lay every frame you have made in Weeks 6 and 7 on one board and walk the path a real person takes: ad → landing page → pricing → sign up → verify → onboard → empty state → first data → dashboard → hit a limit → upgrade → invite a teammate → settings. Every gap you find is a screen that would have been invented badly under deadline. That walk is the exercise; the frames are just the evidence.

Week 8 · Lesson 8.1

Responsive design for the whole web

Here your mobile experience becomes a superpower — you already know small screens. The skill to add: designing the transformations between sizes, for every kind of site.

Watch

▶
Kevin Powell — Responsive Design Made Easy
Powell teaches developers, which is exactly why designers should watch: you'll design better once you know how CSS actually flexes. Also good: his practical guide to responsive web design.

Fluid + breakpoints (how the web actually resizes)

Layouts are fluid by default (percentages, max-widths) and break at defined widths where the arrangement changes. Content determines breakpoints — you add one where the layout starts failing, not at magic device numbers. The working set from Week 2 (390 / 768 / 1280 / 1440) covers real projects; design at 2–3 of them and specify the rules between.

Direction: which end do you start from?

  • Mobile-first — marketing, e-commerce, content, local business: most traffic is phones, and constraint-first forces message clarity.
  • Desktop-first — SaaS apps: work happens at desks; mobile web gets a companion subset (check status, approve, comment — not full admin).
  • Either way, you deliver both. "Is this page usable at 390?" is a question you now ask of every design, including dashboards.

The transformation playbook

PatternDesktop → Mobile
Top navLinks collapse to hamburger sheet/drawer; CTA button survives outside the menu
App sidebarIcon rail (tablet) → hidden drawer or bottom tabs (phone)
Card grid4 → 2 → 1 columns; the grid's column count is the dial
Split heroStacks: text above visual; center-align is acceptable here
Multi-column form pairsSingle column, always
ModalFull-screen sheet
Pricing trioStack with "most popular" first, or horizontal snap-scroll
Dashboard widgetsSingle column, KPI cards 2-up, charts simplified (fewer ticks, bigger touch targets)

Responsive tables (the boss fight)

Tables can't just squish. Choose per table, by how it's used:

  • Priority columns — keep identity + 1–2 key columns, move the rest into the row's detail view. (Most common, usually right.)
  • Horizontal scroll — freeze the identity column, let the rest pan. Honest for truly tabular data; signal scrollability with a cut-off column.
  • Card transform — each row becomes a stacked card (label: value pairs). Good for browse-y lists, verbose for dense data.
  • Skip the anti-pattern: shrinking font until it "fits". 9px type is not a strategy.

Also: touch replaces hover on mobile — every hover-revealed action needs a visible or menu-based fallback; and remember fluid type (clamp()) lets marketing headlines scale smoothly between breakpoints — specify min/max sizes in handoff.

Read

Course
web.dev — Learn Responsive Design (finish it now)

You read 3 units in Week 1. Complete the rest this week.

Article
NN/g — Breakpoints in Responsive Design

Why content, not devices, sets your breakpoints.

The breakpoint set, and what actually changes at each

TokenWidthWhat changes
xs0–639Single column, bottom nav or drawer, tables become cards or scroll, 16 px gutters
sm640Two-up card grids, wider gutters
md768Sidebar can appear as an overlay drawer; forms go two-column where sensible
lg1024The sidebar becomes persistent. The layout stops being mobile.
xl1280Full 12-column layout; content container caps
2xl1440Gutters grow; content does not — never stretch a reading column

Design at 390, 768, 1440 and check 1920. Three frames per screen is the professional minimum; anything else is guessing.

Responsive strategies by component

ComponentStrategy
Data tablePrioritise columns → horizontal scroll with a frozen first column → cards. In that order.
Sidebar navPersistent → overlay drawer → bottom bar (3–5 items only)
ModalCentred dialog → bottom sheet → full-screen with an explicit close
Multi-column formCollapses to single column. Always. Two-column forms cause skipped fields even on desktop.
Dashboard grid4-up → 2-up → 1-up, with KPI cards first and charts below
ChartReduce series, drop gridlines, move the legend below, keep the value labels
Hover-only actionsBecome always-visible or move into an overflow menu — there is no hover on touch
TabsScrollable horizontally, with a fade edge indicating more
Container queries change the rule you learnedA card in a sidebar and the same card in the main column are the same viewport width but very different available widths. Container queries let a component respond to its own container rather than the screen — which is what you actually wanted all along. Design components with a narrow / medium / wide variant rather than a mobile / desktop one, and the same component works everywhere it's placed.

Touch, pointer and input

ConsiderationRule
Target size44 px minimum, achieved with padding not scaling — on desktop too, for imprecise pointers
Spacing between targetsAt least 8 px, so a mis-tap is not a wrong action
Thumb reachOn phones, primary actions sit in the lower third
HoverNever load-bearing. Everything reachable by hover is reachable another way.
Keyboard on mobileCorrect input types and autocomplete attributes; scroll the focused field into view
ZoomNever disable it. 200% text zoom must not cause horizontal scrolling.
Task · ~2 hrsThe three-frame pass Take every screen you've built in Weeks 6 and 7 and produce the 390 and 768 versions. For each, write the strategy you used from the table above. Then check: any hover-only action left? Any target under 44 px? Any two-column form? Any table that just got narrower instead of restructured? Fix them all.

Week 8 · Lesson 8.2

Accessibility that ships

Accessibility isn't a compliance checkbox — it's designing for the full range of human bodies and situations. It also makes everything better for everyone (captions, contrast, keyboard speed).

Watch

▶
WCAG 2.1 Crash Course

WCAG in one paragraph

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines organize success criteria under POUR: Perceivable (can they sense it — contrast, alt text, captions), Operable (can they use it — keyboard, targets, timing), Understandable (can they follow it — plain language, predictable behavior, clear errors), Robust (does it work with assistive tech). Levels A → AA → AAA; AA is the professional and legal standard you design to.

The designer's checklist (what YOU control)

  • Contrast: 4.5:1 body text, 3:1 large text and UI components (Week 4 — you already do this)
  • Color never carries meaning alone: icon+label on statuses, underline-on-hover isn't enough for in-text links
  • Visible focus states on every interactive element — design them, don't let the browser default get stripped
  • Logical tab/reading order noted in specs; keyboard path for every hover-revealed action
  • Touch/click targets ≥ 24×24px minimum, 44px comfortable on touch
  • Real labels on all form fields + specific error messages (Week 5 — already yours)
  • Alt-text intent written for meaningful images; decorative images marked decorative
  • Text resizes to 200% without breaking — another reason for rem-friendly type
  • Motion: no autoplaying carousels without pause; respect reduced-motion preferences for big animations
  • Heading hierarchy is semantic (one H1, ordered levels) — screen readers navigate by it

Make it real, this week

Unplug your mouse for ten minutes and Tab through a site you admire — feel what keyboard users feel. Run WAVE on any page and read its complaints. Then audit one of YOUR Week 6–7 screens against the checklist above and fix what fails. Accessibility learned by audit sticks; accessibility learned by reading evaporates.

Read

Guide
W3C WAI — Designing for Web Accessibility

The official designer-facing starting point.

Reference
WCAG.com — Resources for Designers

Criteria translated into design decisions.

The designer's WCAG shortlist

There are dozens of success criteria. These are the ones a designer owns — get these right and you've handled most of what an audit will find.

CriterionWhat it requiresYou control it by
1.1.1 Non-text contentImages have text alternativesWriting alt text in the spec, and marking decorative images
1.3.1 Info & relationshipsStructure is conveyed programmaticallyReal headings in order, real lists, real tables — specified as such
1.4.3 ContrastText 4.5:1; large text 3:1Your colour ramp — which is why d1.2 builds it from contrast targets
1.4.4 Resize text200% zoom without lossrem-based type, no fixed-height text containers
1.4.11 Non-text contrastUI components and graphics 3:1Input borders, icons, focus rings, chart elements — the most-missed criterion
1.4.12 Text spacingSurvives increased line height and letter spacingNot pinning text into exact-height containers
2.1.1 KeyboardEverything operable by keyboardDesigning the keyboard path, not just the mouse one
2.4.7 Focus visibleA visible focus indicatorDesigning the ring — and never removing it
2.4.11 Focus not obscuredThe focused element isn't hidden behind sticky chromeScroll offset under sticky headers
2.5.8 Target size24 × 24 px minimum (AA); 44 is the practical targetPadding on small controls
3.3.1 / 3.3.3 ErrorsErrors identified and suggestions offeredInline messages saying what's wrong and what valid looks like
3.3.2 LabelsEvery input has a persistent labelNever using a placeholder as the label
2.3.3 Animation from interactionsMotion can be disabledprefers-reduced-motion variants

The one-hour audit

StepDoFinds
1Tab through the whole page, slowlyMissing focus styles, illogical order, keyboard traps, unreachable controls
2Run WAVEMissing alt text, heading-order breaks, unlabelled inputs, contrast failures
3Zoom to 200%Horizontal scroll, clipped text, overlapping elements
4Turn on Reduce MotionAnimations that ignore it; content that never appears
5Greyscale the screenAnything where colour alone carries meaning
6Read it with a screen reader for five minutesEverything the automated tools cannot detect — which is roughly two-thirds of real issues
Why automated tools are only a third of the answerWAVE and Lighthouse catch missing alt text and contrast. They cannot tell you that your alt text says "image", that your tab order jumps around the page, that your modal doesn't trap focus, or that your error message says "invalid input". Those are design failures, and only a human pass finds them.

Designing for specific needs

UserDesign consequence
Low visionContrast, scalable text, no text in images, generous targets
Colour blindness (~1 in 12 men)Never colour alone; test in a deuteranopia simulator; chart palettes distinguishable in greyscale
Blind / screen-reader usersSemantic structure, meaningful alt text, labelled controls, announced state changes
Motor impairmentLarge targets, generous spacing, no precision drag as the only route, no time limits
Cognitive load / dyslexiaPlain language, consistent patterns, no unnecessary time pressure, clear error recovery
Vestibular disordersReduced motion honoured; no large parallax or auto-playing zoom
SituationalBright sunlight, one hand, a cracked screen, a noisy room. Everyone is temporarily disabled.
Task · ~2 hrsAudit your own work, then fix it Run the six-step audit on your Week 7 landing page and your Week 6 dashboard. Log every finding in a table: criterion, severity, fix. Then fix everything. Keep the log — a before/after accessibility audit is one of the most credible artefacts you can put in a portfolio, and almost nobody has one.

Week 8 · Lesson 8.3

Design systems, tokens & handoff

Everything you've built — type styles, color primitives + semantics, spacing scale, component kit — has been a design system growing in secret. Now formalize it and learn to hand it to engineers.

Watch

▶
Design System & Figma Variables Setup — Full Tutorial
Also useful: Build a Design System Ep.1 — Tokens & Variables.

The token pyramid

Primitives (indigo/600, space/4, radius/md) → semantic tokens (action/primary, text/secondary, bg/surface) → component tokens where needed (button/primary/bg). Components consume semantics, never raw values. In Figma this is Variables with modes: a light/dark mode pair on your semantic collection re-themes every screen instantly — the Week 4 promise, delivered.

What a shippable system contains

  • Foundations: color (primitives + semantic, both modes), the dual type scale, spacing scale, radius + elevation scales, grid definitions, icon set.
  • Components with variants covering real states — plus usage documentation: when to use, when not to, content rules ("buttons start with verbs"), a11y notes. Steal the documentation format from Polaris or Atlassian.
  • Patterns: the composed recipes — page header, settings section, table toolbar, empty state, dialog. Systems that stop at atoms leave the hard 50% undone.

Handoff that engineers respect

  • Name layers and components properly; use auto layout everywhere (it translates to flexbox nearly 1:1 — your padding/gap values ARE the spec).
  • Spec the invisible: hover/focus/loading states linked next to the default, responsive behavior per breakpoint ("sidebar → drawer below 1024"), motion (what animates, duration 150–250ms, easing), scroll behavior (what sticks), and every state of every flow (Week 6.3's five states).
  • Content edge cases in the file: longest name, empty avatar, 0 items, 12,847 items.
  • Sit in on implementation. The web designers engineers love are the ones who understand the box model, flexbox, and why "just move it 3px" isn't a thing. (Kevin Powell's channel keeps paying off here.)
Week 8 · Capstone

Capstone: a complete product, end to end

Two weeks (this week + one bonus week — real projects deserve it). One brief, executed completely. This becomes the centerpiece of your web portfolio.

Choose one brief

BriefProductStretch challenge
A — AI SaaS"Brieflow" — AI meeting-notes for agencies: records calls, drafts briefs, tracks decisionsDesign AI states: generating, confidence, human-review
B — Analytics SaaS"Northbeam" — subscription analytics for indie e-commerce brandsChart-heavy dashboard + a report builder
C — E-commerce"Terra" — direct-to-consumer specialty coffee with subscriptionsPLP/PDP/checkout + a subscriber account portal (SaaS patterns inside e-commerce!)
D — Content platform"Fieldnotes" — a magazine + membership site for design writingReading experience + paywall/membership flows

Required deliverables (any brief)

  • Mini design system: tokens (color/type/space/radius, light+dark), 10+ components, documented
  • Marketing site: landing page (full argument structure) + pricing page, at 1440 AND 390
  • Core flows: signup → onboarding → first value (prototyped); plus the niche's money flow (checkout for C, subscribe for D, invite-team for A/B)
  • 5+ app screens: the main workspace (dashboard/table/reader/store account), a record detail, settings, billing — with empty + loading + error states for the two most important screens
  • Responsive spec: the main app screen at tablet + phone, with transformation notes
  • A11y pass: contrast-checked palette, focus states, keyboard notes on one flow

Process (follow it, document it)

  1. Day 1 — Research: 5 competitor teardowns on Mobbin (conventions list + your one deviation), a one-page PRD: who, core job, 3 key flows.
  2. Days 2–3 — Foundations: tokens, type, grid, kit. Boring first = fast later.
  3. Days 4–8 — Screens & flows: wireframe → real components → states. Marketing site last (you'll know the product by then and the screenshots will be real).
  4. Days 9–10 — Polish & package: Refactoring UI pass (spacing, hierarchy, shadows), a11y audit, then a case-study page: problem → process → decisions with rationale → outcomes.
Portfolio framing for the job huntPresent it as decisions, not screens: "Chose desktop-first because…", "Tables use priority-columns because…". Hiring managers for web/SaaS roles screen for exactly this reasoning — your 6 years of mobile + this documented range (SaaS + one other niche) is a strong, honest story.

The capstone, scoped honestly

You now have three tracks' worth of artefacts. The capstone is not "design an app" — it is assemble and finish one product story, then write it up so it hires you.

PieceComes fromFinish it by
Design systemModule d1 practicePublishing the library and scoring it against audit-checklist.md
Marketing siteWeek 7 + module c1–c2Adding the argument structure, the signature move and the reduced-motion variant
Auth & onboardingWeek 7 practiceWriting every word, including the expired-link screen
Core product surfaceWeek 6 table + dashboardAll five states, three breakpoints, dark mode
Settings, billing, teamWeek 7 practiceThe limit-reached → upgrade sequence
Mobile companionModules x1 / x2Five screens, one platform done properly rather than two done thinly
A live artefactModule c4 practiceA real URL. This is what separates you from most portfolios.

The case-study structure that works

SectionLengthWhat goes in it
Hook1 screenThe best visual, plus one sentence on what this is and your role
Context1 screenWho it's for, what the constraint was, what success meant
The problem1–2 screensEvidence, not assertion — a teardown, a metric, a quote
Decisions3–5 screensThe heart of it. For each: the options, what you chose, why, and what it cost. Include a decision you got wrong.
The craft2–3 screensTokens, states, responsive, accessibility, motion spec. The evidence of rigour.
Outcome1 screenWhat shipped, what you'd change, what you learned. Numbers if you have them; honesty if you don't.
Why "decisions" is the section that gets you hiredReviewers can see that your screens look good from the first image. What they cannot see is whether you can think. The decisions section is the only part that demonstrates judgement — and it is the section most portfolios skip in favour of more screenshots. Three well-argued decisions beat twenty polished frames.

Portfolio assembly

RuleDetail
Three case studiesNot seven. Reviewers read two.
Lead with rangeOne product surface, one marketing/craft piece, one system. That trio says "I can do the whole job."
Show process selectivelyThe rejected direction and the thing that tested badly — not every wireframe
Real screens, readable sizeNo 12° floating device mockups
Your own site is a case studyIts load time, accessibility and craft are being judged whether you intend it or not
Write it as you goReconstructing your reasoning six months later never works

Final self-review across everything

CheckPass condition
TokensEvery colour, space and type value in every artefact traces to a semantic token
StatesEvery data surface has all five; every component has all nine
ResponsiveThree breakpoints for every screen, with a named strategy
AccessibilityThe six-step audit run and logged, with fixes
CopyZero lorem ipsum anywhere, including errors and empty states
MotionSpecified with numbers; reduced-motion variants exist
LiveAt least one artefact has a public URL that loads fast on mobile data
Case studiesThree, each with a real decisions section including one thing you got wrong
What you have at the endA published design system, a data-dense product surface with every state, a complete acquisition-to-expansion product story, a native mobile module, an award-rubric-scored craft piece, and a live site. That is not a portfolio of a designer transitioning to web — it is the portfolio of someone who already works there.
Week 8 · Final Exam

Final Exam

16 questions across all eight weeks. Pass at 75%. If you pass honestly, you're ready to call yourself a web designer.

Mobile · iOS Design 1

The iOS platform & HIG philosophy

You've designed mobile for years — this module re-grounds that instinct in Apple's own vocabulary, so your decisions cite the Human Interface Guidelines instead of habit.

In plain words (start here if this feels new)The HIG is Apple's rulebook: a free website explaining how iPhone apps are supposed to look and behave. Designers who follow it make apps that feel "right" to users on day one; designers who ignore it make apps that feel off in ways users can't name. This module walks the rulebook top-to-bottom — nothing here requires code, and every lesson ends in something you actually make.
Warm-up · 20 minBefore reading anything Open three apps on an iPhone (Settings, App Store, and any social app). Just observe and write five sentences: where is navigation? What happens when you tap a row? What slides up from the bottom? You'll recognize everything you wrote in the next five lessons — learning sticks better when you've seen the pattern first.

The three HIG values (everything derives from these)

ValueMeaningIn practice
ClarityLegible at every size; icons precise; functionality obviousDynamic Type respected, SF Symbols over custom glyphs, no mystery-meat controls
DeferenceUI serves content, never competes with itTranslucent bars, edge-to-edge content, chrome that recedes on scroll
DepthLayers and motion communicate hierarchySheets rise over context, push slides deeper, materials blur what's beneath

Units & screens — the numbers you design with

  • Points (pt), never pixels. 1pt = 2px on @2x devices, 3px on @3x. Design at 1x point dimensions; export assets @2x/@3x (or use vectors/SF Symbols and forget scales).
  • Reference frames: 393×852 (6.1" Pro class) is today's default artboard; also test 430×932 (Max) and 375×667 (SE, smallest supported).
  • Safe areas are law: content respects the status bar/Dynamic Island region (top ~59pt on Island devices) and the home-indicator region (bottom 34pt). Backgrounds may run edge-to-edge; touchable content may not.
  • Minimum touch target: 44×44pt — the most quoted rule in the HIG, and it still catches everyone's too-small icon buttons.

App anatomy

Almost every iOS app is one of a few archetypes: tab-based (3–5 top-level areas, the default), hierarchical (single drill-down stack — Settings), page-based (swipeable siblings — Weather), or single-view utility. Choose the archetype first; it dictates the navigation shell everything else lives in. The standard shell: status bar → navigation bar (large title collapsing to inline on scroll) → content → tab bar (49pt + home indicator).

Developer mindsetEngineers build these shells from UIKit/SwiftUI primitives — TabView, NavigationStack, List. When your design matches a system container, it costs hours; when it fights one, it costs weeks. Ask "which system container is this?" for every screen.

Read & watch

Canon
Human Interface Guidelines

The source of truth. Read "Designing for iOS" + "Layout" this lesson; the rest arrives module by module.

Guide
learnui.design — iOS Design Guidelines, illustrated

The HIG condensed into visual patterns with free templates — the best companion read.

Video
WWDC — Design foundations from idea to interface

Apple's designers walking through the reasoning, not just the rules.

Kit
Apple Design Resources (Figma)

Official component libraries and device templates — install now, you'll use them all module.

The units, once and for all

UnitWhat it isYou design in…
pt (point)The logical unit. 1 pt = 1 px at @1x.Points. Always. Your Figma frame is in points.
pxPhysical pixels on the panelNever — except when exporting assets
@2x / @3xScale factor. Most iPhones are @3x; some are @2x.Export raster assets at both. Vectors (SF Symbols, SVG) sidestep this entirely.

Practical consequence: design at 393 × 852 (the current standard iPhone logical size) and everything you draw is in points. A 44 pt tap target is 132 physical pixels on an @3x device — you never need to think about that number again.

Screen anatomy — the regions you must respect

RegionHeightRule
Status bar~54 pt (Dynamic Island devices)Never place content under it. It can turn green/red for calls and recording.
Dynamic IslandSits inside the top safe areaContent routes around it; Live Activities expand from it
Navigation bar44 pt (+ ~52 pt for a large title)Standard. Don't rebuild it.
ContentEverything left16 pt side margins compact, 20 pt regular
Tab bar49 ptPlus the home-indicator inset
Home indicator34 ptNo tap targets here. A swipe up will fire instead of your button.
Safe areas are not marginsA margin is your aesthetic choice; a safe area is a hardware fact. Background colours and images should extend through the safe area to the screen edge — content and controls must not. Getting this backwards is the fastest way to make an app look non-native.

App archetypes — pick one before you draw

ArchetypeStructureExamplesChoose when
Flat / tabbed3–5 peer sections in a tab barApple TV, Cleo, most appsSections are independent and equally important
HierarchicalDrill down through a nav stackSettings, Mail, FilesContent nests naturally
Content-drivenThe content is the navigationPhotos, Books, MusicBrowsing beats searching
Single-taskOne screen, one jobCamera, Compass, a timerAny structure would be overhead
Document-basedBrowser → document → editorCraft, Pages, NotesUsers create and return to artefacts

Most real apps combine two: a tab bar (flat) whose tabs each contain a nav stack (hierarchical). That combination is the iOS default for a reason — decide which of your sections are peers before anything else.

The HIG's actual principles

PrincipleWhat it means in practice
DeferenceThe UI gets out of the way of content. Chrome is thin, translucent, and shrinks on scroll.
ClarityLegibility at every size, meaning carried by type weight and colour rather than by boxes and borders
DepthLayers and motion tell you where you are and where things came from
ConsistencyUse the system component. A custom switch costs you familiarity and buys you nothing.
FeedbackEvery action gets a visible or haptic response within 100 ms
User controlThe user initiates and can cancel. No irreversible action without a way back.
In plain wordsiOS design is mostly subtraction. The platform already supplies navigation, typography, colour, controls and motion. Your job is to add your content, your one accent colour, and the two or three components the system doesn't have. Designers coming from web often add far too much — borders, custom buttons, extra chrome — and the result feels foreign in a way users notice but can't name.

What's changed recently, and why it matters

iOS chrome has been moving toward floating, translucent, rounded elements layered over content rather than opaque bars attached to screen edges. You can see it in the tab bars below: a pill floating above the content, with the content visibly passing beneath. Design consequence: your content must remain legible under translucent chrome, so extend scroll content behind the bar and add bottom padding equal to the bar height plus the safe-area inset. If you design bars as opaque blocks sitting on top of a shorter content area, your app will look a generation old.

Apple TV — floating translucent tab barApple's own current chrome: a floating pill with a separate search affordance, content passing beneath. Craft — document-based appBrowser screen of a document app, with a floating tab bar and a separate + action. Cleo — flat/tabbed with heavy brandingFive tabs, custom type, one accent. Brand carried by typography and colour, not by rebuilt controls.
Warm-up · ~30 minName the archetype Open five apps on your phone. For each, write down: the archetype from the table above, the number of tabs, and whether the chrome is opaque or translucent. Then find one app that picked the wrong archetype — a hierarchical structure forced into tabs, or five tabs where two would do. There is always one.

Mobile · iOS Design 2

Navigation, modality & structure

iOS navigation is a small set of containers with strict rules. Master when each applies and your apps feel native by default.

The navigation containers

ContainerRules
Tab bar3–5 tabs, always visible peers, never hides mid-app, filled/outline SF Symbol + label. Never use it as actions ("Create" as a tab is a smell — unless it opens modally, like Instagram).
Navigation stackHierarchical drill-down: push slides in from the right, back chevron top-left + edge-swipe back (never break the swipe!). Large title → inline on scroll.
Modal sheetSelf-contained tasks that interrupt: compose, filters, settings-of-a-thing. Page sheet with visible parent behind; grabber + detents (medium/large) for resizable sheets; Cancel left, Done/Save right.
Full-screen coverImmersive tasks only: camera, video, onboarding. Needs an explicit close affordance.

Modality: the decision that defines iOS feel

Push = "going deeper into the same journey". Sheet = "a separate task on top". The classic test: if the user should be able to navigate elsewhere mid-task, push; if the task must complete or cancel, sheet. Sheets stack visually (parent recedes) — but never stack more than necessary, and never present a sheet from a sheet when a push inside the sheet's own nav stack would do.

Transient surfaces

  • Alert — critical interruptions only; 2 buttons ideal; destructive action in red; never for confirmations of reversible actions.
  • Action sheet — a choice among actions on something ("Share / Duplicate / Delete"), slides from bottom, Cancel isolated at the bottom.
  • Context menu — long-press on content for secondary actions + preview. iOS's right-click; design one for every content object.
  • Search — lives in the nav bar, expands on tap, with scoped tokens/suggestions; pull-down-to-reveal on lists is standard.

Study these on Mobbin

Apple Store — canonical tab shellLarge title, content-first, floating tab bar + search Notion — actions sheetSelf-contained task surface over dimmed parent

Navigation components — what each one is actually for

ComponentJobRules
Tab barSwitch between peer sections3–5 tabs. Persistent — never hide it inside a tab's own stack. Tapping the active tab scrolls to top; tapping again pops to root.
Navigation stackDrill into detailBack button is titled with the previous screen. Edge-swipe-back must work — if you disable it, users will feel trapped without knowing why.
Large titleAnnounce a top-level screenCollapses to the standard 44 pt bar on scroll. Only on root screens.
ToolbarActions for the current screenBottom of the screen. Not navigation — actions.
SearchFind within the sectionLives in the nav bar, revealed by pulling down, or as a dedicated tab if search is the product
Segmented controlFilter the same content2–4 segments. Not a tab bar substitute — the content type must stay the same.
SidebarMany sections, iPad and largerCollapses to a tab bar on iPhone

Modality — the decision table

PatternUse whenDismissNever
Sheet (medium detent)A short task where the screen behind still matters — pick a filter, confirm detailsSwipe down, tap outside, explicit CancelFor destructive confirmation — too easy to dismiss accidentally
Sheet (large detent)A form or flow of 1–3 screensSwipe down + Cancel/Done in the sheet's own nav barFor content that deserves a URL or a back-stack position
Full-screen coverImmersive or multi-step work — camera, editor, onboardingExplicit Done/Cancel onlyFor anything under three steps
AlertDestructive confirmation or a genuine blockerA button, alwaysFor information you could have shown inline. Alerts are expensive.
Action sheet2–5 choices arising from a specific actionCancelAs a menu of unrelated features
Context menu (long press)Secondary actions on an object, with a previewTap awayAs the only route to an action — it's undiscoverable
PopoveriPad: contextual controls anchored to a sourceTap outsideOn iPhone, where it becomes a sheet anyway
Detents are a design decision, not a defaultA sheet with [.medium, .large] lets the user choose how much context to trade away — and it's why maps and ride-hailing apps feel so fluid. Specify which detents each sheet supports, which one it opens at, whether the grabber is visible, and whether the background dims. Four small decisions that change the whole feel.

Back, cancel and the modal contract

  • Push = "deeper into the same thing." Back is in the top-left, titled, and edge-swipeable.
  • Present = "a separate task." It gets Cancel (left) and Done/Save (right) — never a back arrow.
  • If the user has typed something and swipes to dismiss, show a confirmation action sheet. Silently discarding input is the most-reported iOS bug in usability tests.
  • Never nest a modal inside a modal inside a modal. Two levels is the practical ceiling.

Study these

Strava — small detent over a mapThe map stays the context. A sheet here, not a screen push — because the map is the point. Fi — picker in a sheetThree options as image radios in a short sheet. An action sheet would have been worse: the choice is visual. inDrive — sheet skeletonEven the sheet has a loading state at the correct final height. Note the grabber. Apple TV — tabs + separate searchSearch gets its own affordance rather than a fifth tab. Study that trade.
Task · ~45 minThe modality log For one day, note every modal presentation you encounter on your phone: what kind, what triggered it, how you dismissed it. At the end, mark each as correct or wrong against the decision table. You will find at least two alerts that should have been inline messages, and one full-screen cover that should have been a sheet.
