Mobile · iOS Design 3

Components, controls & haptics

iOS ships a deep standard kit. Using it correctly — sizes, symbols, list styles, feedback — is 80% of looking native.

SF Symbols — your icon system, solved

6,000+ glyphs that align to SF Pro's metrics, scale with Dynamic Type, come in 9 weights × 3 scales, and support monochrome/hierarchical/palette/multicolor rendering. Rules: match symbol weight to adjacent text weight; use fill variants for selected tab items and toggled states; don't redraw what a symbol already expresses. Download the SF Symbols app and browse before you ever draw an icon.

Lists — where iOS apps actually live

StyleLookUse
PlainFull-width rows, sticky headers possibleContent collections (Mail, Music)
Grouped / Inset-groupedRounded cards on gray background (the modern default)Settings, forms, detail pages

Row anatomy: leading icon (optional, 29pt tile), title (17pt), value/detail text (gray), trailing accessory — chevron (navigates), switch (toggles), detail button. Standard row height 44pt+; swipe actions for quick operations (leading = positive, trailing = destructive at the far edge); pull-to-refresh on content lists.

Controls cheat-sheet

  • Buttons: sizes S/M/L; styles plain, gray, tinted (soft fill), filled (primary). One filled per view — the same "one hero action" rule the web track taught.
  • Switch for instant setting toggles (in list rows), checkmarks for selection lists, segmented control for 2–5 exclusive views, stepper/slider for values, pickers — wheel (dates in sheets), menu picker inline in rows.
  • Text fields: 17pt, clear button while editing, appropriate keyboard type per field (email/number/URL) — specify keyboards in your handoff; devs must set them.
  • Haptics pair with meaning: success/warning/error notifications, selection ticks in pickers, impact on drag-drop. Design docs should note haptic moments — engineers won't invent them.

Study on Mobbin

Wispr Flow — inset-grouped settingsSection headers, toggles, helper text under titles Quizlet — action sheetObject actions, Cancel isolated at bottom

Lists — the workhorse of iOS

StyleLooks likeUse for
Inset groupedRounded cards floating on a tinted canvasSettings, profiles, forms — anything with labelled sections
GroupedFull-width sections with headersOlder style; still fine for dense data
PlainEdge-to-edge rows, optional sticky section headersLong homogeneous lists — mail, messages, contacts
SidebarSelectable rows with a highlightiPad navigation

Row anatomy: leading element (icon, avatar, SF Symbol) → label (+ optional secondary line) → trailing element (value, switch, chevron, badge). A chevron promises a push. If tapping the row opens a sheet or toggles something, don't show one — that single mismatch causes more mis-taps than any other list error.

MetricValue
Row height — single line44 pt minimum
Row height — two line~60 pt
Row height — with avatar~72 pt
Inset grouped side margin20 pt
Separator insetAligned to the label, not the screen edge, when there's a leading icon

Swipe actions — power without discoverability

DecisionGuidance
How manyMax 2 per side. Three is unhittable at speed.
Full swipeTriggers the first action on that side. Make sure that action is the safe one, or the common one — never Delete on the leading edge.
ColourDestructive = system red. Everything else uses your tint or a system semantic colour.
LabelIcon + word where the row height allows. Icon alone is a guess.
DuplicationEvery swipe action must also exist somewhere visible — a context menu or a detail screen. Swipe is a shortcut, never the only path.
UndoDestructive swipes need undo. A toast with Undo beats a confirmation alert on every metric.

Controls, and when each is right

ControlUse whenTrap
Button — filledThe one primary actionMore than one filled button per view
Button — tintedSecondary but still prominentUsing it for destructive actions
Button — gray / plainTertiary, toolbars, cancelPlain buttons that look like labels
SwitchImmediate on/offPutting one in a form with a Save button
Segmented control2–4 views of the same contentUsing it as navigation
StepperSmall integer adjustmentsRanges over ~10 — use a field or picker
SliderContinuous, imprecise valuesAnything needing an exact number
Picker / wheelOne of many, in a sheetUnder 5 options — use a menu
Menu (pull-down)Choosing an option or an action, from a buttonMore than ~8 items
Text fieldFree inputWrong keyboard type; missing content-type hints for autofill

Haptics — pair them or they're noise

FeedbackFire on
SelectionPicker tick, segment change, snapping to a value
Impact — light / medium / heavySomething lands, attaches, or is picked up. Weight should match the visual weight.
Notification — success / warning / errorThe outcome of an operation, not the tap that started it

Two rules: haptics accompany a visual change, never replace one; and never fire one on every tap. A phone that buzzes constantly gets its haptics turned off, and then your important ones are gone too.

SF Symbols in practice

Match symbol weight to the adjacent text weight, pick one rendering mode per surface, and prefer a symbol over a custom icon wherever one exists — 6,000+ of them do. Symbols scale with Dynamic Type automatically, which custom icons do not. When you must draw a custom icon, match the stroke weight and optical size of the symbols beside it or it will read as a foreign object.

Study these

Spark Mail — swipe actions, configurableFour swipe slots, each user-assignable. Note the coloured icon previews — teaching by showing. X — destructive swipeRed, full-width, labelled. And the action exists elsewhere too. TextNow — non-destructive swipeSame mechanic, safe action. Compare the colour choice to X's. Todoist — inset grouped rowsSwitches, value rows and chevrons in one screen. Every trailing element promises the right thing.
Task · ~60 minThe chevron audit Screenshot ten list screens across five apps. For every row with a chevron, tap it and record what actually happened — push, sheet, external link, or nothing. Then do the reverse: find rows that push but show no chevron. This mismatch is everywhere, and once you can see it you will never ship it.

Mobile · iOS Design 4

Typography, color & dark mode

On iOS you don't pick sizes and hexes — you pick semantic styles the system already tuned. This is the deepest mindset shift from web design.

In plain wordsInstead of saying "make this text 17px dark gray", iOS designers say "this is Body text, secondary color". The phone then decides the exact pixels — bigger if the user chose large text in accessibility settings, lighter or darker depending on light/dark mode. You design with names, the system handles numbers. Weird for two days, then liberating forever.

Dynamic Type — the eleven text styles

StyleDefault (Large)Typical use
Large Title34pt BoldNav bar expanded title
Title 1 / 2 / 328 / 22 / 20ptSection headings by rank
Headline17pt SemiboldRow titles, emphasis body
Body17pt RegularThe reading default
Callout / Subheadline16 / 15ptSupporting content
Footnote13ptMetadata, timestamps
Caption 1 / 212 / 11ptLabels, image captions

Every style scales automatically with the user's accessibility text size — design your layouts to survive at least one size up. Fonts: SF Pro (Text ≤19pt, Display ≥20pt — the system swaps optical sizes for you), SF Compact (watch), New York (serif companion), SF Mono. Custom brand fonts are fine for display moments; body text in a custom font must still honor Dynamic Type.

Semantic color — name the role, not the hex

  • Label hierarchy: label, secondaryLabel, tertiaryLabel, quaternaryLabel — your four text grays, pre-tuned for both appearances.
  • Backgrounds: systemBackground + secondary/tertiary; the grouped variants for inset-list screens. Fills (systemFill…) for control backgrounds; separator for hairlines.
  • Tint color: ONE accent drives the whole app's interactive color (links, buttons, selected tabs). Your brand color = your tint. System palette (systemBlue, systemRed…) auto-adjusts per appearance.
  • Materials: ultraThin→thick blur materials + vibrancy for text over them — how iOS gets its layered glass look. Use materials for bars/overlays instead of flat translucent fills.

Dark mode, the iOS way

Not inverted, not neutral-flipped: dark mode uses elevated surfaces — base black (systemBackground) with lighter elevated layers for sheets/cards; semantic colors handle 90% automatically. Never hardcode white/black; audit any custom color for both appearances plus Increase Contrast. If you adopted semantic tokens, dark mode is nearly free — exactly the token lesson from the web track, enforced at OS level.

See both appearances side by side

Wispr Flow — light appearanceGrouped backgrounds, secondary text, one big stat Phantom — dark appearanceElevated card groups on near-black, not gray-on-gray
Mini-practice · 30 minName everything Screenshot any app screen from your phone into Figma. Label every piece of text with your best-guess Dynamic Type style name, and every color with its semantic role (label? secondaryLabel? systemGroupedBackground? tint?). Doing this three times makes the vocabulary automatic.
Developer mindsetSwiftUI code reads .font(.headline) and .foregroundStyle(.secondary) — no numbers anywhere. Hand off in those names: "Footnote / secondaryLabel" is implementable in seconds; "13px #8E8E93" forces the dev to reverse-engineer your intent.

Applying the type system (the reference lives in module d3)

Module d3 · iOS Design System carries the full Dynamic Type and semantic-colour tables. This lesson is about using them under pressure. Three habits do most of the work:

HabitWhy
Say the style name out loud when you place text"This is a Headline" forces a hierarchy decision. "This is 17 semibold" doesn't.
Use weight before sizeHeadline and Body are the same size — only the weight differs. That's how iOS separates a row title from its detail without adding a size step.
Cap yourself at four levels per screenTitle, Headline, Body, Footnote. If you need a fifth, the screen is doing two jobs.

The accessibility-size stress test

SettingWhat breaks firstThe fix
Large (default)——
xxxLargeTwo-column rows collideReduce trailing content; allow the label to wrap
AX3Label/value rows must stack verticallyDesign the stacked variant explicitly
AX5Tab bar labels disappear; buttons wrap to 3 linesAccept the system's behaviour; make sure icons still identify the tabs

Design two variants of any row containing a label and a value: horizontal at default sizes, vertical at accessibility sizes. This is roughly ten minutes of work per component and it's the difference between an app that degrades gracefully and one that truncates its own content.

Colour, applied

SituationDo
Choosing a tintVerify it at 4.5:1 against systemBackground in light and dark. Most brand colours need a lighter dark-mode sibling.
Text on your tintCheck the filled-button case: label on tint must clear 4.5:1
Status and stateSystem red/green/orange — users already know them. Custom semantic colours cost recognition.
BackgroundsPick the standard or grouped family per screen and never mix
Dividersseparator, not a hand-picked grey. It adapts to contrast settings.
Anything decorativeAsk whether it survives Increase Contrast. If it vanishes, it was carrying meaning it shouldn't have.

Dark mode, in practice

  • Elevation is lightness. A sheet over a screen is a lighter grey, not the same grey with a shadow. This is why hard-coded darks break: the OS wants to elevate that surface and a literal value refuses.
  • Desaturate. A colour tuned for white will vibrate on near-black. Drop saturation and raise lightness — the same 600→400 move as the web kit.
  • Images need work too. Photos usually survive; illustrations and screenshots with white backgrounds punch holes in a dark screen. Supply dark variants or a subdued container.
  • Pure black is a watch thing, not an iPhone thing. iOS dark backgrounds are very dark greys so elevation has somewhere to go.

Materials

Blur belongs to chrome floating over content — nav bars, tab bars, sheets — and always with vibrancy label styles so text remains legible over whatever passes beneath. Two failure modes to check every time: text over a busy photo (raise the material thickness or add a scrim), and Reduce Transparency turned on, which makes materials opaque and can leave your carefully balanced layout looking flat and wrong.

Study these

Apple Fitness — Apple's own dark disciplineOne accent green; everything else neutral. Note the elevated card greys. Calm — material over imageryChrome floating over photography, with vibrancy carrying the labels. KOHO — high-chroma accent on darkA bright lime CTA on near-black. Measure it — this sits at the edge of comfortable. Apple TV — translucency over full-bleed artContent passes under the tab bar. This only works because the material is doing real work.
Task · ~75 minFour states of one screen Take any screen you've designed. Produce it four times: default light, default dark, AX3 light, and Increase Contrast dark. Fix every break. Then write down which fixes were structural (a row had to stack) versus cosmetic (a colour had to shift) — the structural ones are the reason you do this before, not after.

Mobile · iOS Design 5

Layout, adaptivity & iPad

One design, many rectangles: five phone widths, landscape, iPad splits, and whatever ships next autumn.

Layout constants worth memorizing

ThingValue
Default layout margins16pt (compact) / 20pt (regular+)
Spacing rhythm8pt system: 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 20 / 24 / 32
Nav bar / tab bar heights44pt inline (96+ w/ large title) / 49pt + home indicator
List row minimum44pt
Corner radius feelContinuous curves ("squircle") — use Figma corner smoothing ~60%

Adaptivity model

  • Size classes, not devices: compact vs regular width/height. iPhone portrait = compact width; iPhone landscape (Max) and iPad = regular width → layouts respond to class, not model names.
  • Stretch rules: decide per element — text columns cap (~640pt readable width even on iPad), lists stretch, grids add columns, split view appears (sidebar + detail) at regular width.
  • iPad specifics: sidebars replace tab bars for big apps, popovers replace sheets for small tasks, pointer/keyboard support, Stage Manager arbitrary window sizes — design min-width behavior.
  • Landscape on phone: mostly = shorter compact layout; media apps go immersive. Don't ignore it; QA at 667×375.

Deliverables convention for iOS handoff

Frames at 393×852 for flows + one 430 and one 375 stress test per template; annotate with text-style names, semantic color names, SF Symbol names + weight/scale, spacing in pt, and modality of every surface (push/sheet/full-screen/alert). That vocabulary alone marks you as a designer engineers trust.

Device metrics you'll actually use

ClassLogical size (pt)Design at
iPhone standard393 × 852Your default frame
iPhone Pro Max / Plus430 × 932Check that content doesn't just stretch — use the extra height for more content, not more padding
iPhone mini / SE-class375 × 667–812The stress test. If it works here it works everywhere.
iPad portrait~820 × 1180Regular width — sidebars and popovers become available
iPad landscape~1180 × 820Split view; your app may occupy a third of this
Design the small one firstDesigning at 430 and scaling down guarantees a cramped 375. Designing at 393 and checking 375 gives you a layout that simply gets more comfortable on bigger devices. Always draw the constrained case first — this is the same lesson as mobile-first on web, and designers keep relearning it.

Size classes — the two words that drive adaptivity

ContextHorizontalVerticalWhat you get
iPhone portraitCompactRegularSingle column, tab bar, sheets
iPhone landscape (most)CompactCompactStill single column; nav bar shrinks
iPhone Max landscapeRegularCompactSplit views become possible
iPad full screenRegularRegularSidebar, popovers, multi-column
iPad Slide Over / 1/3 splitCompactRegularYour iPhone layout, on an iPad. This is the case everyone forgets.

Design decisions bind to the size class, not the device. "Show the sidebar on iPad" is wrong; "show the sidebar at regular width" is right — and it automatically does the correct thing when the user drags your app into a third of the screen.

Layout mechanics

MetricCompactRegular
Side margin16 pt20 pt
Inset grouped list margin20 pt20 pt (content column caps)
Reading widthFullCapped — text should not run 1000 pt wide on iPad
Grid columns1–23–4, or list-detail
Minimum tap target44 × 44 pt44 × 44 pt

Landscape and orientation

  • Support landscape unless there's a real reason not to — video, reading and forms all benefit, and locking it out is an accessibility issue for users with mounted devices.
  • In compact-height landscape, vertical space is scarce: shrink the nav bar, hide large titles, and consider moving primary actions to a trailing column rather than stacking.
  • The keyboard eats roughly half the screen in landscape. Every form needs a scroll-to-focused-field behaviour and a way to dismiss.

iPad patterns worth knowing

PatternWhat it isDesign note
Sidebar + detailNavigation column plus contentThe default iPad structure. Collapses to a tab bar or a push stack on iPhone.
Three-columnSidebar → list → detailMail and Notes. Only when the hierarchy genuinely has three levels.
PopoverAnchored floating panelBecomes a sheet at compact width automatically — design both
MultitaskingSplit View, Slide Over, Stage ManagerYour app may be any width at any time. Test at a third-width.
Pointer & keyboardTrackpad hover, ⌘ shortcutsiPad is a hover-and-keyboard platform now. Add hover states and the obvious shortcuts.
Drag and dropBetween appsCheap to support, delightful when present
Task · ~90 minOne screen, four contexts Take your main screen and lay it out at: iPhone 393 portrait, iPhone 375 portrait, iPhone landscape, and iPad regular width. Then the one everyone skips — iPad Slide Over at compact width. Annotate what changed at each and, more importantly, what didn't: the pieces that stayed identical are your real components.

Mobile · iOS Design · Practice

Practice: iOS teardown & rebuild

Same method as the web track: copy the natives until their decisions are your defaults.

Task 1 · ~90 minHIG-vocabulary teardown Pick these two Mobbin screens plus any two apps on your own phone. For each screen, write the native inventory: archetype, nav container, list style, text styles used (guess the Dynamic Type names), semantic colors, symbols vs custom icons, modality of every surface it can open. Wrong guesses welcome — check against the HIG after.
Life Reset — feed + tab bar Phantom — dark-mode grouped settings
Task 2 · ~60 minPattern studies: forms & onboarding Two beginner-critical patterns, straight from Mobbin. For each pair: annotate keyboard type, field anatomy (label? placeholder? floating?), button placement relative to the keyboard, and how onboarding pages communicate progress.
Cuvva — one-field signupEmail keyboard, button above the fold Quizlet — multi-field account formField order, segmented choice, legal text Grab — illustrated onboardingOne idea per page, single CTA Matter — dark onboarding with page dotsProgress dots, primary + secondary CTA pair
Task 3 · ~2.5 hrsRebuild with Apple Design Resources Using the official Figma kit only (no detached components): rebuild your Week-6 SaaS product as a 5-screen iOS app — tab shell, a list screen (inset-grouped), a detail push, a compose sheet with detents, and a settings screen. Both appearances (light + dark via semantic styles). Explore more references on Mobbin's iOS library as you go.
DeliverableTeardown notes + a 5-screen native iOS flow in both appearances, built from unmodified system components.

Rebuild brief — five screens, in this order

#ScreenMust contain
1Tab shell + root listTab bar (3–5 items, SF Symbols), large title collapsing on scroll, plain or inset-grouped list, at least one swipe action, correct separator insets
2Detail (pushed)Titled back button, hero content, at least two Dynamic Type styles, a toolbar or nav-bar action
3SheetMedium detent with grabber, a form using system controls, Cancel/Done, the unsaved-changes confirmation
4SettingsInset grouped, switches with section footers explaining them, one value row with a chevron and one without
5Empty / first runTeaching copy, one primary action, an SF Symbol or illustration

Then the same five in dark mode, and screen 1 at AX3. Twelve frames total. That is a complete, honest iOS case study — most portfolios show three.

Self-review checklist

CheckPass condition
UnitsEverything in points; frame is 393 × 852
Safe areasBackgrounds extend to the edge; no control within 34 pt of the bottom
TypeEvery text layer is a named Dynamic Type style, not a manual size
ColourOnly semantic colours plus one tint; no hand-picked greys
BackgroundsOne family per screen — standard or grouped, never both
ChevronsPresent only where the row pushes
TargetsNothing interactive under 44 × 44 pt
ModalitySheet has Cancel/Done, not a back arrow
Swipe actionsMax 2 per side, and each exists elsewhere too
IconsSF Symbols, weight matched to adjacent text
Dark modeAchieved by swapping semantic colours only — nothing hand-adjusted
AX3Label/value rows stack; nothing essential truncated

Reference set for the rebuild

Screen 1 reference — CleoTab shell with strong branding. Note how the brand lives in type and colour, not in rebuilt controls. Screen 1 alternative — CraftSectioned list under a floating tab bar, with a separate + action. Screen 3 reference — StravaMedium detent, grabber, explicit close. Simple and correct. Screen 4 reference — Wispr FlowGrouped sections with footers doing real explanatory work. Swipe reference — Spark MailFour configurable slots, previewed visually. Dark-mode reference — Apple FitnessApple's own restraint. Match this level of colour discipline.

The teardown, before you build

Task 0 · ~60 minInventory one app in platform vocabulary Pick one well-made iOS app. For five of its screens, write the inventory using only platform words: which navigation component, which presentation style, which list style, which Dynamic Type styles, which semantic colours, which controls, where haptics fire. No adjectives — no "clean", no "modern". If you cannot name a thing in platform vocabulary, that is precisely the gap to go and read about before you build.
Then do the cross-platform memoAfter the Android module you'll rebuild these same five screens in Material. Keep this file — the side-by-side is the single most valuable artefact in the mobile track, and it's what makes you credible in a cross-platform interview.

Reference

Mobile · Android Design 1

Material philosophy: M2 → M3 → You

Material is the most documented design system on earth. Understand its arc — paper metaphor → tonal personalization — and every M3 decision becomes predictable.

In plain wordsMaterial Design is Google's rulebook — the Android sibling of Apple's HIG, but far more prescriptive: it names every color, size and corner radius for you. That makes it the EASIEST platform to learn systematically: when in doubt, the answer is literally written on m3.material.io. This module teaches you to read that site fluently; the design-system track later teaches you to bend it to a brand.

The eras in one table

EraCore ideaTells
Material 1/2 (2014–2021)Digital paper: surfaces with physical elevationDrop shadows for depth, 4dp FAB shadows, purple-teal defaults, sharp-ish corners
Material 3 (2021+)Personal: color from the user, depth from toneTonal surfaces instead of shadows, big rounded corners, pill buttons, dynamic color from wallpaper ("Material You")
M3 Expressive (2025)Emotional range on M3's systemSpringier motion, bolder shapes/type allowed within the token system

You'll still meet M2 in older products — read m2.material.io for maintenance work — but design new things in M3: m3.material.io is your canon for this module.

Units & platform anatomy

  • dp (density-independent pixels) for everything spatial, sp for type (scales with user font size — the Android sibling of Dynamic Type). 1dp = 1px @ mdpi, ×1.5/2/3/4 at hdpi→xxxhdpi. Reference frame: 412×917dp (Pixel class); test 360dp width (compact baseline).
  • System UI: status bar + gesture navigation area; modern apps draw edge-to-edge behind both, insetting content. The back gesture comes from EITHER screen edge — never hang critical swipe interactions off screen edges.
  • Predictive back: the back gesture previews where you'll land — screens need defined back destinations.
  • Minimum touch target: 48×48dp (with ≥8dp between targets).

The three eras, and why you need to recognise all of them

EraMental modelTells
M1 (2014)Digital paper. Ink, shadows, physics.Heavy drop shadows, a circular FAB on everything, bold single-hue app bars
M2 (2018)Paper plus brand. Theming arrives.Primary/secondary colour pair, elevation in dp, outlined text fields, bottom nav with 3–5 items
M3 (2021→)Roles and tones. Personal, adaptive.Tonal surfaces instead of shadows, pill-shaped buttons, dynamic colour, larger corner radii, the nav indicator pill
M3 Expressive (recent)Emphasis and motion as first-classMore shape and size contrast, springier motion, bolder emphasis hierarchy

You will meet all three in the wild — a 2019 codebase is M2 and will stay M2 for years. Being able to name the era in a screenshot tells you which rules apply, and stops you from "fixing" an M2 app into an inconsistent hybrid.

Android's units

UnitUse forNote
dpEvery dimension — spacing, sizes, radiiDensity-independent pixel. 1 dp = 1 px at mdpi (160 dpi).
spText onlyScales with the user's font-size setting. Text set in dp ignores accessibility preferences.
Density bucketsAsset exportmdpi 1× · hdpi 1.5× · xhdpi 2× · xxhdpi 3× · xxxhdpi 4×. Vectors avoid the whole problem.

Design frame: 412 × 917 dp is the current common phone. Same discipline as iOS — you draw in the logical unit and never think about physical pixels again.

Edge-to-edge and gesture navigation

  • Modern Android apps draw behind the status and navigation bars. Your background reaches the physical edge; your content respects insets.
  • The gesture nav bar is a thin handle at the bottom. Keep interactive elements clear of it, and remember the left and right edges are back-gesture zones — a horizontal swipe control placed at the screen edge will fight the system and lose.
  • Predictive back shows a preview of where back will take you as you drag. Design what the user sees during that drag: the previous screen, scaled and revealed.
  • Status-bar icons must contrast with whatever is behind them — that's a design decision (light or dark icons), stated per screen.

The philosophical difference from iOS, stated plainly

iOSAndroid / M3
Brand expressionOne tint on a fixed systemA seed colour generating a whole scheme — or the user's wallpaper replacing it
ElevationLayers and materialsSurface tone
Component philosophyUse the system componentTheme the system component
HardwareA handful of sizesThousands of devices, plus foldables
BackTop-left, per appA system gesture, everywhere, always
MotionInterruptible springsToken-defined easing and duration
In plain wordsiOS asks you to subtract until only your content and one accent remain. Material asks you to configure — pick a seed colour, pick shape and type overrides, and let the system generate a coherent, accessible scheme from them. iOS design is restraint; Material design is parameterisation. Neither is better; using one platform's habits on the other is what looks wrong.
Warm-up · ~30 minDate the screenshot Open Mobbin's Android library and pick ten apps. For each, name the era — M2 or M3 — and cite the evidence: button shape, elevation treatment, nav component, colour-role usage. You'll find plenty of hybrids; note what makes them read as inconsistent.

Mobile · Android Design 2

Android navigation & app structure

Material's navigation kit is richer than iOS's — which makes choosing correctly matter more.

Primary navigation

ComponentWhenRules
Navigation bar (bottom)3–5 top destinations, phonesActive pill indicator, icon+label, 80dp tall; the M3 evolution of M2's "bottom nav"
Navigation railSame destinations on tablets/foldablesLeft vertical strip; pairs with bigger canvases
Navigation drawer6+ destinations or account/workspace switchingModal on phones; standard (pinned) on large screens
TabsSibling views WITHIN a screenPrimary (with indicator) or secondary; swipeable content

Screen furniture

  • Top app bar: four sizes (center-aligned, small, medium, large). Large collapses to small on scroll — Material's counterpart to iOS large titles. Actions right, contextual overflow menu last.
  • FAB: THE distinctly-Android element — one primary creative action floating above content (Compose, New event). Sizes small/regular/large + extended (with label). Don't use it as "the only way" to a feature and don't ship more than one.
  • Dialogs vs bottom sheets: dialogs for focused decisions (M3: 28dp radius, tonal surface); modal bottom sheets for action lists and light tasks (thumb-friendlier — Android leans sheet where iOS leans action sheet); standard bottom sheets persist (music player queue).
  • Snackbar: transient feedback + optional single action ("Undo") — Android's toast, but designed.
Developer mindsetCompose engineers assemble screens from Scaffold slots: topBar, bottomBar, floatingActionButton, snackbarHost, content. Design in those slots and your spec maps 1:1 to the code skeleton.

Navigation components by window size

ComponentWindow classItemsNotes
Navigation bar (bottom)Compact3–5The iOS tab-bar equivalent. Active item gets a pill indicator behind the icon — that pill is the M3 tell.
Navigation railMedium+3–7Vertical strip on the leading edge. Can host a FAB at the top.
Navigation drawer — modalCompactManySlides over content with a scrim. Secondary destinations only.
Navigation drawer — standardExpandedManyPermanently visible beside content
Top app barAll—Four sizes: small (64 dp), center-aligned, medium, large. Medium/large collapse on scroll — the M3 analogue of a large title.
TabsAll2–manyPrimary tabs sit under the app bar for peer content; secondary tabs sit within content. Tabs are not bottom navigation.

The rule that makes adaptivity automatic: bind the navigation component to the window size class, not the device. Compact gets the bar, medium gets the rail, expanded gets the drawer — and the same app handles a phone, an unfolded foldable and a tablet without a separate design.

The FAB, used correctly

VariantSizeUse
Small FAB40 dpCompact layouts, secondary surfaces
FAB56 dpThe screen's single most important action
Large FAB96 dpWhen the action is the entire point of the screen
Extended FAB56 dp tall, label + iconWhen the action needs naming. Can collapse to icon-only on scroll.

One FAB per screen, and only for a constructive action — create, compose, add. Never Delete, never Share, never a navigation target. If the action isn't the primary purpose of the screen, it belongs in the app bar.

Back behaviour — the thing iOS designers get wrong

  • Back is a system-wide gesture and guarantee. Every screen must have a sensible back destination, and it is not always "the previous screen" — it is "up the hierarchy from here".
  • Up vs Back: Up (the arrow in the app bar) moves up the app's hierarchy. Back (the gesture) moves through the user's history. They differ when a user arrives from a notification or a deep link — design that case explicitly.
  • Back on the root screen exits the app. Do not intercept it with a "are you sure you want to leave?" dialog.
  • With predictive back, the user sees where they're going mid-gesture. Any custom back handling must feed that preview or the animation breaks.

App structure decision table

StructureUse whenComponent
3–5 peer sectionsMost appsNavigation bar → rail → drawer by size class
6+ sectionsComplex toolsDrawer, with the top 4 also in a bar
One section, many viewsFeed or document appsTop app bar + tabs
Deep hierarchyFile-like contentApp bar with Up, plus breadcrumb-style titles
Single taskUtilitiesNo navigation component at all

Mobile · Android Design 3

Material 3 components

The M3 kit, component by component — with the rules that make each feel Material rather than merely rounded.

Buttons — five levels of emphasis

StyleLookUse
FilledPrimary color pillTHE action of the screen
Filled tonalSecondary-container pillImportant but not primary
ElevatedSurface + shadowNeeds separation from patterned bg
OutlinedStroke onlyMedium emphasis, pairs with filled
TextLabel onlyLow emphasis, dialogs, inline

40dp tall, fully rounded (20dp radius), label in Label Large, optional 18dp leading icon. Icon buttons come in standard/filled/tonal/outlined variants with a 48dp target.

The rest of the kit — rules that matter

  • Cards: elevated / filled / outlined; 12dp radius; a card is one tappable unit of content, not a page-layout crutch.
  • Chips: assist / filter (checkable) / input (dismissible) / suggestion — 32dp, 8dp radius. Filter chips are Android's inline faceting workhorse.
  • Text fields: filled or outlined (pick ONE family app-wide); floating label animates up; helper/error text below; leading/trailing icons; 56dp tall.
  • Lists: one/two/three-line items, 56–88dp; leading avatar/icon 40dp; trailing meta or control; dividers optional (prefer spacing).
  • Selection: switch (M3 style has a thumb icon option, 52×32dp), checkbox, radio — same semantics you know; segmented buttons (2–5) replace M2 toggle groups.
  • Menus: anchored dropdowns for options/overflow; 4dp radius container, dense rows.
  • Progress: linear/circular, determinate when knowable; skeletons aren't canon Material — Google leans progress indicators + container placeholders.
  • Badges: small dot or numbered, on nav icons.

Every component's full spec (anatomy, measurements, states, tokens) lives at m3.material.io/components — read Buttons, Text fields and Sheets pages fully this week; skim the rest as needed. Notice the state layer model: hover/focus/press = translucent overlays of the content color (8/12/16%) — that's how Material states are generated, not hand-picked.

Buttons — five levels of emphasis

VariantContainerLabelEmphasisUse
Filledprimaryon-primaryHighestThe one primary action
Filled tonalsecondary-containeron-secondary-containerHigh-mediumThe M3-specific middle ground — a strong secondary that doesn't compete
Elevatedsurface-container-low + shadowprimaryMediumWhen a button must separate from a busy or patterned background
Outlinedtransparent + outlineprimaryMedium-lowSecondary actions beside a filled button
TexttransparentprimaryLowestDialog actions, tertiary links, card actions

Default metrics: 40 dp tall, full corner radius, 24 dp horizontal padding, Label Large (14 sp / 500) text, 18 dp icon with 8 dp gap. That pill shape is M3's most recognisable signature — changing it to small is also the fastest way to give a Material app your own voice.

Cards and chips

ComponentVariantsRules
CardElevated · Filled · Outlined12 dp radius. Cards contain related content and at most one primary action. A card is not a container for unrelated things.
Assist chip—Suggests an action ("Add to calendar"). Outlined by default.
Filter chipSelected / unselectedSelected state uses secondary-container plus a check. This is the M3 filter pattern — use it instead of a segmented control.
Input chipWith remove ✕Represents a user-entered value — a recipient, a tag
Suggestion chip—Dynamically generated suggestions, e.g. smart replies

Dialog vs bottom sheet vs snackbar — the decision that defines Android feel

PatternUse whenSpec
Basic dialogA decision that blocks progress; destructive confirmation280–560 dp wide, 28 dp radius, text buttons in the actions row, confirm on the right
Full-screen dialogA complex form on a compact screenApp bar with ✕ and a Save action
Modal bottom sheetA menu of actions, or a short focused task28 dp top radius, drag handle, scrim. This is Android's action sheet.
Standard bottom sheetPersistent secondary content beside the main contentNo scrim; co-exists with the screen
SnackbarBrief confirmation, ideally with UndoBottom, above the nav bar and FAB (which shift up), one action, auto-dismiss 4–10 s
MenuChoosing from a short list, anchored to a trigger4 dp radius, surface-container
Bottom sheet over dialog, most of the timeAndroid's centre-screen dialog is a genuine interruption and reads as heavy. A modal bottom sheet arrives from the bottom, sits under the thumb, and dismisses with a swipe. If the interaction is "choose one of these", it's a bottom sheet. Reserve dialogs for decisions with consequences — and reserve the alert for destructive ones.

Text fields

FilledOutlined
Containersurface-container-highest, 4 dp top radius, bottom indicator lineTransparent, 4 dp radius, 1 dp outline
Reads asMore visually present — good on plain backgroundsLighter — good on dense or card-heavy screens
RulePick one and use it for the entire product. Mixing them is the most common M3 inconsistency.

Anatomy: label (floats up on focus), input, supporting text, optional leading/trailing icons, character counter. Error state colours the label, outline, supporting text and trailing icon in error — all four, or it reads as a rendering bug.

Lists and selection

List items are 56 dp (one line), 72 dp (two lines) or 88 dp (three lines), with a 16 dp leading margin. Selection controls (checkbox, radio, switch) have a 48 dp minimum touch target even though the visual control is smaller — pad, don't scale. Switches in M3 are visually larger than iOS's and show an icon inside the thumb when on; that icon is an accessibility feature, not decoration.

Task · ~90 minTranslate the component sheet Take the button matrix you specced in module d1 (primary / secondary / tertiary / link / destructive) and map each row to its M3 equivalent: filled, filled tonal, outlined, text, and error-coloured filled. Then do the same for your overlays — modal, drawer, popover, toast — mapping to dialog, bottom sheet, menu, snackbar. Where the mapping doesn't fit is the interesting part; write a sentence on each mismatch.

Mobile · Android Design 4

M3 color roles & type scale

Material 3's color system is the most rigorous in the industry — a machine that turns one seed color into a full accessible theme. Learn the machine.

In plain wordsImagine feeding ONE brand color into a machine that spits out ~30 named colors, all guaranteed to be readable on each other, in light AND dark versions. That's M3 color. Your job isn't picking 30 colors — it's picking the one seed, then learning the NAMES of what comes out so you use each in the right place. Try it hands-on first: open the Material Theme Builder link below, paste any color, and watch the scheme generate — then this lesson's tables will make sense.

Tonal palettes → color roles

  • From a seed color, M3 generates 5 tonal palettes (primary, secondary, tertiary, neutral, neutral-variant), each a 13-step tone ladder from 0 (black) to 100 (white).
  • Color roles pick tones from those ladders: primary (tone 40 light / 80 dark), on-primary (100/20), primary-container (90/30), on-primary-container (10/90)… The pattern: every "X" has an "on-X" guaranteed to pass contrast on it. That pairing IS the accessibility system.
  • Surfaces: surface, surface-container (lowest→highest, 5 levels) — elevation expressed by tone, not shadow. outline / outline-variant for strokes; error roles mirror primary's structure.
  • Dynamic color: on Android 12+, the seed can come from the user's wallpaper — design with roles and your app personalizes itself; hardcode hexes and it breaks. Roles > hexes, always.

The M3 type scale

RoleSizes (Large/Medium/Small)Use
Display57 / 45 / 36spHero numerals, splash moments
Headline32 / 28 / 24spPage titles
Title22 / 16 / 14sp (Medium wt)Card & list-section titles, app bars
Body16 / 14 / 12spReading text (Body Large = default)
Label14 / 12 / 11sp (Medium wt)Buttons, chips, nav, captions

Default face is Roboto (or the OEM/system font) — brand faces slot into the same roles. Like iOS: hand off role names ("Title Medium"), not raw numbers; everything is sp so user font scaling works.

Applying the roles (the full tables live in module d4)

Module d4 · Android Design System holds the complete ref/sys/comp architecture and the full role-to-tone mapping. This lesson is about using it on a real screen. Four questions answer nearly every colour decision:

QuestionAnswer
What surface am I on?surface for the screen; a surface-container-* step for anything raised
What text sits on it?on-surface for primary, on-surface-variant for secondary and icons
How much emphasis does this action need?primary (highest) → secondary-container (medium) → outline + primary label (low)
Is it a state or a status?error family for errors; tertiary for a contrasting accent; never invent a colour
The one mistake that marks an amateur M3 screenUsing primary as a background for a large area. primary is tone 40 — a strong, saturated colour meant for small filled elements. Large brand surfaces want primary-container (tone 90 in light, 30 in dark). Flooding a screen with primary is the M3 equivalent of a full-bleed saturated header, and it dates the design instantly.

The emphasis ladder, on one screen

ElementContainerContent
Screen backgroundsurfaceon-surface
Cardsurface-containeron-surface / on-surface-variant
Menu, dialogsurface-container-highon-surface
Primary buttonprimaryon-primary
Tonal button, selected chipsecondary-containeron-secondary-container
Nav indicator pillsecondary-containeron-secondary-container
Error bannererror-containeron-error-container
Divider—outline-variant
Snackbarinverse-surfaceon-inverse-surface + inverse-primary action

Memorise this table and you can colour any Material screen without opening the spec — and every combination is contrast-safe by construction, because the tones were paired that way.

Type in practice

Screen elementRole
Top app bar title (small)Title Large — 22 sp
Collapsed large app barTitle Large; expanded uses Headline Medium
Section headerTitle Small or Label Large, in primary or on-surface-variant
List item titleTitle Medium — 16 sp / 500
List item supporting textBody Medium — 14 sp, on-surface-variant
Paragraph copyBody Large — 16 sp
Button labelLabel Large — 14 sp / 500
Nav bar item labelLabel Medium — 12 sp / 500
Caption / metadataBody Small — 12 sp

Note how much work the Label family does: it exists specifically for interactive text, where a 500 weight aids legibility at small sizes. Using Body Medium on a button is a small mistake that makes the whole app feel slightly soft.

Font scaling — Android's accessibility test

Android font size scales up to 200% (and non-linear font scaling compresses large text less aggressively than small text). Test at 130% and 200%. What breaks: bottom-nav labels, single-line list items with trailing values, chips, and any fixed-height container holding text. The fix is almost always "let it wrap and let the container grow" — never "make the text smaller".

Task · ~60 minColour one screen twice Take a screen you designed for iOS. Colour it once using iOS semantic colours plus a tint, then again using M3 roles from the ladder table. Put them side by side and write three sentences on what each system made easy and what it made awkward. This is the exercise that turns two sets of rules into one mental model.

Mobile · Android Design 5

Layout, density & large screens

Android runs on more rectangle shapes than any platform ever — folding ones included. Material's answer: window size classes and canonical layouts.

Spatial system

  • 4dp base grid (8dp rhythm for blocks): margins 16dp compact / 24dp medium+; gutters 16/24dp; the same proximity-is-grouping law from Week 2.
  • Shape scale tokens: none / xs 4 / s 8 / m 12 / l 16 / xl 28 / full — components reference the scale (cards m, sheets xl top, buttons full).
  • Elevation levels 0–5 expressed as surface-container tones (+ optional shadow at 1–2 levels for M2-flavored brands).

Window size classes (design breakpoints)

ClassWidthLayout response
Compact< 600dpPhone: nav bar bottom, single pane
Medium600–839dpFoldable/small tablet: nav rail, maybe two panes
Expanded≥ 840dpTablet: rail or standard drawer + canonical layouts

Canonical layouts to reach for at medium+: list-detail (master + detail panes), supporting pane (primary + tools), feed (adaptive grid). Foldables add posture: design the two-pane split at the hinge, keep touch targets off the fold line.

Design at these sizes

DeviceSize (dp)Window class
Phone portrait412 × 917Compact
Small phone360 × 780Compact — the stress test
Foldable, folded~360 × 900 (tall and narrow)Compact
Foldable, unfolded~674 × 841Medium — nearly square, which breaks assumptions
Tablet portrait~800 × 1280Medium / Expanded
Tablet landscape~1280 × 800Expanded

Two sizes matter most: 360 dp (if it works there, it works) and 674 dp unfolded (nearly square — a shape no phone or tablet layout anticipates).

Canonical layouts — Google's three answers

LayoutStructureCompact behaviourGood for
List-detailList pane + detail paneList pushes to detailMail, messages, files, settings
Supporting paneMain content + a narrower helper paneHelper becomes a bottom sheetEditors with tools, players with queues
FeedAdaptive grid of cardsSingle columnNews, media, dashboards, galleries

Pick one per screen and the responsive behaviour is already decided. This is Material's most practical idea and the one designers most often skip.

Density and spacing

TokenCompactMedium / Expanded
Screen margin16 dp24 dp
Gutter16 dp24 dp
Grid base4 dp (blocks land on 8)same
Content max widthFullCap it — text should not run the full width of a tablet
Touch target48 × 48 dp48 × 48 dp (40 dp acceptable with a mouse)

Foldables — the specifics

  • The hinge is a real obstruction. Never place a control or important content across the fold. Use it as a natural pane divider.
  • Continuity matters more than layout. When the device unfolds, the user must stay exactly where they were — same item, same scroll position, same text in the field. A layout change that loses state feels like a crash.
  • Postures: tabletop (half-open, horizontal) turns the bottom half into a control surface and the top into a display — video and camera apps get real value from this.
  • Test the unfolded near-square shape explicitly. Layouts tuned for 9:16 and for 16:9 both look wrong at 4:5.

Large screens, properly

Anti-patternDo instead
Stretching a phone layout to fill a tabletUse a canonical layout — show more content, not more whitespace
Bottom navigation on a 1280 dp screenNavigation rail or standard drawer
Full-width paragraphsCap the reading column; put secondary content in the remaining space
Ignoring keyboard and mouseHover states, ⌘/Ctrl shortcuts, right-click menus — ChromeOS and tablets have both
Portrait-onlySupport both orientations; a large screen is often in a keyboard case
Task · ~90 minOne screen, four shapes Take your main Android screen and lay it out at 360 × 780, 412 × 917, 674 × 841 (unfolded), and 1280 × 800. Name the canonical layout you're using. Then draw the transition: what happens to scroll position and selected item at the moment the device unfolds? That transition is the whole large-screen problem in one frame.

Practice: Material teardown & rebuild

Same discipline, other platform — and a comparison exercise that locks both mental models in.

Task 1 · ~90 minMaterial teardown Browse Mobbin's Android library — pick Google-made apps (Gmail, Drive, Calendar) plus one third-party. Inventory each screen in role vocabulary: which nav component, which button styles, which color roles (guess: primary-container? surface-container-high?), which type roles. (Thumbnails for this module can be added to the Images folder later — the practice works from the live links meanwhile.)
Task 2 · ~2.5 hrsRebuild with the M3 kit + your own theme Run your brand color through Material Theme Builder → apply the generated scheme to the M3 Figma kit → rebuild the SAME 5 screens you built in the iOS module: nav-bar shell, list, detail, compose (bottom sheet this time), settings. Light + dark from the roles.
Task 3 · ~45 minThe platform-diff memo One page, side-by-side: tab bar vs navigation bar, sheet conventions, back behavior, type systems, color systems, motion feel. This memo is interview gold and the seed of your cross-platform design sense.

Rebuild brief — the same five screens, in Material

You built these in the iOS module. Rebuild them with M3 vocabulary — same product, same content, platform-native decisions throughout.

#iOS versionMaterial versionThe decisions to get right
1Tab shell + listNavigation bar + listPill indicator on the active item; small or large top app bar; Title Medium row titles; edge-to-edge with correct insets
2Pushed detailDetail with Up arrowUp vs Back distinction; predictive-back preview; collapsing large app bar
3Sheet (medium detent)Modal bottom sheet28 dp top radius, drag handle, scrim; text buttons in the action row
4Inset grouped settingsList with section headersSection header in primary; switches with 48 dp targets; supporting text under each
5Empty stateEmpty state + FABThe FAB is the create action; empty state teaches. Snackbar for the confirmation afterwards.

Plus: light and dark from the roles, and one screen at 200% font scale. Twelve frames again.

UnitsDimensions in dp, text in sp

DimensioniOSMaterial
Primary navigationTab barNavigation bar → rail → drawer by size class
BackTitled back button + edge swipe, per appSystem gesture + Up arrow, with predictive preview
Choices from an actionAction sheetModal bottom sheet
Brief confirmationToast-style overlay or inlineSnackbar with Undo
Type systemDynamic Type styles, ptType roles, sp
Colour systemSemantic colours + one tintRoles generated from a seed; possibly overridden by the user
ElevationLayers, materials, blurSurface tone
Primary action affordanceNav-bar button or a filled button in contentFAB
Motion feelInterruptible springsToken-defined easing and duration; container transform
Then add a tenth row of your own — something you noticed that isn't on this list. That row is the evidence you actually did the work.
Why this memo matters more than the screensAnyone can rebuild a screen in a different style. Being able to explain why each platform made its choice — and when to follow versus when to deviate — is what separates a mobile designer from someone who can operate Figma. This one page comes up in almost every cross-platform interview.

Mobile · Motion 1

Motion languages: iOS vs Material

Both platforms treat motion as meaning — where things come from, what owns what — but they speak different dialects. Design in the native one.

In plain wordsGood motion answers one question the user asks unconsciously: "where did this come from?" A screen that slides in from the right came from the right (and back returns it there). A sheet that rises from the bottom lives below. If you remember only one thing from this module: motion is a MAP, not a decoration.

The dialects

iOSMaterial 3
PhysicsSprings everywhere — critically damped, velocity-preserving, always interruptible (catch a sheet mid-fling)Duration + easing tokens: short 50–200ms, medium 250–400, long 450–600; emphasized easing curve for hero moves
Hierarchy movesPush slides right→left; sheet rises w/ parent receding; zoom from tapped source (app launch, photos)Container transform (element grows into the screen it opens), shared axis (siblings slide X/Y/Z), fade-through
Signature feelFluid, physical, gesture-drivenChoreographed, tonal, expressive (springier since M3 Expressive)

Universal rules

  • Motion explains origin and ownership: a thing should appear from where it conceptually lives and return there. If you can't say what a transition explains, cut it.
  • Enter slow, exit fast: incoming elements get the longer duration/emphasis; outgoing get quick standard easing.
  • Never block: animation must not gate interaction — users can interrupt, cancel, redirect mid-flight.
  • Reduce Motion is non-negotiable: both platforms expose the setting; spec cross-fade fallbacks for anything spatial.

Deep specs: M3 Motion (durations, easing tokens, transition patterns) and the HIG's Motion page. Cite tokens in handoff ("medium2 + emphasized-decelerate"), not "make it smooth".

The two dialects, side by side

iOSMaterial 3
ModelPhysics. Springs with response and damping. Velocity carries through.Choreography. Duration and easing tokens applied to a scripted sequence.
InterruptibilityEssential — you can grab a moving thing mid-flight and reverse itSupported, but less central to the feel
Signature transitionPush/pop with parallax; sheet rise with rubber-bandingContainer transform — a card grows into the screen it opens
Spec language"Default spring, response 0.5, damping 0.825""emphasized easing, medium4 (400 ms)"
Where motion comes fromThe gestureThe token set
Why the difference is real, not cosmeticiOS motion is built around direct manipulation — your finger is attached to the object, so the animation must be able to change its mind at any frame. Material motion is built around meaningful transformation — showing that this card became that screen. Spec them in their own vocabulary and the result feels native; spec a duration curve for an iOS sheet and it will feel subtly dead.

iOS springs, in numbers

SpringResponseDampingFeels likeUse for
Snappy0.30.85Quick, no overshootButtons, toggles, selection
Default0.50.825Smooth, barely settlesMost transitions
Smooth0.51.0No bounce at allAnything where overshoot would look sloppy
Bouncy0.50.65Visible overshootPlayful confirmation — sparingly

Response is roughly how long it takes to get there; damping is how much it wobbles when it arrives (1.0 = no wobble). Two numbers describe every iOS animation you will ever spec.

Material tokens, in numbers

TokenValueUse
emphasizedcubic-bezier(.2,0,0,1)Default for anything visible on screen
emphasized-deceleratecubic-bezier(.05,.7,.1,1)Entering — fast in, gentle stop
emphasized-acceleratecubic-bezier(.3,0,.8,.15)Exiting — gentle start, fast out
short2 / short4100 / 200 msSelection, small components
medium2 / medium4300 / 400 msEntering the screen / container transform
long2500 msFull-screen transitions

The asymmetry is the craft: things enter slower than they leave. Entering deserves attention; exiting should get out of the way.

Material's four transition patterns

PatternRelationshipExample
Container transformA becomes BCard → detail screen; FAB → compose screen; search field → search results
Shared axisSpatial or hierarchical relationshipX for lateral steps (onboarding), Y for hierarchy (up/down a level), Z for depth (into a section)
Fade throughNo relationshipSwitching bottom-nav tabs
FadeEntering or leaving on topDialogs, menus, snackbars

Naming the relationship first, then picking the pattern, is the entire method. If you can't name the relationship, the transition is decoration.

Motion as a map — the one idea that generalises

Every transition should answer "where did this come from?" A sheet rises from below because it lives below. A pushed screen enters from the trailing edge because it lives one step forward. Reversing the animation must reverse the meaning. When you find a transition where the reverse looks wrong, the mental model is broken — that's a diagnostic, not an animation problem.

Reduced motion

NormallyWith Reduce Motion on
Slide / pushCross-fade
Zoom / scaleCross-fade
ParallaxNone
Auto-playing loopsStatic first frame
Spring overshootLinear settle or instant

Reduce Motion does not mean "no feedback". Keep the state change; remove the travel. And remember that for some users motion causes actual nausea — this is an accessibility requirement, not a preference toggle.

Mobile · Motion 2

Micro-interactions, gestures & haptics

The feel of a great app lives in the sub-second layer: press states, drags that track the finger, and vibration that lands exactly on meaning.

The micro-interaction inventory (spec these for every app)

  • Press feedback: iOS = subtle scale/opacity; Material = ripple/state layer. Instant (<100ms perceived).
  • Gesture-driven motion: the element FOLLOWS the finger 1:1 (sheet drag, swipe actions, pull-to-refresh), then springs to the nearest rest state using release velocity. Rubber-banding at limits.
  • State changes: like→liked (bounce), add-to-cart (fly to tab badge), toggle thumbs — 150–300ms, one clear peak.
  • Loading: skeletons/placeholders for structure, spinners for short unknowns, progress for knowables, optimistic UI for user's own actions.
  • Haptics choreography: success/warning/error notifications, selection ticks, impact weights (light/medium/heavy) on drops and detents. Pair haptic + visual + (optional) sound at the SAME instant; overuse numbs.
Do
  • Derive animation from gesture velocity
  • Give every interactive element a pressed state
  • Spec haptic moments in your handoff doc
  • Keep micro-motion under 300ms
Don't
  • Animate for decoration ("delight" with no meaning)
  • Lock the UI while animating
  • Fire haptics on every tap
  • Ship spinner-only loading for >2s waits

The anatomy of a micro-interaction

PartQuestionExample — pull to refresh
TriggerWhat starts it?The user drags the list past its top edge
RulesWhat can happen?Past a threshold it commits; released early it springs back
FeedbackWhat does the user perceive?The indicator rotates with the drag, then a haptic tick at the threshold
Loops & modesWhat if it repeats or fails?Spinner loops while loading; on failure it settles with an error row

Dan Saffer's four-part model. Most broken micro-interactions are missing part four — nobody designed what happens when it fails or when the user does it twelve times in a row.

The gesture vocabulary, and what each costs

GestureDiscoverabilityRule
TapHigh44 pt / 48 dp minimum, always
ScrollHighNever nest two scrollable areas on the same axis
Swipe on a rowMediumMust exist elsewhere too. Max 2 actions per side.
Long pressLowSecondary actions only. Give haptic feedback at the moment it registers, or it feels broken.
Drag to reorderMediumNeeds a visible handle, a lifted state, and a live gap where it will land
Pinch / rotateMedium in contextOnly where a spatial mental model exists — maps, images, canvases
Edge swipeSystem-ownedDo not compete with it. On both platforms the screen edges belong to the OS.
ShakeVery lowUndo only, and never the only route
The hidden-gesture ruleEvery gesture must have a visible equivalent. Gestures are accelerators for people who already know your app — they are never the primary path, and a feature reachable only by long-press effectively does not exist for most users. This is also an accessibility requirement: many users cannot perform precise or sustained gestures at all.

Haptics — a shared vocabulary

MomentiOSAndroid
Value ticks past a stepSelection feedbackCLOCK_TICK / segment tick
Something attaches or landsImpact — light / medium / heavyConfirm / reject constants
Operation succeededNotification successConfirm
Operation failedNotification errorReject
Long press registeredImpact mediumLong-press constant

Three rules: haptics accompany a visual change, never substitute for one; weight should match visual weight (a heavy impact for a small toggle feels wrong); and never fire one on every tap — a constantly buzzing app gets its haptics disabled, taking your important ones with it.

Loading and progress — the perception layer

WaitShow
< 100 msNothing — this reads as instant
100 ms – 1 sInline feedback on the control that was tapped
1 – 10 sSkeleton matching the real layout, at the real dimensions
> 10 sDeterminate progress, a description of the current step, and a way to leave

Two perception tricks worth knowing: an optimistic update (change the UI immediately, reconcile later) makes an action feel instant — at the cost of owing a graceful rollback. And a progress bar that accelerates toward the end is perceived as faster than a linear one, even at identical total duration.

The micro-interactions worth designing properly

InteractionWhat good looks like
Pull to refreshIndicator tracks the drag, haptic at threshold, spring back on release, clear completion
Toggle / switchThumb travel under 200 ms, colour and position change together, haptic on commit
Add to cart / favouriteImmediate state change, a small scale pulse, the counter animating from the item
Delete a rowRow collapses rather than vanishing; an undo affordance appears in the same frame
Form validationError appears on blur, not on keystroke; clears the instant the input is valid
ReorderLift with shadow and slight scale, live gap at the drop target, settle with a spring
Empty → first itemThe empty state animates out as the first row animates in — the single most satisfying moment in most apps
Task · ~90 minDocument three micro-interactions in four parts Pick three interactions from your app. For each, write out trigger, rules, feedback, and loops-and-modes — including the failure case and the twelfth-repeat case. Then specify the numbers: duration or spring, easing token, and which haptic fires when. A developer should be able to build it from your page without watching a video.

Mobile · Motion 3

Prototyping in Figma & beyond

Prototype fidelity is a dial: turn it only as high as the question you're answering requires.

The Figma toolkit

  • Smart Animate — matches layer names across frames and tweens position/size/opacity/rotation. Your workhorse for transitions and component state changes; set spring or custom cubic-bezier per platform dialect.
  • Drag triggers + overlays — sheets, drawers, swipe actions; position overlays manually for detent states.
  • Variables + conditionals — real logic: cart counts, toggled states, branching flows, "if empty show empty-state". This upgraded Figma into a genuine flow-testing tool.
  • Device preview — ALWAYS judge motion on the phone via the Figma app; trackpad lies about scale and spring feel.

When Figma isn't enough

NeedTool
Sensor/gesture-rich, multi-screen logic, data inputsProtoPie
Timeline-crafted hero animationsAfter Effects (+ Lottie export for devs)
TRUE spring feel + production handoffSwiftUI / Compose previews — pair with an engineer; motion specced in code is motion shipped
Practice · ~2.5 hrsOne flow, two dialects Prototype your compose flow from the iOS and Android modules: iOS version — sheet with detents, spring feel, interruptible drag; Android version — FAB container-transform into full-screen compose, M3 durations/easing. Test both on-device; note in one paragraph what each platform's dialect made you feel.

Choose the fidelity for the question you're asking

QuestionFidelityTime
Does this flow make sense?Clickable wireframes, no motion~1 hour
Can people complete the task?Realistic screens, basic transitions, real copyHalf a day
Does this feel right?Smart animate with correct curves and timing1–2 days
Does the gesture feel right?ProtoPie / Origami, or a real device buildDays
Will engineering build it correctly?A spec document with numbers, plus a short reference videoHours

Fidelity is a cost, not a virtue. The most common prototyping mistake is animating something before anyone has agreed the flow.

Figma: what it does well, and where it stops

CapabilityUse forWatch out
Smart animateAny transition where elements persist between framesMatching is by layer name — identical names across frames or nothing tweens
Easing & spring curvesMatching your motion tokens exactlySet a custom bezier rather than "ease out"; the defaults are not your tokens
VariablesReal state — toggles, counters, form values, themesKeep a small named set; variable sprawl is unmaintainable
Conditional logicBranching on state — "if signed in, go here"Excellent for demoing logic; still not a real app
Interactive componentsHover, press, toggle states inside one componentBuild once, reuse everywhere — this is the biggest time saver
Scroll behaviourSticky headers, horizontal carousels, parallaxNested scrolls are fragile; simplify
Device previewAlways — test on the actual phoneTiming that feels right on a laptop often feels slow in the hand
Where Figma genuinely stopsGesture-driven, interruptible motion — the thing that is iOS. If your interaction requires the animation to track a finger and reverse mid-flight, Figma cannot represent it. That's the moment to move to ProtoPie or Origami, or to sit with an engineer and build it. Knowing this boundary is more useful than any technique.

The tool ladder

ToolStrengthReach for it when
FigmaFast, shared, no new file format90% of the time
ProtoPieSensors, real gesture tracking, device featuresContinuous gestures, drag-driven motion, hardware input
Origami StudioPatch-based logic, very close to native behaviourComplex conditional interaction; teams that already use it
Rive / LottieProduction-ready vector animationIllustrated loaders, icon transitions, empty-state animation that ships
SwiftUI / Compose previewsThe actual platformPairing with an engineer — often faster than a high-fidelity prototype, and the result is real

The under-used option is the last one. An hour beside an engineer with a SwiftUI or Compose preview frequently beats a day of prototype-building, and what you end up with is shippable rather than disposable.

Motion specs engineers can actually build from

FieldExample
TriggerTap on card
Properties animatedPosition, corner radius, opacity of the container; cross-fade of content
Duration / spring400 ms — md.sys.motion.duration.medium4
Easingemphasized — cubic-bezier(.2,0,0,1)
StaggerChildren 50 ms apart, top to bottom
ReverseSame curve, 300 ms (medium2)
InterruptionReverses from current position
Reduced motionCross-fade, 150 ms
HapticImpact light, at the moment the container reaches full size

Nine rows. Attach a short screen recording as reference, but the numbers are the contract — a video alone leaves every value to be guessed.

Task · ~3 hrsPrototype one flow, then spec it Take the sheet-presentation flow from your iOS rebuild. Build it in Figma with smart animate and a spring curve that matches the default iOS spring. Add a variable so the form's state persists, and conditional logic so an incomplete form shows an error instead of dismissing. Preview it on your phone and tune the timing there, not on your laptop. Then write the nine-row spec above for the presentation and the dismissal.
Done when: the timing feels right in your hand, and the spec has numbers in every row.

Watch · Lesson 1

watchOS deep dive

The Apple Watch is not a small phone — it's a glance machine. Every watchOS rule flows from one number: interactions should finish in under ten seconds.

In plain wordsNobody "uses" a watch app the way they use a phone app. They glance at it mid-conversation, mid-run, mid-meeting — two seconds, wrist down. So watch design is really the art of choosing the ONE number and ONE button that matter, and making them readable at arm's length. If your watch design needs explaining, it's already failed the glance.

Platform facts

  • Canvas: 40–49mm cases → roughly 162×197pt to 205×251pt; rounded-rect display; design edge-to-edge (black bg merges with the bezel — pure black is the frame).
  • Inputs: tap, Digital Crown (precise scroll/zoom WITHOUT covering the screen — support it for every scrollable), long-press sparingly, side button, plus your phone for anything long-form.
  • Type: SF Compact (tuned for small sizes); text starts ~12pt supporting, body 15–16pt; large bold numerals are the watch's signature typography move.
  • Always-On: your app shows a dimmed state constantly — design it: simplified, redacted-if-private, no second-ticking animations.

The watchOS surfaces

SurfaceJobDesign notes
App (List/Page)Vertical list drill-down OR horizontally paged siblingsFull-width tappable rows ≥44pt; one idea per screen
ComplicationsWatch-face data slots (corner, circular, rectangular, bezel families)THE most-used surface — one metric, ruthlessly abbreviated, tap = deep link
Smart Stack widgetsCrown-scroll cards under the faceGlanceable card; relevance-ranked by system
NotificationsShort look (banner) → long look (scrollable detail + actions)Design the long look; 1–3 action buttons

The honest strategy: most "watch apps" should be a great complication + notifications + a two-screen app. Canon: the HIG's Designing for watchOS section.

Surfaces, ranked by how often people actually see them

RankSurfaceSeenDesign consequence
1Complication on the watch faceDozens of times a dayThis is your product for most users. One number or one glyph.
2Smart Stack widgetSeveral times a dayAppears contextually. Must be readable in half a second.
3Notification (short look)OftenSystem-generated — you supply the title and the icon
4Notification (long look)When they raise their wristYou design this. Content, then actions.
5The app itselfRarelyDesign it, but do not assume it's the main event
The mistake that defines bad watch designDesigning the app first. On a watch the app is the least-visited surface. Design the complication first, the widget second, the notification third — and only then the app. Teams that invert this ship watch apps nobody opens twice.

Complication families — you must design all four

FamilyShapeHolds
accessoryCircularSmall circleA gauge, a ring, one glyph, or 1–3 characters
accessoryCornerCorner arcIcon plus a short curved label
accessoryRectangularWide rectangleUp to three lines — the richest family
accessoryInlineSingle line beside the timeOne short string with an optional glyph

You cannot ship only the one you like. Users choose their own watch face, and a missing family means your app simply isn't available on it. Design all four, and design the placeholder / no-data state for each — that's the state a user sees the moment they add it.

Navigation on watchOS

ModelUse whenNotes
List (vertical)Default for almost everythingFull-width rows, ~50–60 pt tall, crown-scrollable
Page-based (horizontal)2–4 peer views with no hierarchyPage dots at the bottom. More than four and people get lost.
HierarchicalDrill into detailKeep to two levels. Three is too deep for a wrist.
Tab-styleRareOnly when the app genuinely has peer sections

The Digital Crown

The crown is a precision input on a device with no room for precision touch. Use it for: scrolling long lists, adjusting a value, and zooming. Always pair crown movement with selection haptics at each step — without the tick, the crown feels like it isn't connected to anything. And whatever the crown adjusts must also be adjustable by touch, for users who cannot rotate it comfortably.

Always-On — the state your screen spends most of its life in

In Always-OnWhat to do
Luminance drops sharplyReduce brightness of large fills; keep type white
Refresh rate drops to ~1 HzNo animation. Seconds hands and counters go static or coarse.
Sensitive dataRedact it — you choose what's hidden, or the system will choose badly
Burn-in riskShift content position slightly; avoid large static bright areas
ControlsDim or hide buttons — they aren't tappable until the wrist is raised

Design the always-on variant of every screen that can stay open. This is the single most-skipped watchOS deliverable, and it's the state a passer-by actually sees.

Case sizes and type

Two size families in practice: smaller cases (40/41/42 mm) and larger (44/45/46/49 mm). The system scales SF Compact text styles between them, which is exactly why you bind to text styles and never to point values. Design at the smaller case — if your layout survives there, the larger one simply gets more comfortable.

Warm-up · ~30 minThe wrist audit If you have a watch, note every interaction you have with it for one day: what surface, how long, whether you completed it on the wrist or reached for your phone. If you don't have one, do this with a colleague's or watch three reviews closely. Almost every interaction will be under ten seconds and on a complication or a notification — which is the whole argument of this module, delivered by your own data.

Watch · Lesson 2

Wear OS deep dive

Wear OS is Material for a circle. The round display isn't a constraint to fight — it's the layout system.

Round-first layout

  • Circular canvas (typical 192–228dp diameter): content narrows toward top and bottom — lists SCALE and curve items as they approach edges (the ScalingLazyColumn pattern: center item full-size, neighbors shrink/fade). Design lists with that taper in mind.
  • Curved elements: text and progress arcs along the bezel; page indicators curve; time sits top-center.
  • Margins are percentages (~5.2% of diameter) not fixed dp — corners of a square layout literally don't exist here.
  • Inputs: tap, rotary (crown/bezel — the Digital Crown twin; support it), physical buttons; wrist gestures on some devices.

The Wear OS surfaces

SurfaceAnalog ofNotes
TilesSmart Stack widgetsSwipeable full-screen glances right of the face; template-driven; one task/metric + one tap action
ComplicationsSame concept as watchOSData slots on faces: short text, ranged value (arc), icon types
AppswatchOS appsM3-flavored components from the Wear Compose kit: chips (list rows!), cards, buttons ≥48dp, dialogs
Ongoing activitiesLive Activities-ishPersistent chip on the face during runs/timers/playback

Color: true black backgrounds (AMOLED battery + bezel blending) with vivid accents; the Wear M3 ColorScheme is dark-only by design. Type: larger relative sizes than phone; nothing under 12sp; test at arm's length. Canon: developer.android.com/design/ui/wear.

Round-first, and the maths that follows

ConstraintNumberConsequence
Screen widths~192 dp small · ~227 dp largeDesign both. The gap is bigger than it sounds at this size.
Side margin~5.2% of widthPercentage, not dp — the same layout must fit both sizes
Top / bottom margin~10%Curvature eats the top and bottom of a rectangle hardest
Usable content column~70% of widthAnything wider clips at the corners
Touch target48 × 48 dp (40 dp only where space forces it)Larger than the phone rule, on a smaller screen
Why percentage margins, not dpA 16 dp margin is 8.3% of a 192 dp screen and 7.0% of a 227 dp one — so a layout tuned for one looks wrong on the other, and content clips at the curve on the smaller device. Percentage margins keep the optical inset constant across sizes. This is the single most Wear-specific layout rule.

Surfaces, ranked

RankSurfaceDesign note
1TileA swipeable glanceable panel. Your most-seen surface after the watch face. Design at both screen sizes.
2ComplicationOn the watch face. Multiple types — short text, ranged value, monochromatic image.
3NotificationWith actions. Keep to two.
4Ongoing activityPersistent during a live session — a workout, a timer, navigation. Shows on the watch face.
5The appOpened deliberately, briefly
—Watch faceA separate product with its own rules. Treat as its own system.

ScalingLazyColumn — design for the scaling, don't fight it

Wear's standard list scales and fades items as they approach the top and bottom edges, so the centre item is always the most prominent. Consequences for your design:

  • The first and last items are clipped by default unless you add top and bottom spacers. Always add them.
  • Never put critical information in an item that will sit at an edge — it will be visually de-emphasised.
  • Item content must survive being scaled down; a two-line row at 85% scale can drop below the legible floor.
  • Design the list at both screen sizes; the number of visible items differs.

Colour and shape

TokenValueWhy
background#000000OLED — black pixels are off. Free contrast, free battery.
surface / surfaceContainerVery dark neutral, 8–15% lightnessCards need to separate from black without lighting up the panel
primaryBrand tone 80Inverted from the phone: light-on-dark for legibility
onPrimaryBrand tone 20Dark text on a light button
Corner shapefullRound hardware, round components. Rectangles look foreign here.

There is no light mode. One theme, on black, always.

Rotary input

Wear devices have a rotating crown or bezel. Every scrollable surface must respond to it, with haptic feedback at each detent. Rotary is often the only comfortable input while walking or exercising — if a screen can only be operated by touch, it fails in exactly the situation the device exists for.

Power as a design constraint

ChoiceBattery cost
Black backgroundEffectively zero
Large light fillHigh — this is why cards are 10–20% white, not solid
Continuous animationHigh — keeps the display and CPU awake
Frequent data refreshHigh — batch and cache instead
Ambient mode with static contentLow — design for it deliberately

On a phone, battery is engineering's problem. On a watch it is a design problem, because your colour and motion choices directly determine whether the device lasts the day — and a watch app that costs the user their battery gets uninstalled regardless of how good it looks.
