Watch · Lesson 3

Shared watch patterns & constraints

Strip the branding and both platforms converge on the same physics: tiny canvas, two-second attention, battery as a design material.

The universal laws

  • The 10-second task: if a flow needs more, it belongs on the phone. Design the handoff explicitly ("Continue on phone").
  • One thing per screen: a metric, a decision, a confirmation. Information density is the enemy here — the exact inverse of your SaaS instincts.
  • Glance hierarchy: the ONE number huge and bold; label small; context (trend arrow, ring) visual not verbal.
  • Targets & type floors: ≥44pt/48dp targets (fingers don't shrink with screens); nothing below ~12pt/sp; prefer bold weights — thin fonts die on tiny OLEDs.
  • Battery is UX: black backgrounds, minimal always-on states, no gratuitous animation — a beautiful app that kills the battery gets uninstalled by lunch.
  • Haptics > sound: the wrist tap is the primary output channel; notifications must earn it (interruption budget is tighter than phone).
  • Companion split: setup, auth, long forms, browsing = phone app; capture, glance, control, log = watch. Write the split down before designing screens.

Round vs rect quick math

Corner content on round displays: the largest inscribed square of a circle of diameter d has side d·0.707 — anything outside that square risks clipping. Center-anchor your critical content; let decoration bleed.

Learning materials for this track

Canon
HIG — Designing for watchOS + the Complications and Widgets pages

Short reads; the complication families table is worth printing.

Canon
Wear OS design guidance

Tiles, complications, ongoing activities — with downloadable Figma kit.

Patterns
Mobbin — search any fitness/timer app and study its watch screenshots on the app's page

Watch thumbnails can be added to your Images folder later, same as Android.

The ten-second budget

SecondsWhat must have happened
0–1Wrist raised, screen on, the one number or state is readable
1–3If more detail is needed, one tap has produced it
3–7An action is taken — one tap, or a crown adjustment plus a tap
7–10Confirmation, and the arm comes down
> 10This task belongs on the phone.

Apply it as a test, not a guideline: state in one sentence the single task each screen exists for. If the sentence needs an "and", split the screen or cut it.

Round-layout maths — the practical version

RuleWhy
Content lives inside ~70% of the screen widthA rectangle inscribed in a circle loses its corners
Margins as percentages, not fixed unitsOne layout must fit two (or four) case sizes
Nothing important in the cornersThey clip, and on watchOS the curvature is aggressive
First and last list items need spacersOtherwise they can never scroll fully into view
Full-width rows over side-by-side elementsTwo columns on a 190 dp round screen is a target-size failure
Curved text only where the platform provides itHand-curved type is unreadable and inaccessible

Type and target floors

watchOSWear OS
Smallest usable textFootnote — 12 ptLabel Small — 12 sp
Default bodyBody — 16 ptBody Large — 16 sp
The glanceable numberLarge Title — 34 ptDisplay Large — 40 sp
Minimum target44 × 44 pt48 × 48 dp (40 dp only under duress)
TypefaceSF CompactRoboto (or a brand face, cautiously)

Note that your smallest watch text is roughly your phone's caption size — the scale doesn't shrink proportionally with the screen, because the eye-to-wrist distance doesn't shrink either.

Splitting the product between wrist and phone

Belongs on the watchBelongs on the phone
Checking a single status or numberBrowsing, comparing, exploring
Starting or stopping somethingConfiguring how it works
Responding to a prompt — accept, snooze, logAny text entry longer than a canned reply
Capturing a moment — a rep, a note, a check-inReviewing history in depth
Live sessions — workout, timer, navigationAccount, billing, settings

Rule of thumb: the watch handles one verb per surface. The phone owns nouns and configuration. Products that try to mirror the phone app onto the wrist end up with a worse version of both.

Input, ranked by comfort in motion

InputComfort while movingUse for
Rotary / crownHighestScroll, adjust, zoom — always with haptic detents
Large tap targetHighThe primary action, full-width
VoiceHighAny text entry. Make it the default, not a fallback.
Canned repliesHighMessaging — 3–4 contextual options
SwipeMediumPage changes only. Never a hidden action.
Scribble / keyboardLowLast resort, never required
Long pressVery lowAvoid entirely

Notifications — the surface you actually design

The short look is system-generated from your app icon and title. The long look is yours: a heading, the essential content, and at most two actions plus Dismiss. Rules — lead with the content, not your branding; make actions verbs; and make sure the notification is useful without opening the app, because most of the time it won't be opened.

Task · ~45 minThe one-verb exercise Take your SaaS product and write down ten things a user does with it. Score each against the ten-second budget. You should end with one that genuinely belongs on a wrist — maybe two. Write its verb in one sentence. That sentence is the brief for the next lesson's build, and the discipline of cutting nine ideas is the actual skill.

Practice: one app, both wrists

Design the watch companion for your course-long SaaS product — twice.

Task 1 · ~30 minThe split memo List every feature of your product; assign each to phone-only / watch-glance / watch-action. Choose the ONE metric and the ONE action that define the watch experience.
Task 2 · ~90 minwatchOS set Design: one rectangular + one circular complication, a Smart Stack widget, a 2-screen app (glance → action), and a long-look notification. 45mm frame (198×242pt), SF Compact, black background, always-on dimmed variant of the glance.
Task 3 · ~90 minWear OS set Same content as Task 2 but circular (224dp): a Tile, two complications (short text + ranged value), a 2-screen app using chip-style rows with the edge taper, an ongoing-activity chip. Note where the round canvas forced different decisions.
DeliverableSplit memo + both platform sets + a 5-line comparison. Watch thumbnails from Mobbin can be added to the Images folder later — design from the official galleries meanwhile.

The brief — one verb, two platforms, every surface

Use the single verb you isolated in the last lesson. Build the whole product around it, on both platforms.

#DeliverablewatchOSWear OS
1Token sheetSF Compact styles, black + tint, 44 pt targets, ~8–10 pt marginsWear M3 roles on black, 48 dp targets, ~5.2% margins
2Glanceable surfaceAll four complication families + Smart Stack widgetTile (both screen sizes) + complication
3Main screen45 mm and 41 mm227 dp and 192 dp
4Action / adjust screenCrown-driven, with haptic detents specifiedRotary-driven, same
5Always-on / ambientDimmed, redacted, no animationAmbient variant
6NotificationLong look with two actionsExpanded notification with two actions
7Live sessionLive ActivityOngoing activity
8Empty / no-dataIncluding the complication placeholderIncluding the tile placeholder

Roughly twenty frames. Small screens make this far faster than it sounds — and the completeness is what makes it credible.

Self-review checklist

CheckPass condition

Ten-second budgetThe main task completes inside it, hand on the wrist
BackgroundPure #000000, both platforms
Type floorNothing below 12 pt / 12 sp
Targets44 pt / 48 dp minimum, achieved by padding
Round safetyContent within ~70% width; nothing important in corners
List edgesSpacers so first and last items scroll clear
ComplicationsAll four families, each with a placeholder state
Always-onDesigned, dimmed, redacted, static

The cross-device memo

Task · ~45 minOne product, four screens wide You now have the same product designed for web (Weeks 6–7), iOS (x1), Android (x2) and watch (x4). Write one page comparing how the same task appears on each:
DimensionWhat to state
What the surface showsEverything / a screen's worth / a glance
Primary inputMouse + keyboard / thumb / thumb / crown
Session lengthMinutes / a minute / seconds
Information densityHow many facts are on screen at once
What was cut, and whyThe most important column
What was added because the platform allowed itHaptics, complications, hover, keyboard shortcuts
This memo is the capstone of the entire mobile and watch track. Anyone can resize a layout; explaining what survives contact with each platform — and what each platform makes newly possible — is the thing that gets a multi-platform designer hired.
Portfolio noteA watch case study is rare and disproportionately memorable. Very few designers have one, and almost none have all four complication families plus a designed always-on state. Twenty small frames, one clear argument, and it will be the piece reviewers remember.

Design Systems · SaaS 1

System architecture & tokens

This module builds an Untitled-UI/Linear-grade system from nothing. It starts where engineers start: with the token architecture, because a design system IS a data structure that happens to look good.

In plain wordsThink LEGO. A design system is the box of bricks (buttons, inputs, colors, spacing rules) plus the instruction book, so every screen anyone builds afterwards snaps together from the same parts. "Tokens" are just NAMED values — instead of remembering "our borders are #EAECF0", everyone (designers AND developers) says border-primary, and if the value ever changes, it changes everywhere at once. That's the entire trick; the rest of this module is doing it thoroughly.

The three-layer token pyramid (the industry consensus)

LayerContainsExampleWho touches it
1 · PrimitivesRaw values, exhaustive, meaningless alonegray-700 = #344054, spacing-4 = 16pxOnly the system team, rarely
2 · SemanticRoles that point at primitives; THE theming layertext-secondary → gray-700, bg-brand-solid → brand-600Themes remap these (dark mode = new pointers)
3 · ComponentPer-component decisions pointing at semantics (only where needed)button-primary-bg → bg-brand-solidComponent authors

Components consume layer 2/3 — never layer 1. That single discipline is what makes rebrands one-day jobs and dark mode a remap instead of a redesign. You met this idea in Week 8; this module industrializes it.

Naming — the API of your system

  • Pattern: category-concept-property-variant-state, only as many segments as needed: bg-primary, text-error-primary, border-brand-solid-hover.
  • Name by purpose, never appearance: bg-success not bg-green (the day success becomes teal, appearance-names lie).
  • Pick conventions ONCE and write them down: singular vs plural, "fg" vs "text", scale numbering (100s like Tailwind vs t-shirt sizes). Consistency beats cleverness — devs will autocomplete these names hundreds of times a day.

In Figma, in code

  • Figma: two variable collections — "Primitives" (locked/hidden from most editors) and "Semantic" with modes = Light/Dark. Component tokens usually live as component-level decisions, not variables.
  • Code mirror: CSS custom properties, a Tailwind theme config, or a tokens JSON in the W3C DTCG format transformed by Style Dictionary. Ask your engineers which; align names EXACTLY — the whole point is one vocabulary.
  • Versioning: systems ship like software — changelogs, deprecation (mark old, alias to new, remove later), semver thinking. Breaking a token name breaks every file that uses it.

Study the masters

Kit
Untitled UI

The de-facto reference SaaS system for Figma. Open the free version and read its variable collections like source code — this module constantly cross-references it.

Book
Atomic Design — Brad Frost (free online)

The mental model underneath every system: atoms → molecules → organisms → templates.

Book
Design Systems — Alla Kholmatova (Smashing)

The organizational half: shared language, adoption, governance.

The three tiers, with real names

Everything in this module is built on one rule: each tier may only reference the tier below it. Break that rule and you get a system where changing the brand colour requires opening forty components.

TierHoldsExample nameWho reads it
1 · PrimitiveRaw values. A hex, a pixel count, a millisecond. No opinion about use.color.brand.600
space.4		Only the semantic tier. Never a component. Never you, while designing a screen.
2 · SemanticRoles. What the value is for. This is the tier you design with.action-primary-bg
text-secondary
border-focus		Every component. Every screen. This is the public API of your system.
3 · ComponentLocal exceptions a role can't express.button-height-md
table-row-height		One component each. If you're adding many, your semantic tier is missing a role.
The alias-chain trapSemantic tokens must point at primitives, never at other semantic tokens. button-bg → action-primary-bg → brand-600 looks tidy and is a maintenance bomb: two years later nobody can answer "what actually changes if I edit this?" One hop. Always.

Naming grammar — pick one and never deviate

A token name is a sentence with a fixed word order. The grammar below covers every token you will ever need on web:

SlotAnswersValues
categoryWhat kind of thing?color · space · radius · shadow · font · z · duration
role / conceptWhat is it for?bg · text · border · action · focus · viz
variantWhich flavour?primary · secondary · brand · danger · subtle
stateWhen?(rest) · hover · active · disabled · selected
scaleHow much?25…950 · sm/md/lg · 1…32

So: action-primary-bg-hover = action · primary · background · on hover. And bg-danger-subtle = background · danger · the quiet version. Read either one aloud and a developer knows exactly what it does.

Do
  • Name for role — text-secondary survives a rebrand
  • Keep the word order identical across every token
  • Spell it out; bg is fine but bgSecInv is not
  • Leave the resting state unnamed (action-primary-bg, not …-default)
Don't
  • Name for appearance — gray-text dies the day you go dark-mode
  • Encode the value — blue-button lies the moment marketing picks purple
  • Mix conventions — btnPrimaryBG next to text-primary
  • Create a token used exactly once

How this lands in Figma

CollectionModesContainsPublished?
Primitives1 (no modes)Every colour ramp, the spacing scale, radiiHidden from publishing — designers should never pick from here
SemanticLight · Dark (add Brand A/B later)Every role, each one an alias to a primitiveYes — this is what teams consume
ScaleCompact · Comfortable (optional)Spacing and sizing that changes with densityYes

The step everyone skips: in the Semantic collection, set each variable's value to a variable alias pointing at the matching primitive, not to a raw hex. If you paste hex values into the semantic tier you have built two disconnected palettes that will drift within a month.

Design Systems · SaaS 2

The color system, end to end

A production color system is ~150 decisions made once. Here is every decision, in build order.

Step 1 — Primitive ramps (base colors)

  • Ramps of 11–12 steps: 25, 50, 100 … 900, 950 (Untitled UI's scale). Build: gray (choose a temperature — blue-gray reads "product", true gray reads "editorial"), brand, error (red), warning (amber), success (green), + 2–4 accents for data-viz/tags.
  • Craft rule: brand-600 = your brand color for light-mode solids; steps must hold hue identity from 25 to 950 (adjust hue ±2–8° and saturation along the ramp; naive lightness-stepping goes muddy in the middle). Sanity-check against Radix Colors — the most perceptually engineered open ramps.
  • Alpha ramps for gray + white (gray-alpha-50…900): overlays, hover-on-anything, borders on images — the pros' secret for surfaces that work on any background.

Step 2 — Semantic roles (the layer devs consume)

GroupRoles (typical Untitled-style set)
Texttext-primary · secondary · tertiary · disabled · placeholder · on-brand · error/warning/success-primary
Backgroundbg-primary (page) · secondary · tertiary · active · disabled · overlay · brand-solid · brand-soft · error/warning/success-soft&solid
Borderborder-primary · secondary · disabled · brand · error
Foreground (icons)fg-primary … fg-quaternary · fg-brand · fg-white
Focusfocus-ring (brand @ 4px, 24% alpha) · focus-ring-error

Step 3 — The light/dark mapping table

RoleLightDark
bg-primarywhitegray-950
bg-secondarygray-50gray-900
text-primarygray-900gray-50
text-secondarygray-600gray-400
border-primarygray-200gray-800
bg-brand-solidbrand-600brand-500 (brighter on dark)
bg-error-softerror-50error-950

Notice the inversion is asymmetric — dark mode brightens accents one step and never uses pure black text-inversions. This table (extended to every role) IS your dark mode; build it in Figma modes so every component flips by selection.

Step 4 — Verification & data-viz

  • Contrast-check every text/bg PAIR the semantic layer allows: primary-on-primary, secondary-on-secondary, on-brand-on-brand-solid… ≥4.5:1 body, 3:1 large/UI. Both modes.
  • Data-viz palette: 6–8 categorical hues equidistant in hue, similar lightness, colorblind-tested (Viz palettes in Untitled UI are a good crib); sequential + diverging ramps for heat/deltas.

Build the ramp on contrast, not on feel

Most designers make a ramp by nudging lightness until it looks even. It never is — and each hue ends up with different usable steps, so green-600 fails contrast while blue-600 passes. Fix it by defining the ramp by target contrast against white, then solving for the colour. Every hue's step 600 then behaves identically.

StepContrast vs whiteSafe for
25 · 50 · 1001.03 – 1.18Page and card backgrounds, subtle tints
200 · 3001.42 – 1.95Borders on light surfaces; fills and text on dark
4002.75Large graphics, dark-mode body text
5003.85Non-text UI — icons, borders, focus rings (clears the 3:1 bar)
6005.20Buttons, links, body text — clears AA 4.5:1
7007.20Text — clears AAA 7:1
800 · 900 · 950 · 10009.6 – 17.6Headings, dark-mode surfaces

Learn those three bold rows and colour decisions stop being decisions: 500 for non-text, 600 for interactive, 700 for text.

The kit's ramps (verified, copy them)

StepNeutralBrandSuccessWarningDanger
50#F5F6F6#F5F5FA#F1F7F4#F8F6F1#F9F5F5

Notice green jumps hard between 200 and 300. That is not a bug — pure green is intrinsically light, so hitting a contrast target forces a bigger hue-lightness move. Every ramp system hits this; the honest ones admit it.

Semantic mapping — the table your whole product runs on

Semantic tokenLightDarkUsed by
bg-canvasneutral-50neutral-1000The page behind everything
bg-surfacewhiteneutral-950Cards, panels, table bodies
bg-surface-raisedwhiteneutral-900Menus, popovers, modals
bg-hoverneutral-100neutral-900Row and item hover
text-primaryneutral-900neutral-50Headings, body
text-secondaryneutral-700neutral-300Labels, supporting copy
text-tertiaryneutral-600neutral-400Metadata, placeholders
border-subtleneutral-200neutral-800Dividers, row rules
border-defaultneutral-300neutral-700Inputs, card edges
border-focusbrand-600brand-400The focus ring, everywhere
action-primary-bgbrand-600brand-400Primary buttons, active nav
action-primary-fgwhiteneutral-1000The label on top of it
bg-brand-subtlebrand-100brand-950Selected nav item, info card
text-dangerdanger-700danger-300Error text
Why dark mode flips the step, not the tokenIn light mode the brand button is brand-600 with white text. In dark mode a 600 on a near-black surface is a muddy bruise, so the token re-points to brand-400 — and because 400 is light, the label flips to neutral-1000. Both pairs land above 5:1. The button component never changed; one variable did.

Rules the ramp doesn't teach you

  • Dark mode is not inversion. Surfaces get lighter as they rise (canvas 1000 → surface 950 → raised 900). Shadows barely read on dark; elevation becomes tone.
  • Desaturate on dark. A colour that sings on white screams on black. That's why dark mode uses 300/400 steps, which are less saturated at the same contrast.
  • Never carry meaning in colour alone. Every status gets an icon or a word too — for colour-blind users and for greyscale printouts.
  • Alpha tokens matter. Overlays, scrims and hover washes need alpha variants so they work over any surface. Add bg-hover-alpha: rgb(neutral-900 / 6%) when solid hovers fight your imagery.

Data visualisation palette

Chart colours are a separate palette with a different job: distinguishable, not hierarchical. Six categorical series, in order — brand-500, info-500, success-500, warning-500, danger-500, brand-800. Test them three ways: greyscale, deuteranopia simulation, and side-by-side as 4px lines (thin strokes lose colour identity fast).

See the same system in both modes

Plain — Preferences (light)Almost no colour. Hierarchy done entirely with neutrals + one accent on the toggle. Supabase — Preferences (dark)Study the surface steps: canvas, card, input. Three distinct greys, no shadows. Mixpanel — Dark dashboardA real data-viz palette under pressure: many series, one background. Posh — Dark analyticsNear-black canvas, single accent hue. Count how few colours are actually in play.
Task · ~60 minRe-point one token, watch a product change Open saas-tokens.css from the kits folder in any text editor. Change only the six --c-brand-* values in the primitive tier to a different hue (pick one, run it through a ramp generator, keep the same contrast targets). Save. Every button, link, focus ring, selected row and subtle brand background updates — and nothing else does. That five-minute experience is the entire argument for this module.

Design Systems · SaaS 3

Typography that scales

Systemized type = a fixed menu of styles so complete that nobody ever needs a one-off size again.

The two-axis scale (Untitled UI pattern)

StyleSize / LineNotes
Display 2xl → xs72/90 · 60/72 · 48/60 · 36/44 · 30/38 · 24/32Marketing + dashboard hero numbers; tracking −2%
Text xl → xs20/30 · 18/28 · 16/24 · 14/20 · 12/18Product UI; md(16) marketing body, sm(14) app default

Each size × weights regular/medium/semibold/bold = the full menu (~44 styles). Name as Display md/Semibold, Text sm/Regular. Add purpose-bound aliases sparingly (e.g., Code = mono sm).

System rules

  • One family (+ optional display face + mono). Must ship tabular figures for the dashboard half of your life.
  • Responsive behavior is a mapping, not new styles: "Display xl at desktop → Display md at mobile" — publish the map (marketing sizes step down 1–2 levels below 768px; product UI mostly doesn't change).
  • Dev mirror: sizes in rem, the scale as Tailwind fontSize config or CSS vars; line-heights baked into the token (size+line+tracking travel together, always).
  • Text color comes from the color system's text-* roles — type styles NEVER embed color.

The full scale — every row has a job

Two families, one file. Display sizes are for marketing pages and page titles; text sizes are for product UI. A scale with eleven steps sounds like a lot until you try to build a pricing page and a data table from the same six.

TokenSizeLine heightWeightTrackingUse it for
display-2xl72 px90 px (1.25)700-0.02emMarketing hero, once per site
display-xl60 px72 px (1.2)700-0.02emHero on secondary pages
display-lg48 px60 px (1.25)700-0.02emSection headline
display-md36 px44 px (1.22)600-0.02emMarketing page title
display-sm30 px38 px (1.27)6000App page title
display-xs24 px32 px (1.33)6000Section title, modal title
text-xl20 px30 px (1.5)6000Card title, big metric label
text-lg18 px28 px (1.55)6000Subsection heading, lead paragraph
text-md16 px24 px (1.5)4000Body — marketing and long-form
text-sm14 px20 px (1.43)4000Body — app UI, table cells, buttons
text-xs12 px18 px (1.5)5000Labels, badges, captions, table headers
Why 14 px is the app default and 16 px is the web defaultProduct UI is scanned, dense and read at close range with a mouse in hand; 14 px lets a table row stay 48 px tall. Marketing copy is read, in paragraphs, often on a phone — 16 px is the floor for comfortable reading. Same system, two defaults, documented so nobody has to ask.

Line height is a function of size, not a number you pick

Size rangeLine-height ratioReasoning
≥ 48 px (display)1.1 – 1.25Big type already has visual space; loose leading looks disconnected
24 – 36 px1.25 – 1.35Transition zone
16 – 20 px1.5Reading comfort — the WCAG 1.4.12 baseline too
12 – 14 px1.4 – 1.5Small text needs proportionally more air, not less
Single-line UI (buttons, table cells)1.0 – 1.2, or fixed heightLine height here is a layout tool, not a reading tool

Tracking follows the same inverse law: big type gets tighter, small type gets looser. Anything at 12 px in all-caps wants +0.04em or it turns into a smudge.

Responsive type — two strategies, know when to use each

Stepped (breakpoint swaps)Fluid (clamp())
Howdisplay-lg at ≥1024 px, display-md belowclamp(2rem, 1.46rem + 2.19vw, 3rem)
Use forProduct UI — predictable, easy to spec, easy to QAMarketing — no awkward jumps mid-resize
Watch outThe jump at the breakpoint is visible if the gap is > 8 pxUsers who zoom can get stuck — always set the min in rem, never vw alone

The kit ships fluid tokens for marketing in marketing-web-tokens.css and fixed tokens for app UI in saas-tokens.css. That split is deliberate — copy it.

The five type rules nobody writes down

  • Tabular numerals for anything comparable. Tables, prices, metrics, timers. font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums. Without it, digits jitter as values update and columns stop lining up.
  • Measure caps at 65–75 characters. On a 1440 px screen that means your paragraph column stops long before the container does. Use max-width: 65ch, not a pixel guess.
  • Two weights is a system; five is a mood board. 400 and 600 will carry an entire product. Add 700 only for display.
  • Never centre more than three lines. Ragged left edges destroy scanning speed.
  • Truncation is a spec, not an accident. Decide per component: single-line ellipsis, two-line clamp, or wrap. Then decide what the tooltip says.

Font stack decisions

SlotRecommendationWhy
UI / bodyInter, or the system stackDesigned for screens at small sizes; huge weight range; free; has tabular figures
Display / brandOne distinctive face, used above 30 px onlyThis is where brand lives. It does not belong in a table cell.
MonoJetBrains Mono / SF Mono / ui-monospaceCode, IDs, API keys, anything the user might copy

Performance is a design decision too: every weight is a file. Two weights of one variable font beats five static files, and a variable font lets engineering use any weight without asking you for another export.

Design Systems · SaaS 4

Spacing, grids, radius, shadows, z-index

The unglamorous scales that make 400 screens feel like one product.

The scales (steal these, then own them)

ScaleValuesNotes
Spacing0 · 2 · 4 · 6 · 8 · 12 · 16 · 20 · 24 · 32 · 40 · 48 · 64 · 80 · 96 · 128Named spacing-0.5…32 (÷4 = Tailwind numbering devs already speak)
Radiusnone · 2 · 4 · 6 · 8 · 10 · 12 · 16 · 24 · fullSemantic aliases: radius-input(8) · radius-card(12) · radius-modal(16); nested = outer − padding
Shadowsxs · sm · md · lg · xl · 2xl (two-layer, low alpha)Semantic: shadow-card(sm) · dropdown(lg) · modal(2xl); dark mode: shadows fade, borders/tone take over
Widthscontainer-sm 640 · md 768 · lg 1024 · xl 1280 · paragraph 45ch+ sidebar-width, modal sizes sm 400/md 480/lg 640
Z-indexdropdown 1000 · sticky 1100 · overlay 1200 · modal 1300 · popover 1400 · toast 1500 · tooltip 1600The scale nobody designs and everybody fights about — publish it and end the z-index:99999 wars

Grids for product vs marketing

  • App frame: fixed sidebar token (e.g., 280px) + fluid content with max-width option; content grid inside = 12-col/24px for dashboards, plain stacks for settings/forms.
  • Marketing: your Week-2 grid, tokenized: container-xl + 12 cols + gutter token + section-spacing scale (64/96/128/160).
  • Focus ring spec lives here too: 2px ring offset 2px in focus-ring color — one definition, every component inherits keyboard accessibility.
Developer mindsetEvery scale above becomes ~ten CSS variables or one Tailwind config block. When a designer uses 13px padding, the dev must either break the system or negotiate — spacing OFF the scale is a bug report against the design, not a nitpick.

Spacing — one 4 px base, and a documented job per step

A spacing scale is not "multiples of 8". It is a short list of allowed values — short enough that picking one is instant and every designer picks the same one.

TokenValueUse it for
space-14 pxIcon-to-label inside a badge; optical nudges only
space-28 pxIcon-to-label in a button; gap between chips
space-312 pxInput padding-x; label-to-field
space-416 pxThe default gap. Between form fields, between cards in a grid
space-520 pxRare — use when 16 crowds and 24 sprawls
space-624 pxCard padding. Grid gutter. Between grouped sections in a form
space-832 pxBetween distinct content blocks on a page
space-1040 pxPage content top offset
space-1248 pxBetween major page sections (app)
space-1664 pxSection rhythm on marketing, small screens
space-20 / space-24 / space-3280 / 96 / 128 pxMarketing section padding at desktop
The proximity law is the real ruleSpacing communicates grouping. The gap inside a group must always be smaller than the gap around it. A label 12 px above its input, and 24 px to the next field — read at a glance, that's four fields. Make both gaps 16 px and it reads as eight loose things. Most "this feels messy" feedback is this one mistake.

Grid and layout constants

TokenValueNote
container-max1280 pxApp content cap; marketing goes wider
container-gutter24 px16 px below 768 px
grid-columns124 at mobile, 8 at tablet
grid-gutter24 pxMatches space-6 — no coincidence
sidebar-width240 pxCollapsed: 64 px
topbar-height56 pxSticky; sets your scroll offset

Radius — personality in one scale

TokenValueApplied to
radius-none0Full-bleed media, table cells
radius-xs4 pxBadges, tooltips, checkbox
radius-sm6 pxButtons, inputs, selects — the workhorse
radius-md8 pxSmall cards, menu items
radius-lg12 pxCards, panels
radius-xl16 pxModals, drawers, large surfaces
radius-2xl24 pxMarketing feature cards, media
radius-full9999 pxAvatars, pills, switch, radio

Radius is one of the fastest brand levers you have: set buttons to radius-full and the product reads friendly and consumer; set them to radius-none and it reads technical and serious. Change it in one token and evaluate the whole product — that's the exercise.

Nesting rule: an inner radius should be the outer radius minus the padding. A 12 px card with 8 px padding wants inner elements at ~4 px. Concentric corners look intentional; parallel ones look like a mistake.

Shadows — an elevation ladder, not decoration

TokenMeaningValue
shadow-xsResting on the surface0 1px 2px 0 rgb(16 20 28 / .05)
shadow-smCard, slightly lifted0 1px 3px 0 rgb(16 20 28 / .10), 0 1px 2px -1px rgb(16 20 28 / .10)
shadow-mdHovering / dropdown0 4px 8px -2px rgb(16 20 28 / .10), 0 2px 4px -2px rgb(16 20 28 / .06)
shadow-lgPopover, menu0 12px 16px -4px rgb(16 20 28 / .08), 0 4px 6px -2px rgb(16 20 28 / .03)
shadow-xlDrawer0 20px 24px -4px rgb(16 20 28 / .08), 0 8px 8px -4px rgb(16 20 28 / .03)
shadow-2xlModal over a scrim0 24px 48px -12px rgb(16 20 28 / .18)
shadow-focusFocus glow (paired with the ring)0 0 0 4px rgb(98 85 236 / .24)
  • Two layers, always. A tight dark shadow for the contact edge plus a wide soft one for ambient light. One-layer shadows look like stickers.
  • Tint the shadow with your neutral hue, never pure black. rgb(16 20 28 / …) here — a cool near-black that matches the neutral ramp.
  • In dark mode, shadows stop working. Replace elevation-by-shadow with elevation-by-surface-tone: canvas 1000 → surface 950 → raised 900. Keep a hairline border for definition.

Borders

TokenWidthWhere
border-subtle1 pxDividers, table row rules — barely there by design
border-default1 pxInputs and cards at rest
border-strong1 pxHovered input, emphasised outline
border-focus2 px, 2 px offsetFocus ring — must reach 3:1 against both adjacent colours

Z-index — the layer contract

TokenValueLayer
z-base0Page content
z-docked10Sticky table header, floating action bar
z-dropdown1000Select menus, comboboxes
z-sticky1100Sticky top bar
z-banner1200Announcement bars
z-overlay1300Modal scrim
z-modal1400Modal / drawer panel
z-popover1500Popovers inside a modal
z-toast1600Toasts — above modals, always
z-tooltip1700Tooltips — above everything

Gaps of 100 are intentional: they leave room to slot something in later without renumbering. The day someone writes z-index: 9999 in your codebase is the day this table stopped being enforced.

Motion tokens

TokenValueUse
duration-instant75 msFocus ring, hover colour
duration-fast150 msButton states, tooltips, checkbox
duration-normal250 msDropdowns, accordions, toasts
duration-slow400 msModals, drawers, page transitions
ease-standardcubic-bezier(.2,0,0,1)Default for anything on-screen
ease-deceleratecubic-bezier(0,0,0,1)Things entering
ease-acceleratecubic-bezier(.3,0,1,1)Things leaving
ease-springcubic-bezier(.34,1.56,.64,1)Playful confirmation — sparingly

Every duration token collapses to 1 ms under prefers-reduced-motion. That is one media query in the kit, and it makes the entire system compliant.

Task · ~45 minThe hardcoded-value hunt Open any screen you designed in Weeks 5–7. Select every element and check: is each gap, radius and shadow a value from these tables? Log every violation. Then fix them and note which ones you can't fix without a new token — those are the genuine gaps in your scale, and the only legitimate reason to add a step.

Design Systems · SaaS 5

Core component specs

A component spec answers four questions: anatomy, variants, states, and content rules. Engineers read variants as props — spec in their shape and handoff becomes trivial.

Button — the reference spec (copy this rigor everywhere)

AxisValues
hierarchy (prop)primary · secondary · tertiary · link · destructive
size (prop)sm 36 · md 40 · lg 44 · xl 48 (px height; padding 12/14/16/18×2)
icon (prop)none · leading · trailing · icon-only (square, tooltip required)
statedefault · hover · focus (ring) · active · disabled · loading (spinner, width locked)
content rulesVerb-first labels · no wrapping · sentence case

In Figma: ONE component set, those axes as variant properties + boolean icon slots; every layer bound to semantic tokens. 5×4×4×6 = 480 combinations from one component — that's the leverage.

The core kit — spec highlights per component

  • Input: anatomy label / field / leading icon / trailing action / hint / error; sizes sm-md-lg matching buttons (forms align!); states default·hover·focus·filled·error·disabled·readonly; error replaces hint, never both.
  • Select & Combobox: input anatomy + menu (radius-input, shadow-dropdown, max-height + scroll, checkmark selected); combobox adds type-ahead + empty result state.
  • Checkbox / Radio / Switch: 16–20px marks, 44px row targets; indeterminate checkbox for "some children"; the switch=instant rule from Week 5 is now a documented content rule.
  • Badge/Tag: sizes sm/md; soft (color-50 bg + color-700 text) and solid variants; optional dot / dismiss X; semantic color prop, not arbitrary.
  • Avatar: 16→64px scale; image → initials → icon fallback chain; status dot slot; stack group with +N overflow.
  • Tooltip: side.align prop (top.center…), max-width 240, delay 300ms, never interactive content inside.
  • Dropdown menu: item anatomy (icon+label+shortcut+submenu-chevron), destructive item style, separators, 6px item radius inside 8px container.
Developer mindsetName variant properties EXACTLY as the code API will: variant, size, state, iconLeading. When Figma props equal React/Compose props, Code Connect and dev-mode handoff become copy-paste. Audit target: Untitled UI's button set — count its properties and match that discipline.

The button, fully specified

If you can spec a button completely, you can spec anything — it contains every problem the rest of the library has, in miniature. Here is the whole matrix, in tokens.

VariantRestHoverActiveDisabledUse when
Primarybg action-primary-bg
fg action-primary-fg		bg action-primary-bg-hoverbg action-primary-bg-activebg bg-disabled
fg text-disabled		The one action this screen exists for. Max one per view.
Secondarybg bg-surface
border border-default
fg text-primary		bg bg-hover
border border-strong		bg bg-activefg text-disabled, border border-subtleThe realistic alternative — Cancel, Back, secondary path
Tertiary / ghosttransparent
fg text-secondary		bg bg-hover
fg text-primary		bg bg-activefg text-disabledToolbar actions, table row actions, low-stakes repeats
Linkfg text-brand, underline on hoverfg text-brand + underlinefg brand-800fg text-disabledNavigational, inline in a sentence
Destructivebg action-danger-bg
fg action-danger-fg		bg danger-700bg danger-800bg bg-disabledDelete, remove, revoke — never the default focus
SizeHeightPadding XGapFontIconRadius
sm32 pxspace-36 pxtext-sm / 60016 pxradius-sm
md (default)40 pxspace-4space-2text-sm / 60020 pxradius-sm
lg48 pxspace-5space-2text-md / 60020 pxradius-sm
The two states everyone forgetsLoading — the label swaps for a spinner and the width locks, or your layout jumps and the user clicks the wrong thing. Focus-visible — a 2 px ring at 2 px offset, on every variant, tested against both the button fill and the page behind it. A ghost button on a white page and a ghost button on a grey toolbar need the ring to clear 3:1 in both places.

Text input — every state, in order

StateBorderBackgroundTextAlso
Restborder-defaultbg-surfacetext-primaryPlaceholder text-tertiary
Hoverborder-strongbg-surface—Cursor: text
Focusborder-focus 2 pxbg-surface—shadow-focus glow
Filledborder-default—text-primaryClear button appears if clearable
Errorborder-danger——Icon + message in text-danger below; aria-invalid, aria-describedby
Successsuccess-600——Only when confirmation genuinely helps (username availability)
Disabledborder-subtlebg-disabledtext-disabledNot focusable, not submitted
Read-onlynonetransparenttext-primaryFocusable and selectable — this is the difference from disabled

Anatomy, top to bottom: label (text-sm/500, never a placeholder standing in for one) → optional hint (text-xs, text-tertiary) → field (40 px, space-3 padding-x) → message slot that is always reserved, so the layout does not jump when an error appears.

Selection controls

ControlSizeRadiusSemanticsUse when
Checkbox16 px (20 px target padding to 44)radius-xsHas an indeterminate state — spec itZero-to-many, independent options
Radio16 pxradius-fullCannot be unselected once set — give a defaultExactly one of 2–5 visible options
Switch36 × 20 px, thumb 16 pxradius-fullTakes effect immediately — no Save buttonOn/off system settings
Select40 pxradius-smNative on mobile; custom listbox needs full ARIAOne of 6+ options
Segmented control32/40 pxradius-smRadio semantics with tab-like looks2–4 mutually exclusive views
Switch vs checkbox is a behaviour question, not a style questionA switch changes something now. A checkbox records an intention that a Save button commits later. Put a switch inside a form with a Save button and users will believe it already applied — then be annoyed when it didn't. This one distinction resolves about half of all settings-page bugs.

The small components

ComponentSpec essentialsTrap
Badge20/24 px tall, text-xs/500, radius-full or xs, subtle bg + matching 700 textColour alone carrying status — add the word
Avatarsizes 24/32/40/48/64, radius-full, initials fallback, group stacking with -8 px overlap and a "+N" chipNo fallback for missing images
Tooltiptext-xs, dark surface, radius-xs, 300 ms open delay / 0 ms close, 8 px offsetPutting actions or essential info inside — touch users never see it
Menu item32/36 px tall, icon + label + optional shortcut, bg-hover on hover and on keyboard focusHover and keyboard highlight looking different
Spinner16/20/24 px, 800 ms linear loop, currentColorUsing it for waits over 1 s — use a skeleton instead

See real component systems under load

WorkOS — form cardNote the disabled primary button: the form's state is visible before you type. Coinbase — modal formLabel above field, one primary action, generous 44px+ targets. Linear — PreferencesSwitches (instant) and selects (instant) — no Save button anywhere. Deliberate. Luma — SettingsTheme picker as image radios; per-row selects. Two selection patterns, one page.
Task · ~3 hrsSpec the button, then build it Open component-spec-template.md from the kits folder. Fill it in completely for your Button — all thirteen headings. Only then open Figma and build it: 5 variants × 3 sizes × 9 states, as one component set with properties named the way code will name them (variant, size, disabled, loading, iconLeading). Every colour bound to a semantic variable. If you find yourself picking a hex, stop — you're missing a token.

Design Systems · SaaS 6

Complex components, patterns & docs

Molecules become organisms: the composed components where most systems go vague — and where Linear-grade systems shine.

Composed component specs

  • Table: the Week-6 masterclass, tokenized — header cell / cell / row components; density prop (relaxed 48 / compact 36); column types (text, number-right-tabular, status-badge, actions); sort indicators; selection column + bulk bar; sticky header; pagination footer component; skeleton row variant.
  • Modal & Drawer: size prop (sm/md/lg/full); slots header/body/footer; overlay token; focus-trap + Esc as documented behavior; drawer widths 400/480/640.
  • Tabs: underline / pills / segmented variants; overflow behavior specced (scroll, not wrap).
  • Toast: semantic variants; placement token; duration 4–6s; action slot (Undo); stacking limit 3.
  • Date & range picker: calendar grid anatomy, presets column ("Last 30 days"), disabled dates, the input formats.
  • Command menu (⌘K): the Linear signature — input + grouped results + shortcut hints; empty & loading states.
  • Empty states: a real component (illustration slot / title / body / actions) so every team stops hand-rolling them.

Patterns & templates layer

Above components, publish page recipes: page header (title + meta + actions), settings section, filter bar, form layout (single column, 640 max, section groups), list page, detail page, dashboard grid. Templates are where consistency is actually won — two composed screens that both obey the components can still disagree; recipes prevent it.

Documentation standard (per component page)

SectionContains
OverviewWhat it is, when to use, when NOT to (link the alternative)
AnatomyNumbered diagram of parts
Variants & propsThe API table — mirrors code
BehaviorStates, keyboard map, focus order, motion
ContentVoice, casing, max lengths, truncation
AccessibilityRoles/labels, contrast notes, screen-reader behavior

Benchmark your docs against Polaris and Atlassian — you studied them as a consumer in Week 5; now you're the author.

The data table — the hardest component in SaaS

Tables are where systems break, because a table is not a component: it is a dozen components that must agree. Spec these ten things or engineering will invent them.

CapabilitySpec
Row densityCompact 36 px · Default 48 px · Comfortable 60 px. A user preference, persisted.
Header40 px, text-xs/500, text-secondary, uppercase optional, sticky on scroll
SortClick header toggles asc → desc → none. Arrow icon shows current state. Sorted column header gets text-primary.
SelectionCheckbox column, 44 px wide. Header checkbox = select-all-on-page with an indeterminate state. Selecting reveals a bulk-action bar — spec where it appears and what it covers.
Row actionsGhost icon buttons revealed on hover and on keyboard focus, plus an always-present overflow menu. Hover-only actions are inaccessible.
Column controlResize (drag handle, min width), reorder, show/hide. Persist per user.
OverflowPer column: truncate with tooltip, wrap to 2 lines, or horizontal scroll with a frozen first column. Decide once, per column type.
PaginationPage size selector + range label ("21–40 of 312"). Or infinite scroll — but then you owe a "load more" fallback and a working keyboard path.
NumbersRight-aligned, tabular numerals, consistent decimal places, units in the header not the cell.
StatesLoading (skeleton rows, same height), empty (three kinds — see below), error, partial/stale.

Overlays — one decision table, argued once

PatternUse whenNever whenDismiss
ModalA short, focused, blocking task — confirm, quick create, destructive checkThe task is long, or the user needs the page behind itEsc, scrim click, ✕, Cancel
DrawerA longer form or a detail view where page context still mattersThe content deserves its own URLEsc, scrim click, ✕
PopoverSmall contextual controls anchored to a trigger — filters, date pickerIt contains a form with more than three fieldsEsc, outside click
Inline expandEdits belonging to a row or cardIt pushes everything below off-screenSave / Cancel
Full pageMulti-step, shareable, or resumable workIt's a two-field editNavigation

Every overlay owes you the same six things: a focus trap, focus returned to the trigger on close, Esc to dismiss, a scroll lock on the body, aria-modal plus a labelled title, and a documented behaviour for what happens if the user has unsaved changes.

Feedback — pick the right channel

ChannelScopeDurationUse for
Inline messageOne fieldUntil fixedValidation. Always the first choice.
ToastApp-wide4–6 s, pausing on hoverConfirmation of a completed action; must be dismissible and must never carry the only copy of important info
BannerPage or appUntil dismissed or resolvedSystem status, plan limits, required action
DialogBlockingUntil answeredDestructive confirmation only — and put the object's name in the sentence

Toast spec: 380 px wide, top-right or bottom-centre (choose one for the whole product), stacks to max 3, z-toast, role="status" for success and role="alert" for errors, an Undo action wherever undo is technically possible. Undo beats confirm. A dialog costs every user a click to protect against a rare mistake; undo costs only the person who made it.

Command menu — the power-user surface

Once your app has more than about 20 destinations, a command menu stops being a flourish and starts being the primary navigation for your best users.

  • Trigger: ⌘K / Ctrl-K, plus a visible search affordance for people who don't know the shortcut.
  • Structure: input → grouped results (Actions, Recent, Pages, Search results) → footer showing key hints.
  • Behaviour: fuzzy match, keyboard-only navigation, Enter executes, Esc closes, first item selected by default. The highlight must be identical for mouse hover and arrow-key focus.
  • Content: every item needs an icon, a label, and — where ambiguous — a context breadcrumb. Show shortcuts inline; the menu teaches them.
Vapi — command menuGrouped Actions / Recent / All Pages, with section context on every row. Juicebox — command menuNote the left bar marking the focused row, and the key-hint footer teaching shortcuts. StackAI — command menuTwo-line rows with descriptions — richer, slower to scan. A real trade-off.

Empty states — three different components wearing one name

KindMessage jobPrimary action
First runTeach what will live here and why it's worth creatingCreate — plus a template or sample-data shortcut
Cleared outCongratulate, don't instruct. They know what this is.Quiet; maybe "View archived"
No resultsSay what was searched and offer an escapeClear filters · broaden search · create with this name
Laravel Cloud — first-run emptyIllustration, one sentence, one button. Plus a toast confirming the delete that caused it. Hashnode — empty guideThe illustration previews the thing you'd create. Cheap, effective. Contractbook — empty teamDashed container makes the emptiness intentional rather than broken.

Page templates — the layer above components

A mature system ships templates, not just parts. Six cover almost all of SaaS: list/index, detail, settings, dashboard, wizard, auth. Each template fixes the page header, the action placement, the empty and loading states and the responsive behaviour — so a new feature takes an afternoon instead of a week of layout debate.

Documentation standards

Every component page carries the same nine sections, in the same order: purpose · anatomy · properties · states · sizing · behaviour · accessibility · do/don't · related. That order is itself a design decision — it front-loads what a developer needs and back-loads what a designer needs. Add a changelog and a status (draft / review / stable / deprecated) so consumers know what they can rely on.

The real definition of doneA developer can build the component without asking you a single question. Run that test on your own docs by handing a spec to someone and answering nothing.
Task · ~3 hrsSpec the table, then design its five states Write the full table spec against the ten capabilities above. Then design the same table five times: ideal, loading (skeleton rows at exact row height), empty-first-run, no-results, and error. Then design the bulk-action bar that appears on selection. Most designers have never drawn four of these six — which is exactly why they get invented badly in code.

Design Systems · SaaS · Practice

Practice: build & publish your system

The capstone of this module is a real, publishable system file — the single most valuable portfolio artifact a product designer can own.

Task 1 · ~2 hrsFoundations file Collections: Primitives (color ramps incl. alpha, spacing, radius, shadow styles as effects) + Semantic with Light/Dark modes (the full mapping table from lesson 2). Type styles: the full two-axis menu. Publish as a library.
Task 2 · ~3 hrsComponent file Build to spec: Button (full matrix), Input, Select, Checkbox/Radio/Switch, Badge, Avatar, Tooltip, Dropdown menu, Tabs, Modal shell, Toast, Table (header/row/cell + density). Every fill/stroke/text bound to semantic variables — switch the page to Dark mode and NOTHING should need manual fixing. That's the pass/fail test.
Task 3 · ~1 hrAudit against the masters Open Untitled UI (and linear.app in devtools) beside your system. Three columns: what they have that you missed / what's identical (validation) / what you deliberately did differently and why. Fix the misses that matter.
DeliverableA published two-file system (foundations + components) that survives the dark-mode flip test, plus the audit memo. Rebuild one Week-6 dashboard screen using ONLY the system to prove coverage.

Start from the kit, not from zero

Files for this practiceIn the Design System Kits folder beside this course file: README.md (read first) · saas-tokens.css · saas-tokens.json (DTCG) · saas-tokens.figma.json (variable import) · saas-tokens.tailwind.css · component-spec-template.md · audit-checklist.md. These are a working system, not a demo — your job is to make them yours.

The build, in six checkpoints

Checkpoint 1 · ~90 minFoundations into Figma Create the file [Your Brand] Design System with pages: 0 · Getting started, 1 · Foundations, 2 · Components, 3 · Patterns, 4 · Templates, 5 · Changelog.
Build three variable collections — Primitives (no modes), Semantic (modes: Light, Dark), Scale. Import saas-tokens.figma.json, then re-point every semantic variable to a primitive alias. Verify by switching the mode: if anything doesn't change, it's still a hardcoded hex.
Done when: flipping one mode switch turns your whole Foundations page dark, correctly.
Checkpoint 2 · ~60 minDocument the foundations On page 1, build swatch sheets for every ramp (with the step→contrast table from lesson d1.2), the full type scale rendered live, the spacing scale as visual bars, the radius scale, the shadow ladder, and the z-index list. This page is what you show in an interview — make it presentable.
Done when: someone who has never seen your system can pick the right token from this page alone.
Checkpoint 3 · ~4 hrsThe eight core components Button · Input · Select · Checkbox/Radio/Switch · Badge · Avatar · Tooltip · Menu item. Each one: full variant set, every state from the d1.5 tables, all colours bound to Semantic, auto-layout throughout, properties named as code will name them.
Done when: you can build a settings screen using only instances, changing nothing but content.
Checkpoint 4 · ~4 hrsThe five complex components Data table (with all ten capabilities from d1.6) · Modal · Tabs · Toast · Empty state (all three kinds). Then assemble two page templates: a list page and a settings page, built exclusively from your instances.
Done when: the table renders correctly in all five screen states without detaching anything.
Checkpoint 5 · ~2 hrsWrite the docs Fill component-spec-template.md for Button, Input and Table — completely, all thirteen headings. Write the 0 · Getting started page: what this system is, how to use the variables, how to request a change, what "stable" means.
Done when: you hand the Button spec to a friend and they ask you zero questions.
Checkpoint 6 · ~90 minAudit, fix, publish Run audit-checklist.md end to end and score yourself honestly. Fix every ✗ in sections 1–3 (tokens, colour, components) before publishing. Then publish the library, install it in a fresh file, and rebuild one Week 7 screen from it.
Done when: the rebuilt screen took under 30 minutes. That number is the whole return on this module.

Benchmark against the professionals

Open Untitled UI, Shopify Polaris and Adobe Spectrum side by side with your file. For each of your eight core components, list three things they specified that you didn't. Those thirty-odd items are your v1.1 backlog — and the honest measure of the gap between a UI kit and a design system.

Portfolio noteThis module produces the strongest single artefact in the whole course. A published Figma library with documented tokens, a filled spec sheet and a scored audit is the piece that gets design-system roles. Screenshot the foundations page, the button matrix and the table's five states — that's three slides of a case study you now own.

Design Systems · Websites 1

Marketing system foundations

A marketing site system shares your SaaS foundations but obeys different physics: pages ship weekly, non-designers edit content, and type must be fluid.

What changes vs the app system

ConcernApp systemMarketing system
TypeFixed sizes per breakpoint mapFluid: sizes as clamp(min, vw-based, max) — Display 2xl might be clamp(40px, 5vw+16px, 72px). Publish min/max pairs per style.
Spacing4px component scale+ a section-spacing scale (section-sm 64 · md 96 · lg 128 · xl 160, halved on mobile) — the rhythm OF the page
LayoutApp shell + templatescontainer tokens + the 12-col grid + full-bleed-background/contained-content as a codified pattern
ColorStrict semantic rolesSame roles + section themes: light / gray / dark / brand section variants every block must support
ArtIcons, product shotsArt-direction slots: defined image ratios, illustration style rules, screenshot framing recipes (browser chrome, tilt, glow)

Reuse layer 1 primitives from your SaaS system verbatim — one brand, one set of ramps. The marketing system is a second SEMANTIC + component layer on the same foundation, not a second brand.

What changes when the system leaves the app

Product system (d1)Marketing system (d2)
TypeFixed scale, swapped at breakpointsFluid — clamp() from 390 px to 1440 px
SpacingComponent-level, 4 px baseSection-level rhythm — 48→160 px, fluid
ContainerOne max width, one gutterFive: prose · narrow · default · wide · full-bleed
ComponentsTake props (variant, size, state)Take content (eyebrow, headline, media, CTA, proof)
VariationRigidly constrainedArt-directable within slots
ColourLight + dark modesSection themes — default · alt · inverse · brand
MotionState transitionsScroll reveals — and never above the fold

Both systems share the same primitives. The kit reflects this: marketing-web-tokens.css loads on top of saas-tokens.css and only adds what marketing needs.

Fluid type — the tokens and the maths

clamp(min, preferred, max): the browser uses preferred unless it falls outside the bounds. The preferred value mixes a rem base with a vw slope so the type grows with the viewport.

TokenRangeclamp()
--fluid-display-2xl40 → 72 pxclamp(2.5rem, 1.29rem + 4.95vw, 4.5rem)
--fluid-display-xl36 → 60 pxclamp(2.25rem, 1.41rem + 3.43vw, 3.75rem)
--fluid-display-lg32 → 48 pxclamp(2rem, 1.46rem + 2.19vw, 3rem)
--fluid-display-md28 → 36 pxclamp(1.75rem, 1.42rem + 1.33vw, 2.25rem)
--fluid-lead18 → 20 pxclamp(1.125rem, 1.04rem + 0.33vw, 1.25rem)
--fluid-body16 → 17 pxclamp(1rem, 0.96rem + 0.17vw, 1.0625rem)
The zoom trapAlways express the min in rem, never in vw alone. A pure-vw size ignores the user's browser zoom, which breaks WCAG 1.4.4 (resize text to 200%). The rem floor is what keeps fluid type accessible.

In Figma you cannot express clamp(). Design at three widths — 390 · 834 · 1440 — and put the clamp values in the handoff note. That note is the deliverable; the frames are just evidence.

Section rhythm — the layout system of a marketing page

TokenRangeUse
--section-pad-sm48 → 72 pxDense utility sections — logo wall, breadcrumb strip
--section-pad-md64 → 112 pxDefault for every content section
--section-pad-lg80 → 160 pxHero, final CTA — the two sections that get room
--section-gap48 pxHeadline block → content within a section

A long page stays readable because of alternation, not decoration: default surface → alt tint → default → inverse. Three or four alternations across a page give the eye somewhere to rest and make each section feel finished.

Containers

TokenWidthUse
--container-prose65chBlog posts, docs — measure-bound, not pixel-bound
--container-narrow720 pxCentred hero copy, CTA blocks
--container-default1200 pxStandard section content
--container-wide1440 pxFeature grids, logo walls, screenshots
--container-full100%Full-bleed media and colour bands

Gutters: 20 px mobile, 40 px desktop. Note these are wider than the app's 16/24 — marketing pages breathe, apps pack.

Task · ~60 minMeasure a real page against these tokens Open linear.app or vanta.com with DevTools. Measure: section top/bottom padding at 1440 and at 390 · container max width · hero headline size at both widths · gap between headline and subtext. Write the numbers down, then compare to the tables above. Where they differ, decide whether it is a better decision or just a different one — and be able to say why.

Design Systems · Websites 2

Sectionized components & content props

The unit of a marketing system isn't the button — it's the SECTION. Design sections as components with content props and a marketer can assemble a landing page without you.

The section library (each with variants + theme prop)

  • Nav: simple / with-dropdown / mega; transparent-over-hero + solid-on-scroll behavior documented.
  • Hero: centered / split / with-form / full-bleed — props: eyebrow, title, body, primary+secondary CTA, media slot.
  • Logo bar · Feature trio · Zig-zag row · Bento grid · Stats band · Testimonial (single/wall) · Pricing (cards + comparison) · FAQ (accordion) · Final CTA · Footer (slim/mega).
  • Every section supports the four section themes and defines its mobile stacking — that's what makes assembly safe.

CMS thinking (the developer-mindset core of this module)

Engineers will bind your sections to CMS models: every text you drew becomes a field with a max length, every image a slot with a ratio, every list a repeatable (3–6 items). Design the worst legal content for each prop — longest headline, 6 features, missing image — and the section must survive. A section that only works with the lorem you chose isn't a component; it's a poster.

Practice · ~2 hrsAssemble-without-designing test Build 8 sections as components with content props + theme variants. Then rebuild your Week-7 landing page purely by INSTANTIATING them — zero detaching. Anything you had to detach reveals a missing prop; fix the component, not the page.

Sections as components with content slots

A marketing system's unit is not the button — it is the section. Spec each one as a component whose props are content slots, and a page becomes an ordered list of sections a marketer can reorder without you.

SectionContent slotsVariants
Navlogo · links[] · dropdown mega-panel · CTA primary · CTA secondarytransparent-over-hero · solid · sticky-condensed · mobile drawer
Heroeyebrow · headline · subhead · CTA primary · CTA secondary · media · proof stripcentred · split L/R · full-bleed media · video
Logo walllabel · logos[] (6–12)static · marquee · grid
Featureeyebrow · headline · body · bullets[] · media · linkmedia-left · media-right · media-below · 3-up grid
Testimonialquote · avatar · name · role · company logo · metricsingle large · 3-up cards · carousel · logo+quote strip
Pricingtiers[] (name · price · period · description · features[] · CTA · badge) · toggle · comparison table3-tier cards · 4-tier · table-only · cards + table
FAQitems[] (question · answer)accordion · two-column · linked to docs
CTA bandheadline · body · CTA primary · CTA secondarydefault · inverse · brand · with media
Footerlogo · columns[] (title · links[]) · newsletter · social · legal · localecompact · full · with newsletter
Why slots and not just "design the page"Because a marketing site changes weekly and you will not be there for most of it. If the pricing section is a component with a tiers[] slot, adding a fourth plan is a content edit. If it's a hand-built frame, it's a design ticket — every time, forever.

Pricing — the hardest marketing section

It carries the most decisions per pixel. Spec: tier count (3 is the sweet spot; 4 needs a comparison table), the recommended badge and how it visually elevates one card, monthly/annual toggle plus how the saving is expressed, feature lists as "everything in X, plus…" versus full lists, and what happens when a tier is "Contact us" instead of a number.

Vanta — 3-tier cards"Everything in X, plus…" pattern. Middle card elevated by border, not colour. OpenTable — badged tiersEvery tier gets a badge, which weakens all three. A real, instructive mistake. Sprig — feature comparisonGrouped feature blocks with aligned rows across all three columns.

Footer — the section that proves your system works

It is the densest, most link-heavy, most-often-neglected surface on a site. If your tokens hold up here they hold up anywhere.

Maze — 5 columns + newsletterOversized wordmark as a brand moment. Count the column rhythm. Employment Hero — max densitySix columns, region picker, consent checkboxes, locale selector. Everything, at once. In Common With — editorialSame slots, completely different personality. Type and rules only.

CMS thinking — write the content model

Every slot needs three answers before it ships: required or optional, character limit, and what happens when it's missing. Write them as a table next to each section. It looks bureaucratic and it saves the site — because a headline slot with no maximum length will receive an eighty-word headline, and you will not be in the room.

SlotRequiredLimitFallback
Hero eyebrowNo24 charsHide, close the gap
Hero headlineYes60 chars (2 lines at 1440)—
Hero subheadNo140 charsHide, headline gains bottom margin
Hero mediaNo16:9 or 4:5Layout falls back to centred variant
Testimonial metricNo12 charsHide row

Marketing motion

One pattern, three tokens: fade + 24 px rise, 600 ms, cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1), 80 ms stagger between siblings, triggered once at 20% visibility. Never animate above the fold — the hero must be readable the instant the page paints. And every value collapses to zero under prefers-reduced-motion.

Task · ~4 hrsBuild the section library Build nine section components — nav, hero, logo wall, feature, testimonial, pricing, FAQ, CTA band, footer — each with named content-slot properties and its variants. Then compose two complete landing pages from instances only: your SaaS product, and one page in a totally different industry (a restaurant, a law firm, a fitness studio). Same components, different content and one changed brand token.
If the second page needs a new component, your slots were too narrow. That failure is the real lesson of this exercise — go back and widen them.

Design Systems · iOS 1

iOS-native tokens & the SwiftUI mindset

On iOS you don't invent a token system — Apple already ships one inside the OS. An iOS design system is a thin, disciplined brand layer over the system tokens.

The system IS the token set

Your SaaS tokeniOS-native equivalent
Type scaleThe 11 Dynamic Type styles (LargeTitle…Caption2) — never freeze px sizes
text-primary/secondary…label / secondaryLabel / tertiaryLabel / quaternaryLabel
bg rolessystemBackground trio + systemGroupedBackground trio
borderseparator / opaqueSeparator
brand-solidONE tint color (your only real brand decision)
Elevation/overlayMaterials (ultraThin→thick) + vibrancy
Icon systemSF Symbols with weight/scale/rendering config
Spacing8pt rhythm + 16/20 layout margins (convention, codify yours on top)

What you ADD: tint, custom semantic accents mapped for both appearances + Increase Contrast, brand display font (headers only; body stays Dynamic-Type-capable), spacing conventions, and any product-specific components (charts, cards) — each built FROM the system tokens.

Developer mindsetSwiftUI has no stylesheet — styling is semantic modifiers: .font(.headline), .foregroundStyle(.secondary), .background(.regularMaterial). A custom "12.5px #6B7280" has NO natural home in that code; "subheadline / secondaryLabel" is one line. Your system's quality is measured by how rarely a dev must leave Apple's vocabulary.

Dynamic Type — your type tokens, already built

You do not build a type scale on iOS. You adopt one, and the OS resizes it for every user. Sizes shown at the Large (default) setting.

Text styleSizeLine heightWeightUse for
Large Title34 pt41 ptRegularScroll-to-top screen title
Title 128 pt34 ptRegularSection screen title
Title 222 pt28 ptRegularProminent card heading
Title 320 pt25 ptRegularSub-section heading
Headline17 pt22 ptSemiboldRow title, emphasised body
Body17 pt22 ptRegularDefault reading text
Callout16 pt21 ptRegularSlightly de-emphasised body
Subheadline15 pt20 ptRegularSecondary row text
Footnote13 pt18 ptRegularTimestamps, attribution
Caption 112 pt16 ptRegularCaptions, tags
Caption 211 pt13 ptRegularSmallest permissible label
The test everyone skipsSet your device to AX3 and open your design. Rows must reflow to vertical stacks — label above value — not truncate. If your two-column row becomes an ellipsis at AX3, the layout is wrong, not the setting. Roughly a third of iPhone users run larger-than-default text.

Semantic colours — the real iOS token sheet

GroupTokensRule
Textlabel · secondaryLabel · tertiaryLabel · quaternaryLabel · placeholderTextFour levels only. If you need a fifth, your hierarchy is too deep.
Background — standardsystemBackground · secondarySystemBackground · tertiarySystemBackgroundUse on screens not built from grouped lists
Background — groupedsystemGroupedBackground · secondarySystemGroupedBackground · tertiarySystemGroupedBackgroundUse on Settings-style inset-grouped screens
FillssystemFill → quaternarySystemFillLayered fills for chips, thumbnails, small controls
Separatorsseparator · opaqueSeparatorThe first lets background through; the second doesn't
TinttintColor / accentColorYour brand. Very nearly the only colour you supply.
The grouped/standard mistakeMixing the two background families is the most common iOS colour error, and it is invisible in light mode. In dark mode the grouped canvas is darker than the standard one, so a card that looked fine suddenly floats on the wrong grey. Pick one family per screen and stay in it.

Dark mode is two systems, not one

iOS dark mode has a base and an elevated level. Anything presented over content — sheets, popovers, alerts — automatically uses elevated variants. This is precisely why hard-coding a dark grey breaks: the OS wants to lighten that surface and your literal value refuses. Elevation on dark is expressed as a lighter surface, exactly like the web kit's bg-surface-raised.

Materials and vibrancy

.ultraThinMaterial → .thinMaterial → .regularMaterial → .thickMaterial → .ultraThickMaterial. Always pair with vibrancy label styles so text stays legible over whatever is behind. Materials belong to chrome floating over content — nav bars, tab bars, sheets — never to the content itself.

SF Symbols as icon tokens

AxisValuesRule
WeightUltralight → BlackMatch the weight of the text beside it
ScaleSmall · Medium · LargeMedium default; Large for standalone actions
RenderingMonochrome · Hierarchical · Palette · MulticolorPick one per surface and hold it
Variable value0.0 – 1.0Progress-style symbols (wifi, volume, battery)

The SwiftUI mindset

SwiftUI code reads almost exactly like a good design spec: .font(.headline), .foregroundStyle(.secondary), .background(.regularMaterial). Semantic names, not numbers — which means if your spec says "17 pt, #3C3C43 at 60%", you have made the developer's job harder. Say "Subheadline, secondaryLabel" instead and the code writes itself. This is the single highest-leverage habit change for a designer moving to native work.

Reference sheetDesign System Kits/ios-tokens-reference.md holds all of the above plus layout metrics, motion springs and the short list of what you actually supply versus what you inherit.

Design Systems · iOS 2

Library from Apple Design Resources

Your iOS library starts as Apple's official kit, re-themed — not a from-scratch rebuild.

Build order

  • 1. Import the Apple Design Resources Figma libraries (iOS UI kit + SF Symbols). These carry correct metrics for bars, lists, sheets, keyboards.
  • 2. Tokenize: recreate the semantic color table as Figma variables with Light/Dark modes (Apple publishes the exact values); bind the kit's detachable pieces to your variables where you extend them.
  • 3. Brand layer: tint variable; your accent set; brand type style aliases pointing at Dynamic Type sizes; app-specific components (stat card, chart frame, paywall) built from system parts.
  • 4. Templates: tab shell, list screen (plain + inset-grouped), detail push, sheet (med/large detents), settings, onboarding, paywall — each in both appearances at 393×852 + one 375 stress frame.

Handoff mapping table (publish this with the library)

Design elementDev receives
Text style "Headline".font(.headline)
Color "text/secondary".secondary / UIColor.secondaryLabel
Row spacing 16default List insets — "no custom padding"
Sheet medium→large.presentationDetents([.medium,.large])
Symbol "gearshape, semibold, medium"Image(systemName:) + config

What Apple actually ships you

ResourceContainsUse it for
iOS UI Kit (Figma)Every system component, both appearances, real Dynamic Type stylesYour library's foundation — never redraw a tab bar
Device templatesCurrent iPhone and iPad frames with correct safe areasLayout and App Store screenshots
SF Pro / SF Compact / SF MonoThe system faces, all weights and optical sizesInstall locally before you design anything
SF Symbols library6000+ symbols with configurationIcons — before you draw a single custom one
watchOS / iPadOS / macOS kitsSame, per platformModule d5 and any multi-device work

Structure your iOS library

Three layers, and the discipline is knowing which layer a thing belongs to:

LayerContentsRule
1 · Apple, untouchedTab bar, nav bar, alerts, action sheets, pickers, switches, system list rowsNever restyle. Restyling these is how apps end up feeling wrong.
2 · Apple, themedButtons (tint), segmented controls, list rows with your content, sheetsChange the tint and the content. Not the metrics.
3 · YoursYour card, your empty state, your chart, your onboarding, your brand illustrationThis is where the whole design system lives. Spec it fully.
Why so little is "yours"Because the value of designing on iOS is that a billion people already know how it works. Every system component you replace is a small tax on every user. Spend your design budget on layer 3, where it buys something.

Handoff — map every spec to a SwiftUI concept

You sayThey write
"Body, secondary".font(.body).foregroundStyle(.secondary)
"Grouped inset list"List { }.listStyle(.insetGrouped)
"Sheet, medium detent".sheet { }.presentationDetents([.medium])
"Standard margins".padding() — already 16/20 pt by context
"Card on secondary grouped background".background(Color(.secondarySystemGroupedBackground))
"Symbol, matches label weight"Image(systemName:).imageScale(.medium)

Write your specs in the left column. A developer reading it has nothing to translate — and nothing to translate means nothing to get wrong.

Study real iOS systems

Todoist — grouped settingsGrouped background family, section footers explaining each switch. Textbook. Gentler Streak — themed rowsSystem list metrics kept; only the tint and typography carry the brand. Wispr Flow — cards over groupedCustom card rows inside a grouped screen. Layer 3 done well.
Task · ~2.5 hrsBuild layer 3 Import the Apple iOS UI Kit into a fresh Figma file. Set your tint colour once. Then design only your layer 3 components: card, list row variant, empty state, chart, onboarding page. Every text layer bound to a Dynamic Type style; every colour either semantic or your tint. Then duplicate the page and switch to dark — if you have to change anything by hand, you used a literal somewhere.

Design Systems · iOS 3

Theming the iOS way

iOS theming is deliberately narrow — and that narrowness is the design system.

  • Tint is the theme: one accent propagates to buttons, links, toggles, selection, nav items. Multi-accent brands pick ONE for interaction and demote the rest to illustration/data colors.
  • Dark = elevated stack: base systemBackground (true black-ish) → secondary/tertiary elevate; sheets get the elevated variant automatically. Custom surfaces must define both appearances + both elevation levels — a 4-value table per surface.
  • Accessibility variants are part of the theme: Increase Contrast (borders appear, colors deepen), Bold Text, Reduce Transparency (materials → solid). Ship a variant table for your custom colors across these — Apple's own colors already comply.
  • What you DON'T theme: control shapes, nav metrics, motion physics. Fighting those reads as broken, not branded. Brand lives in tint, type display moments, iconography style, illustration, and tone of voice.
Practice · ~2 hrsRe-skin proof Take your x1 practice screens; swap the tint + accent variables to a totally different brand. If the app rebrands convincingly from variables alone, your iOS system works. Then flip Increase Contrast mentally: audit which custom colors would fail and add their variants.

Theming iOS: change the tint, not the system

LeverWhat it movesCost of overusing
Tint / accentEvery button, link, selected state, switch, slider, active tabNone — this is the intended lever
Display typefaceTitles above 20 pt onlyBody in a custom face loses Dynamic Type reliability
Corner radius on your cardsLayer-3 componentsNothing, as long as system sheets keep their radius
Illustration & icon styleEmpty states, onboarding, marketing surfacesNothing — this is where brand should live
Restyling system componentsEverythingHigh. Users feel it as "this app is weird" without knowing why

One tint, one display face, one illustration style. That is a complete iOS brand system — and products like Todoist, Things and Bear are built on exactly that much.

Dark mode variants

Your tint needs a dark-mode sibling. A 600-level brand colour that reads confidently on white will look muddy on near-black; go two steps lighter and slightly less saturated — the same 600 → 400 move from the web kit. Verify both against the surface they sit on: 3:1 for a filled control, 4.5:1 for tinted text.

Apple Fitness — darkApple's own tint discipline: one accent green, everything else neutral. Calm — dark with imageryElevated surfaces over photography; note the tab bar material. KOHO — high-chroma accent on darkA bright lime CTA against near-black. Check its contrast yourself — this is the edge of safe.

Accessibility variants your system owes

SettingWhat your design must do
Increase ContrastSemantic colours shift automatically — but your tint and custom colours don't. Supply a high-contrast variant of each.
Reduce TransparencyMaterials become opaque. Verify text on your blurred chrome still works when the blur is gone.
Reduce MotionSlides become cross-fades. Parallax and auto-playing motion stop.
Bold TextEverything gains weight. Tight layouts break — test it.
Larger Text (AX1–AX5)Rows reflow to vertical stacks. Never truncate essential content.
Button ShapesText buttons gain visible backgrounds. Confirm your layout absorbs that.

Six settings, six variants to check. Do it once as a checklist page in your library and it becomes a five-minute pass instead of a rediscovery every project.

Task · ~90 minThe six-setting audit Take your layer-3 components from the last lesson. Produce a single Figma page showing each one under: default, dark, Increase Contrast, Bold Text, AX3, and Reduce Transparency. Mark every failure. Fix the failures. This page is a portfolio piece in its own right — very few designers have one.
