Craft · No-Code Build · Practice

Practice: build and publish a real site

The capstone of this track. Not a mockup — a live URL you can send to someone.

Checkpoint 1 · ~30 minPick the project and the tool Choose one: your own portfolio, the Week 7 landing page, or a real site for a person or business you know (the strongest option — real content, real constraints, real feedback). Then answer the four decision questions from lesson c4.1 in writing and commit to a tool.
Checkpoint 2 · ~2 hrsModel the content first Before opening the builder: list every collection, every field, every field's type, limit, and required/optional status. Write the absent-state rule for each optional field. Then write the real copy for the whole site. Building before the copy exists is why so many portfolio sites never launch.
Checkpoint 3 · ~6–10 hrsBuild it Structure and layout first, at desktop; then tablet and mobile. Use the token values from your design-system kit for type, spacing, radius and colour — that's what they're for. No motion yet.
Done when: the site is complete, responsive, and boring. Motion goes on a finished skeleton, never on a half-built one.
Checkpoint 4 · ~3 hrsAdd the craft layer Now add, in this order: scroll reveals with a consistent stagger; the sticky nav condense; one signature moment (a Unicorn Studio hero, a Spline object, a Rive icon set, or one GSAP sequence); page-transition treatment; and hover states everywhere including the animated link underline.
Budget: one heavy effect. Everything else must be cheap.
Checkpoint 5 · ~2 hrsThe pre-launch pass Run the full lesson c4.3 sequence: SEO fields on every page, OG image designed and verified, images converted and lazy-loaded, fonts subset, Lighthouse on mobile, WAVE for accessibility, tab through the whole site, reduced-motion check, 404 page, and cross-browser testing. Record your Lighthouse scores before and after the fixes.
Checkpoint 6 · ~1 hrPublish, then get scored Connect a domain and publish. Then score it yourself against the Awwwards rubric — Design 40%, Usability 30%, Creativity 20%, Content 10% — and have two other people do the same blind. Write down the three lowest-scoring items and fix them.
Optional: submit it. Even a rejection returns a jury score, which is more specific feedback than most designers ever receive.

Self-review

CheckPass condition
ConceptOne sentence, written down, and every section obeys it
ContentReal copy and real imagery. Zero lorem ipsum, zero stock-photo placeholders.
TypeTracking corrected at display sizes; headline line breaks controlled at both widths
PaletteThree colours or fewer, all contrast-passing
MotionOne signature effect; consistent stagger and easing everywhere else
Reduced motionComplete, usable page — not a broken one
PerformanceLighthouse mobile 90+ on all four categories
CLSUnder 0.1 — every image and embed has explicit dimensions
KeyboardWhole site navigable, focus always visible
DetailsFavicon, OG image, 404, selection colour, animated link underline
MobileTested on a real mid-range phone on real mobile data
Portfolio noteA live URL beats twenty Figma frames. Present it as a case study: the concept sentence, the content model, the before/after Lighthouse scores, the one signature effect and why, the reduced-motion variant, and your rubric scores. That structure shows judgement, not just taste — and judgement is what gets hired.

AI · Design Process 1

What AI is actually good at — and what it isn't

Roughly 72% of designers now use generative AI in their work, and those who do report meaningfully higher job satisfaction. But the gap between designers who get real leverage from it and those who get slop is not the tool — it's knowing precisely where the line falls.

In plain wordsA language model is a very fast, very well-read assistant with no judgement, no memory of your project, and a habit of stating guesses as facts. It is superb at volume, structure and first drafts. It is unreliable at truth, taste and context. Every technique in this module is a way of using the first three while covering for the last three.

The capability map

AI is genuinely good atAI is unreliable at
Generating 20 variations when you have 2Telling you which of the 20 is right
Summarising and clustering large volumes of textKnowing which cluster actually matters to the business
Rewriting, reformatting, converting between structuresFacts, statistics, citations — it will invent them fluently
First drafts of copy, specs, research plans, test scriptsFinal copy in a specific brand voice, unedited
Explaining a domain you're new to, fastBeing correct about that domain at the edges
Boilerplate: alt text, edge-case lists, naming, tokensAnything requiring your design system's actual rules
Playing devil's advocate against your own thinkingHaving an opinion worth deferring to
Code for prototypes and throwaway buildsProduction code without review
The rule that governs this whole moduleAI produces the draft; you produce the judgement. Every time you accept an output without evaluating it against something real — a user, a metric, your design system, a domain expert — you have outsourced the part of the job you are actually paid for. Nielsen Norman Group's own position is worth internalising here: AI is an extraordinarily capable intern, not a designer.

Prompting, for designers specifically

Most "prompt engineering" advice is noise. Five things account for nearly all of the quality difference:

MoveInstead ofDo this
1 · Give it a role and a standard"Write some onboarding copy""You are a product writer for a B2B analytics tool. House style: sentence case, verb-first, under 12 words per line, no exclamation marks."
2 · Provide the actual contextDescribing your productPaste the real thing — your token file, your component spec, your research notes, three real user quotes
3 · Specify the output shape"Give me ideas""Return a markdown table: column 1 the pattern, column 2 when to use it, column 3 the trade-off. Exactly 8 rows."
4 · Ask for range, then narrow"What's the best approach?""Give me 8 distinctly different approaches, including two you'd normally advise against. Then argue against your own top pick."
5 · Make it show its reasoningAccepting the answer"For each recommendation, state what evidence it rests on and how confident you are. Mark anything you're inferring rather than citing."

Two more habits worth building: iterate rather than re-prompt ("that's too corporate — make version 3 harsher and cut it by half" beats starting again), and keep a prompt library. The prompts you refine over a project are reusable assets, and they compound faster than any individual output.

The failure modes, named

FailureLooks likeGuard
HallucinationConfident, plausible, false. Fake statistics, invented citations, non-existent WCAG criteria.Never accept a number or a source without checking it yourself. Ask for the source and then open it.
Regression to the meanEvery output looks like every other product. Generic layouts, generic copy.Use it for range and structure; supply the taste yourself. Generic in, generic out.
SycophancyIt agrees with your bad idea enthusiasticallyAsk it to argue the opposite case before you ask what it thinks
Context blindnessAdvice that ignores your constraints, your users, your systemGive it the constraints explicitly — every time, in every new conversation
Stale knowledgeOutdated platform guidance, deprecated APIs, old pricingVerify anything time-sensitive against primary docs
Averaged biasPersonas and imagery that flatten toward a dominant defaultName the diversity you need explicitly, and check the output for who's missing

Tooling: what to actually have open

JobTools
General reasoning, writing, analysisClaude, ChatGPT, Gemini — pick one as your primary and learn it deeply rather than sampling all three
Inside FigmaFigma AI — rename layers, content-aware fill, auto-layout suggestions, First Draft, Figma Make
Research synthesisDovetail, Marvin, Notably, Condens, Looppanel
Image & asset generationMidjourney, Firefly, Ideogram (for text in images), the image tools inside your primary assistant
Prototype & codev0, Lovable, Figma Make, Cursor, Claude Code

Task · ~45 minBuild your first two prompt assets Write two reusable prompts and save them somewhere permanent. (1) A critique prompt: role, your product's constraints, your design principles, and an instruction to critique a screen against them and rank issues by severity. (2) A range prompt: role, context, and "give me 8 distinctly different approaches including two you'd advise against, then argue against your own favourite."
Run both against a screen you designed in Week 6. Note which one produced something you'd act on — and which produced confident nonsense. Both results are the lesson.
AI · Design Process 2

AI for research & discovery

Research is where AI gives the largest genuine speed-up and carries the largest risk of quietly corrupting your work. The techniques below are ordered by how safe they are.

The safety ladder

UseRiskVerdict
Transcribing and tagging interviewsLowDo it. Pure time saving, easily checked.
Clustering findings you already collectedLow–mediumDo it, then verify every cluster against the raw quotes
Drafting discussion guides and screenersLowDo it, then edit hard — AI writes leading questions by default
Desk research and competitive teardownsMediumDo it, verify every claim against the primary source
Summarising support tickets, reviews, NPS at volumeMediumDo it — this is a genuine superpower — but read a random sample of raw items yourself
Generating personas from real dataMedium–highOnly as a first draft. Personas are a decision, not an output.
Generating personas from nothingHighDon't. This is fiction wearing a research costume.
Synthetic users / simulated interviewsVery highUseful for rehearsing your questions. Never as evidence. It tells you what a model predicts an average person would say — which is the exact opposite of research.
The synthetic-user trapIt is now trivially easy to "interview" twelve fictional users and produce a beautiful insights deck by lunchtime. It will be internally consistent, plausible, and evidence-free — and stakeholders often cannot tell the difference. If you take one thing from this module: never present model output as user evidence. Label it. The credibility you lose when someone finds out is not recoverable.

Desk research, done properly

StepPrompt shape
1 · Map the space"List the 10 main players in [domain], with one line each on their positioning. Mark which you're confident about and which you're inferring."
2 · Find the vocabulary"What terms do practitioners in [domain] use that an outsider would get wrong? Give me 15, with the common mistake beside each."
3 · Surface the constraints"What regulatory, technical or workflow constraints shape products in [domain]? Which are hard constraints and which are conventions?"
4 · Generate the question list"Based on the above, what are the 12 things I most need to ask a real practitioner? Rank by how much the answer would change a design decision."
5 · VerifyTake every factual claim and check it against a primary source. Delete what you can't confirm.

Step 4 is the point. AI is at its best turning "I know nothing about logistics software" into a good question list for a real expert in twenty minutes. It is at its worst replacing that expert.

Interview work

StageHow AI helpsGuard
Discussion guideDrafts structure and probesIt writes leading and double-barrelled questions. Rewrite every one; ask it to flag its own leading questions and it will find several.
RehearsalRole-play a difficult participant so you practise your follow-upsThis is legitimate and genuinely useful — it is practice, not data
TranscriptionFast, cheap, mostly accurateCheck names, jargon and numbers
Tagging & codingFirst-pass codes across many sessionsRead the raw transcripts of at least two sessions yourself before you trust any cluster
Quote retrieval"Find every moment someone struggled with export"Excellent. Verify each quote is real and in context.

The research tool landscape

ToolStrength
DovetailThe established repository; AI-assisted coding of structured studies. Strong when research is a formal, ongoing practice.
MarvinAI analysis plus research ops — scheduling, participants, recruitment. Better value for small teams.
NotablyAI-first and lightweight. Fastest path from transcripts to themes.
CondensStructured synthesis; strong for teams that want rigour over speed
LooppanelCall recording and analysis; good for interview-heavy work
Your general assistantHonestly, for a solo designer with 8 transcripts, pasting them into Claude or ChatGPT with a good synthesis prompt gets you 80% of the way for free

Task · ~2 hrsThe verification exercise Pick a domain you know nothing about. Run steps 1–4 of the desk-research sequence. Then take every factual claim in the output and try to verify it against a primary source. Log what held up, what was unverifiable, and what was simply wrong.
Most people find 10–25% of confident claims don't survive checking. That number is the single most useful thing you will learn in this module, because it calibrates how much you should trust the next output.
AI · Design Process 3

AI for ideation, IA & content

This is where AI earns its keep with the least risk: nothing here is presented as truth, and everything gets filtered by you.

Ideation: use it for range, not for answers

TechniquePrompt shape
Forced range"8 distinctly different approaches to [problem]. Two must be ones you'd normally advise against. No two may share a core mechanic."
Constraint injection"Now solve it with no modals." / "Now assume the user is on a phone, one-handed, in a hurry." / "Now assume they do this 200 times a day."
Analogy transfer"How would a code editor solve this? A kitchen? An air-traffic control system?"
Inversion"Design the worst possible version of this screen." Then invert each failure — it surfaces assumptions faster than brainstorming.
Steelman the rejected option"Make the strongest possible case for the approach I dismissed."
Pre-mortem"It's six months later and this feature failed. Give me the 10 most likely reasons, ranked."
Why "8 approaches" beats "the best approach"Asking for a recommendation gets you the statistical average of everything ever written about the problem — which is exactly the generic result people complain about. Asking for range uses the model for what it's actually good at (breadth) and leaves the selection to the person with context. Almost every disappointing AI design output is a range question asked as a recommendation question.

Information architecture

JobHowGuard
First-pass sitemapGive it the feature list; ask for 3 different groupings with the logic behind eachIt groups by topic; users group by task. Check against real user language.
Navigation labels"12 alternatives for this label, ranked by how likely a non-expert is to understand it"Test the top 3 with real people — a five-minute first-click test settles it
Card-sort analysisCluster open card-sort results and name the groupsVerify against the raw sorts
Flow mapping"Map every path from [entry] to [goal], including error and abandonment branches"Excellent for finding the branches you forgot — this is one of the highest-value uses in the whole module
Edge-case enumeration"List every state this screen can be in, including failure, permission, empty and stale states"You will get 15 and 3 will be ones you'd have shipped without

UX writing — the highest-leverage use of AI in design

SurfaceAsk for
Buttons & CTAs10 options under 3 words, verb-first, ranked by clarity not cleverness
Error messagesThe what-happened / why / what-next formula, in your voice, without blame
Empty statesThree versions — first run, cleared out, no results — each with a different job
OnboardingCopy for each step, plus a critique of whether the step earns its place
Tooltips & helper textOne sentence each; ask it to flag any that are explaining a bad interface rather than a complex one
Microcopy consistencyPaste every string in the product; ask for inconsistencies in tense, person, capitalisation and terminology

That last row is the underrated one. Pasting an entire product's strings in and asking "what's inconsistent here?" finds things no human review catches — and it takes four minutes.

Give it your voice, or it will give you its ownAI's default register is upbeat, slightly corporate, faintly American, and allergic to full stops in headlines. If you don't supply a voice document — three rules and five before/after examples — every product you touch will slowly converge on that register. The voice doc is a ten-minute artefact that pays for itself immediately.

Task · ~90 minVoice doc, then a full copy pass Write a one-page voice document for your Week 7 product: three rules, five before/after examples, and a banned-words list. Then paste every string from your product plus the voice doc, and ask for (1) inconsistencies, (2) a rewrite of the ten worst strings, (3) a flag on any copy that's compensating for a confusing interface.
Fix the interface problems it finds. Those are worth more than the copy.
AI · Design Process 4

AI for visual design & assets

The most hyped area, and the one with the widest gap between demo and daily reality. Knowing exactly which features hold up is the whole lesson.

Figma AI: what holds up daily vs. what's a starting point

FeatureVerdict
Rename layersUse daily. Cleans a messy file in seconds. Pure time back.
Content-aware fillUse daily. Realistic placeholder content instead of Lorem and grey boxes.
Auto-layout suggestionsUse daily. Especially on imported or inherited files.
Visual search / find similarUseful in large files — finds the component you know exists somewhere
First DraftGood start, weak finish. Generates a working layout from a prompt. It does not know your design system, so spacing, type scale and components come back as Figma defaults.
Figma MakePrompt-to-working-prototype with code. Genuinely useful for throwaway prototypes and first-pass UI with no system behind them.
The restructuring taxThe honest failure mode of AI layout generators: the output looks 80% right and is built on none of your foundations. Rebuilding it onto your tokens and components can cost more time than the generation saved. Use generators where no system exists yet — early exploration, a pitch, a throwaway prototype. Once you have a design system, hand-assembling from your own components is usually faster and correct.

Where AI genuinely helps visual work

JobHow
Realistic contentGenerate 40 plausible rows — real names, real ranges, edge cases like a very long name, a null, a zero. Designing on real-shaped data catches layout failures Lorem hides.
Exploration breadthSix directions for a hero in an hour, to react to. You pick; it produces.
Imagery & textureBackgrounds, abstract art direction, mood boards, illustration style exploration
Photo workExtend, clean up, remove objects, match grade across a mismatched set — this alone lifts stock imagery to "curated"
Icon draftsFirst-pass concepts to redraw properly. Never ship raw — generated icons won't share optical weight.
Alt text at volumeDraft alt text for 200 images, then edit. Accessibility work that used to get skipped for time.
Design-system choresNaming tokens, writing component descriptions, drafting documentation, generating the states checklist
CritiquePaste a screenshot plus your design principles and ask for a ranked critique. Genuinely useful as a second pair of eyes at 2am.

Image generation, practically

ToolBest at
MidjourneyAesthetic quality and art direction. Best for mood, texture and stylised imagery.
Adobe FireflyCommercially-safer training data, and it lives inside Photoshop where the editing happens
IdeogramText inside images — still the thing most generators fail at
Your primary assistantQuick iterations in the same thread as the reasoning. Convenience beats quality for exploration.

Prompt structure that works for design imagery: subject → composition → lighting → colour → medium → mood → technical. "A ceramic vessel, centred, three-quarter view, soft north-facing window light, warm neutral palette, editorial product photography, calm and expensive, shallow depth of field, 4:5." Vague prompts produce the generic AI look everyone can now spot instantly.

The consistency problem is the real limitationGenerating one beautiful image is easy. Generating twelve that look like the same shoot is hard — and twelve is what a real site needs. Practical answers: generate one hero and use photo editing for the rest; impose a single grade and grain over everything; or use AI for backgrounds and texture only and commission the imagery that carries meaning.

Rights and disclosure — know this before a client asks

QuestionWhere it stands
Can I use AI images commercially?Tool-dependent. Check the specific terms; Firefly markets commercial safety explicitly. Enterprise clients increasingly ask in writing.
Who owns the output?Varies by tool and jurisdiction, and purely AI-generated work may not be copyrightable in some places. Assume you cannot protect it.
Can I paste client work into a model?Check first. NDAs and enterprise policies routinely prohibit it. Use enterprise tiers with training opt-out where available.
Should I disclose?Yes, if asked, and proactively for imagery of people. Being caught not disclosing costs far more than disclosing.
Portfolio?Say what you used and what you did. "AI-assisted, I directed and rebuilt" is a strong answer. Silence, then discovery, is not.

Task · ~2 hrsThe head-to-head Take one screen from your Week 7 project. Build it twice: once with First Draft or Figma Make from a detailed prompt, once by hand from your own component library. Time both, including the time to bring the generated version onto your tokens and components.
Then write which you'd use, and in what situation. Most designers find the generator wins decisively before a system exists and loses decisively after — and knowing exactly where your own crossover point sits is what makes you fast.
AI · Design Process 5

AI for prototyping & design-to-code

The area that has changed fastest. A designer can now produce a working, deployed, interactive product from a prompt — which changes what a prototype is.

In plain wordsThese tools take a description (or a Figma file) and give you back a real running app, not a clickable picture. That means you can test with something that actually works — real data, real states, real errors. The catch: the code is a prototype's code. It gets you to a validated idea, not to production.

The tools, and what each is for

ToolProducesReach for it whenNotes
v0 (Vercel)React components styled with shadcn/uiYour team already lives in that ecosystem; you want polished front-end fastToken-based pricing since Feb 2026; Team around $30/user/month. Figma import is on paid plans.
LovableFull-stack apps — front end and back endYou need auth, a database, real data flowingPro around $25/month with credit limits; Figma imports consume credits scaling with design complexity. v2 cut errors sharply.
Figma MakePrototype + code, inside FigmaVisual exploration without leaving your working fileBest when the design doesn't need to survive
Cursor / Claude CodeEdits to a real codebaseYou're working with engineers on the actual productThe most powerful option, and the one that requires the most comfort with code
Google StitchUI from promptsFast explorationNewer entrant; worth a comparison run

A structural change worth knowing: Figma's MCP server arrived in beta in early 2026, with bidirectional Claude Code integration following shortly after. That means an AI coding tool can read your actual Figma file — components, variables, structure — rather than guessing from an image. It is the difference between "make something that looks like this screenshot" and "build this using these components and these tokens", and it is why design-system rigour is becoming more valuable, not less.

Where AI prototyping genuinely wins

SituationWhy
Testing with real interactionA working prototype with real data surfaces problems a Figma prototype hides — typing, validation, loading, empty results
Settling an argumentBuild both versions in an afternoon instead of debating for a week
PitchingA working demo persuades in a way frames never do
Learning what your specs feel likeBuilding one thing you designed permanently improves how you spec everything after
Internal toolsSometimes the prototype genuinely is good enough to ship internally
Component explorationGenerate ten variants of a component as real code and interact with all ten

Where it fails, honestly

LimitDetail
It won't match your design systemUnless you feed it the system — via MCP, a token file, or pasted component code
Accessibility is inconsistentGenerated markup often misses focus management, labels and keyboard paths. Audit before testing with anyone.
Production readinessSecurity, performance, error handling, tests. This is prototype code.
Complexity ceilingFine for a few screens; degrades as the app grows and the model loses the thread
Cost is realCredit and token pricing means iteration has a running meter. Budget it like any other tool.
It doesn't know your usersIt generates a defensible average, which is exactly what your research existed to move you away from
Never let a generated prototype become the designThe seductive failure: the prototype looks like it works, so it ships. Then someone discovers there's no keyboard path, no error handling, no empty state, and the spacing is arbitrary. Treat these as throwaway by default. If it's going to ship, it gets rebuilt properly on your system — and you say so out loud at the start, before anyone gets attached.

Working with engineers, now

ChangeWhat it means for you
Your design system became machine-readableTokens and named components now feed the tools directly. Sloppy naming has a new, immediate cost.
Specs are consumed by modelsPrecise, structured specs (the tables in modules d1 and c2) produce better generated code. Vague specs produce vague code.
The prototype is now a shared artefactYou can hand an engineer a working reference instead of a description
Your leverage moved upLess time producing screens, more time on the decisions about the screens. That's the job getting more senior, not disappearing.

AI in the Design Process Quiz

AI · AI Products 1

Designing AI features: chat, assist & agent

Using AI to design is one skill. Designing products that contain AI is a different and now far more valuable one — Gartner projects that around 40% of enterprise applications will embed task-specific agents by the end of 2026, up from under 5% a year earlier. Almost all of them need an interface layer that did not exist before.

In plain wordsWhen AI is inside your product, you are designing something that is sometimes wrong, takes unpredictable amounts of time, and does things the user didn't watch. Classic UI assumes none of those. This module is the set of patterns that handle them.

Three shapes, three different design problems

ShapeWhat it isCore design problem
AssistAI embedded in an existing task — autocomplete, suggested reply, smart default, summarise-thisMaking the suggestion easy to accept, easy to reject, and obviously optional
ChatA conversational surface with a defined scopeCommunicating capability — users cannot see what it can do
AgentAn autonomous system taking multi-step actions across toolsTransparency and control — the user isn't watching every step
The central tension of agent UXThe more autonomous the agent becomes, the less the user understands what is happening. Your entire job is resolving that tension: giving people confidence, control and clarity while still letting the thing do its work. Every pattern below is an instrument for that one trade-off.

Assist patterns — the safest and most under-designed

PatternRules
Inline suggestion (ghost text)Visually distinct from typed content. One key to accept, one to dismiss. Never blocks typing.
Suggested actions / smart replies3–4 max. Always editable before sending — never a one-tap send.
Summarise / explainAlways keep the source visible or one click away. A summary that replaces the source is a trap.
Smart defaultsPre-filled but obviously changeable, and marked as a suggestion rather than a fact
Rewrite / toneShow the original beside the rewrite. Undo must restore exactly.
The entry pointDon't hide AI behind a sparkle icon with no label. Users don't know what it does, so they don't press it.

Chat patterns

ProblemPattern
Capability transparency — users can't see what it can doAn empty state that teaches: 4–6 example prompts covering the real range, plus a plain statement of scope and limits
The blank inputSuggested starting prompts, contextual to what the user was just doing
WaitingStream the response. Show what it's doing if there are steps. Never a bare spinner over 2 seconds.
Confidence displayDistinguish "I know this" from "I'm inferring". Cite sources for factual claims and make them clickable.
RecoveryRegenerate, edit-and-resend, thumbs feedback, and a clear route to a human or to a non-AI path
Long outputsProgressive disclosure — the answer, with depth available. Not a wall of text.
Memory & contextShow what it remembers, and let the user delete it
AccessibilityStreaming text needs live regions; don't announce every token. Keyboard path through the whole conversation.

Agent patterns — the new discipline

RequirementWhat you design
Show the plan firstBefore acting, state the steps. For anything consequential, require approval.
Live progressWhich step, of how many, doing what. Not "thinking…" for 90 seconds.
Explain the choiceWhy this tool, this source, this action — available without being forced on everyone
Intervention pointsPause, redirect, or stop mid-process. Not just cancel-and-lose-everything.
Permission tiersRead freely; ask before writing; always ask before anything irreversible, financial or public
The audit trailWhat did it actually do? Reviewable afterwards, in plain language.
Graceful failurePartial completion is the normal case. Show what succeeded, what didn't, and what state things are in now.
UndoWherever technically possible. Where it isn't, that action needs explicit confirmation naming the consequence.

Read that table beside the five-states matrix from Week 6 and the error taxonomy beside it. Agent UX isn't a new discipline so much as the old disciplines under much harder conditions — more states, longer waits, less certainty, higher stakes.

Task · ~2 hrsThree shapes of the same feature Take one job in your Week 7 product — say "explain this metric" or "find the customers at risk". Design it three ways: as an assist (inline, in the existing UI), as a chat surface, and as an agent that does it autonomously. For each, draw the empty state, the working state, and the failure state.
Then write which you'd ship and why. Nine times in ten the answer is assist, and being able to argue that against a stakeholder who wants a chatbot is a genuinely valuable skill right now.
AI · AI Products 2

Trust, control & designing for being wrong

Conventional software either works or throws an error. AI features are confidently approximate. Designing for that is the whole craft.

The trust equation

IngredientHow you design itFailure
Calibrated expectationSay what it can and can't do, up front, in plain wordsOverpromising in onboarding, then a wrong answer feels like a betrayal
Visible reasoningSources, steps, "based on…" — available, not forcedA black box the user can't audit
ControlEdit, redirect, stop, undo, turn it off entirelyAutonomy the user didn't ask for
ConsistencySame input, similar quality; behaves the way it did last timeErratic quality — the fastest way to lose trust permanently
Graceful wrongnessBeing wrong quietly and correctably rather than confidently and irreversiblyAn error the user only discovers downstream
Trust is asymmetricIt builds slowly across many correct answers and collapses on one confident, consequential error. That asymmetry should drive your design: bias the whole system toward being obviously uncertain rather than occasionally, invisibly wrong. A feature that says "I'm not sure — here are the three sources" survives being wrong. One that states it flatly does not.

Communicating uncertainty without a percentage

MethodUse whenWatch out
Hedged languageAlmost always — "this looks like", "based on…"Hedging everything is as useless as hedging nothing
Source citationAnything factualLinks must be real and must open. Fabricated citations destroy trust instantly.
Multiple optionsWhen there's no single right answerPresenting three options implies you can't tell — which is honest
Visual confidenceHighlighting, opacity, a badge on low-confidence itemsNever colour alone; and users read a number as more precise than it is
Explicit abstention"I don't have enough information"The most under-used and most trust-building output a system can produce
Human handoffHigh-stakes or repeatedly failingMust be genuinely available, not a dead end

Feedback loops

Thumbs up/down is the minimum and it is nearly useless on its own — it tells you something was wrong, not what. Design a ladder: rate → pick a reason → correct it inline → the correction visibly changes future behaviour. The last rung is what makes people bother. Close the loop visibly: "Got it — I'll use your phrasing from now on" is worth more than a hundred silent thumbs.

The cost-of-error matrix — run this before you design anything

If it's wrong, the cost is…Design response
Trivial (a bad suggestion)Full autonomy, easy dismissal, no confirmation
Annoying (wrong tag, bad summary)Easy correction, visible undo
Costly (wrong data sent to a customer)Review before commit, explicit approval step
Irreversible (deleted, published, paid)Never autonomous. Human confirmation naming the specific consequence.
Dangerous (medical, legal, financial advice)Don't ship it as an authority. Provide information, cite sources, route to a professional.

This single table resolves most arguments about how much autonomy a feature should have — and it moves the conversation from opinion to consequence.

The ethics that will land on your desk

IssueYour responsibility as the designer
DisclosureUsers know when they're interacting with AI, and when content was AI-generated
DataClear about what's sent to a model, retained, and used for training — with a real opt-out
BiasTest outputs across demographics. A model trained on averages will produce averaged, exclusionary results.
Dark patternsDon't use AI's fluency to manipulate. A persuasive machine is a new kind of dark pattern.
DependencyDesign so skills aren't atrophied and the non-AI path still exists
AccessibilityAI features must meet the same bar. Streaming text, dynamic content and voice interfaces all have specific requirements.
Environmental costInference isn't free. "Should this be AI at all?" is a legitimate design question.
The question to ask first, every time"Does this need to be AI?" A great deal of what ships as an AI feature would be better as a good filter, a sensible default, or a well-designed form. AI is expensive, non-deterministic and hard to debug. Reach for it when the problem is genuinely fuzzy, open-ended or high-volume — not because it's on the roadmap.

Task · ~90 minDesign the wrong answer Take the AI feature you designed in the last lesson. Now design its four failure states: (1) confidently wrong, (2) partially right, (3) unable to answer, (4) the user disagrees and corrects it. Write the exact copy for each, and design the correction loop — including how the user sees that their correction landed.
Then run the cost-of-error matrix on the feature and write one sentence justifying the level of autonomy you gave it.
AI · AI Products 3

How working designers actually use AI

Cutting through both the hype and the backlash: here is what the workflow looks like in practice for designers who are getting real leverage.

The realistic day

MomentWhat AI is doingTime saved
Starting a new domainBriefing you, building a question list for a real expertHours — and a better first conversation
After 8 interviewsTranscribing, tagging, first-pass clusteringRoughly a day, per study
Stuck on a flowEnumerating branches, states and edge cases you forgotMinutes, and it catches real gaps
Filling a table with contentGenerating realistic data with awkward edge casesHalf an hour, and better designs
Writing every stringDrafting, then checking consistency across the whole productHours — the single biggest daily saving
File hygieneRenaming layers, fixing auto-layout, drafting component docsConstant small returns
Before a reviewCritiquing your own work against your principles; generating the questions you'll be askedBetter reviews, fewer surprises
HandoffDrafting specs, alt text, edge-case lists, changelog entriesHours
Deciding anythingNothing. That's still you.—
Notice the shape of that listAlmost every real saving is in volume work around the design, not in the design itself. Research admin, content, documentation, edge-case enumeration, file hygiene. The design decisions — what to build, for whom, at what cost — are untouched. That is the actual state of the craft in 2026, and it is why designers who use AI well end up doing more design, not less.

Four working styles you'll encounter

StyleHow they workWhere it breaks
The acceleratorAI for every draft, every volume task; keeps all judgementNowhere, mostly. This is the productive default.
The explorerGenerates enormous range early, then designs properly from what it surfacedCan mistake breadth for insight if they skip research
The builderPrototypes in v0/Lovable/Cursor; tests working software instead of framesPrototype creep — the demo becomes the product
The abstainerDeliberately doesn't use it; protects craft and tasteIncreasingly hard to sustain on volume work — but their taste is often the best in the room, which is the real lesson

The useful synthesis: be an accelerator on volume, an explorer at the start, a builder when a question needs settling, and an abstainer on anything that defines the product's voice or point of view.

What is genuinely changing about the job

ShrinkingGrowing
Producing screens from a known specDeciding what to build and why
Manual research adminJudging which insight matters
Drafting documentationSystems thinking — because machine-readable systems now feed the tools
Producing many variations by handTaste — choosing well from infinite options
Pixel execution as a differentiatorDesigning AI features themselves
—Facilitation, argument, saying no

Every row in the right-hand column is a senior skill. That is what the adoption data reflects: the designers reporting higher satisfaction are the ones who handed off the volume and kept the judgement.

Team and portfolio practice

SituationDo
Client or employer confidentialityAsk before pasting anything. Use enterprise tiers with training opt-out. Assume the default is no.
Presenting AI-assisted workSay what you used and what you did. "I used AI for range and content; the system, the decisions and the craft are mine."
Research findingsLabel anything model-generated. Never present it as user evidence.
PortfolioShow the decisions. Reviewers assume tooling; they're hiring judgement. A case study that shows you rejected an AI output and why is stronger than one that hides the tool.
InterviewsExpect "how do you use AI?" Have a specific, honest answer with an example of where it failed you.
Your teamWrite down where AI is and isn't allowed. Ambiguity is where the incidents happen.

Habit
Rebuild one thing you already designed, using AI, every month

Tool news decays in weeks. Judgement about where AI helps your work compounds — and only comes from doing it on work you can already evaluate.

Task · ~45 minWrite your own AI practice statement One page: where you use AI and where you deliberately don't; how you verify output; what you will and won't paste into a model; how you disclose it in work and in your portfolio; and one example of a time it was confidently wrong and how you caught it.
This is a real interview answer, a real team document, and — more usefully — the exercise that forces you to have an actual position rather than a vibe.
AI · AI Products · Practice

Practice: one project, start to finish, with AI

Run a complete project using AI at every stage where it genuinely helps — and document exactly where it didn't. That documentation is the deliverable.

Pick the projectEither a new small product, or — better — redo your Week 6–7 project. Redoing something you already designed by hand is the only way to honestly measure what AI changed, because you have a baseline to compare against.
Checkpoint 1 · ~2 hrsDiscovery Use AI to brief yourself on the domain, map competitors, and produce a ranked question list for a real practitioner. Then talk to one real person — 30 minutes is enough.
Log: every factual claim AI made, whether it survived verification, and what the real person said that no model would have.
Checkpoint 2 · ~2 hrsSynthesis Feed in your interview notes plus any real reviews or support tickets you can find. Get clustered themes. Then read the raw material yourself and mark which themes were real, which were plausible-but-absent, and which the model missed entirely.
Log: the precision and recall of the machine synthesis, in your own words.
Checkpoint 3 · ~2 hrsIdeation & IA Use the forced-range, constraint-injection and pre-mortem prompts. Get 8 approaches; pick one and write why. Map every flow branch and enumerate every screen state.
Log: which branches and states AI surfaced that you had missed.
Checkpoint 4 · ~3 hrsDesign Write your voice doc. Generate all copy against it. Generate realistic content with edge cases. Build the screens on your own design system — use First Draft only where nothing exists yet. Run an AI critique against your design principles before you show anyone.
Log: time spent, and how much of the generated layout survived contact with your tokens.
Checkpoint 5 · ~3 hrsPrototype & test Build a working prototype in v0, Lovable or Figma Make. Audit it: keyboard, focus, contrast, 390 px, empty submit. Fix what you can. Then put it in front of two real people.
Log: what the working prototype revealed that a Figma prototype would have hidden.
Checkpoint 6 · ~2 hrsAdd one AI feature — properly Design one AI feature into the product. Run the cost-of-error matrix. Choose assist, chat or agent and justify it. Design the empty state that teaches capability, the working state, the four failure states, and the correction loop.
Log: the autonomy level you chose and the consequence that justified it.
Checkpoint 7 · ~90 minWrite the honest report One page, with numbers where you have them:
SectionContents
Where AI clearly wonStage, task, time saved, quality effect
Where it was neutralLooked useful, wasn't
Where it actively hurtWrong output you nearly used; generic direction you had to undo
Verification costHow long checking took — subtract it from the time saved and report the net
What only a human didBe specific. This is the most valuable paragraph you will write this year.
What you'd do differentlyYour own practice statement, revised

Self-review

CheckPass condition
Real evidenceAt least one real human was spoken to; no synthetic users presented as research
VerificationEvery factual claim checked against a primary source; failures logged
VoiceA voice doc exists and the copy follows it — nothing in default assistant register
System integrityFinal screens sit on your tokens and components, not generator defaults
Prototype auditKeyboard, focus, contrast and responsive all checked before testing with people
AI featureCost-of-error matrix run; all four failure states designed; correction loop closes visibly
DisclosureThe case study states what was AI-assisted and what wasn't
HonestyThe report includes at least one thing AI got confidently wrong
Why this is the strongest case study in the courseEvery designer now claims to use AI. Almost none can show a measured, honest account of where it helped, where it cost them, and what only judgement could do. That report is evidence of exactly the thing hiring managers are trying to assess and cannot — and it will be the piece they remember.
